NOTES BY " MUST."

The week-end matches have done the Warrington Football Club good service. Huddersfield's visit on Saturday demonstrated what a long way from the first- class our senior team is, and the Wakefield match on Monday made equally clear the paucity of the reserves. Nothing is more obvious than that the Club has a lot of hard.w.rk in store to raise the standard of the game locally,to the heights it reached a few years back.

No one expects the team-building to be completed in a season. It is 1;1,t very long since even Rudders- field were a secood-rate side. Did they not come to Warrington once and receive a beating of 50 points to nil, Jack Fish scoring 30 of the points? But the progress of the Wirepullers needs to be consistent to give encouragement. Just now it looks as if there was a slackening of effort on the part of the men at the helm—though appearances are often deceptive. The only captures of the season alymt which any song needs be made are flose of Rushton, Nicholas, R Thomas and Cox. These men have all proved their usefulness, but the two half backs are a long way from being class enough for Warrington. This posi- tion is still the weakest in the t earn, and the most vital. We also require anothir forward or two of the right stamp, and a couple of w;ng threequarters who can run. How slow our backs really are was demonstrated beyond question by the men f rcm Huddersfield. So far, we have not really got beyond the foundations in team-building. Substantial pro- gress is expected before the Cup-tie registrations are to hand. Time is getting short.

Saturday's match was one of the best! That Warrington were beaten by 21 points to 6 does not alter the fact in the least. They were no match for Huddersfield, 'tis true, but they played a plucky and sportsmanlike game from start to finish and had more of the play than the score would suggest. In cne position they were fully the equds of their famous visitors, viz., forward. The hc me six did magnificent work, and it was only in the back divisions that there was such a marked disparity between the teams. The work of the Huddersfield backs was a thing of beauty. They showed how regularly tries follow perfect corn- bination,and displayed to the full the possibilities of the professional Rugby game. When one remembers that the Fartown men twice proved their superiority over the Australasians, it may be assumed that they are to-day tbe firreit team in the world. I would give something to see them opposed to the South Africans, who are making such a " show " of the Rugby Union teams. The " Boks " would have their eyes opened !

The men who most'took the eye on Sathrday, were Wagstaffe and Mcorhouse, the home-grosn products of Huddersfield schoolboy football. The cleverness of these two Yorkshire lads aroused some comforting reflections; all the stars do not scintillats round the Southern Cross. Clark, tLe Cumberland forward, was an absentee, and one also missed the robust play of Wrigley at centre. The new Australian, Gleeson, made a good impression though I should question the claim that he is the fastest man in the Northern linicn. He can travel, certainly, but there would have been more scoring with Wrigley in his usual place.

The most striking object lesson Warrington got was in half-back play. Grey and Davies proved that it is possible to make openings without running round the scrimmage, and at the same time avoid being tackled. These two are probably the brainiest pair playing, and yet their game is one of method mote than men. They aim at keeping the ball on the move, and abandon the sensational break-away which is the be-all-and end-all of some half-back's aspirations. The game is an easy game for themselves—with a modicum of risk and a maximum of effectiveness. Note how far back Davies stood the same applies to Johnny Thomas— and you will realize that half-backs of the Warrington type (the average type) make a mistake in lying close to the scrum and trying to break through before part- ing with the ball. Of course, the pace of the handling and the pace of the players had a lot t') do with the success of the methods employed, but those methods are not at all difficult of imitation by half-backs with ideas. At Wilderspool if nowhere else the scheme of attack needs remodelling.

One might have expected that Saturday's object lesson would have had some reflex on Warrington's play in the match on Monday, but instead they gave the worst exhibition of the season. The team was disorganised by the absence of Brookes,Dickenson,and Mclntyre, the two latter only expressing their inability to play on the morning of the match. The Committee were thus in a quandary, and had to resort to the expedient of playing Clare, Jordan, and Povey. Wakefield were no better represented, for both the regular halves and wings were unavailable, but they proved good enough to beat Warrington by 11 points to 3.

It was a humiliating exhibition the Wirepullers gave. The forwards were again in excellent form, but the backs might as well have been novices for all idea of combination they displayed. Nicholas and Rushton were equally had at half back, while in the three- quarters Tranter stood alone. Now and then Jolley gave him some support, but in the main it was single- banded work. He was responsible for the few thrills the Warrington men raised. Clare was, as usual, too cumbersome, and it is a grave reflection on the Club's reserve strength that he should be first choice among the juniors. Woodburn and Waywell would have been acquisitions on Monday, but were are they ? Until we have better men we might as well keep these two in training.

Wakefield succeeded because they possessed men who could play an average game with few mistakes. The centres, Poynton and Lynch, were too much for the weak Warrington defence, and their efforts carried the side to victory. Kershaw, the international forward, deputised at half-back and was a good deal more use than the Warrington pair, both of whom seem to be going back instead of improving

This looks like being a woeful week for the Wire- pullers. They have already lost two matches, and can hardly hope to succeed at Broughton to-day. Changes in the team had been made, but though they are justified they are hardly likely to effect the result. Young Brown and Daintith are selected for the half back positions and merit the honour. Nicholas goes back to the "A " team and Rushtcn is to have a rest. Unfortunately Renwick is not considered quite sound yet. He is badly missed. Brookes' knee injury may keep him out for a month.
The team will he: Jolley, full back; Mclntyre Tranter, Dickenson and Clare, three-quarters ; Brown and Daintith, half backs; G Thomas, R Thomas, Cox, Skelhorne, Fearnley and Cheaters, forwards.

The "A " team will turn out at home-against the Rangers "A " with the following thirteen: Broan, full back; Davies, Jordan, Hudson and Manchester, three-quarters; Nicholas and Douglas, half backs; Critchley, Harmer, Naylor, Gibbs, Bevan and Arnold, forwards.

div.head: IMPS AT A WHIST DRIVE.
div.p: IMPS AT A WHIST DRIVE.
TO-DAY'S MATCHES.
The list of fixtures for to-day, together with the results of the correspeuding games last season, is as follows :

Dewsbury l6 Leeds 5 Hunslet l9 Huddersfield Bramley Halifax 5 Oldham 3 Hull Kinaston Rovers... 17 Keighley Leigh 26 Batley Rochdale Hornets 2l Barrow Wakefield Trinity l4 Wigan Bradford York l5 Hull Broughton Rangers Salford l3 St Helens l5 Runcorn

which was loudly cheered. Half-time : Huddersfield 4 tries (12 points) ; Warrington, nil. The resumption of play soon found Warrington further in arrears. Grey, Davies and Wagstaffe worked the hall across to Moorhouse who beat Mclntyre at bait way and then punted past Jolley. In the race for the ball Moorhonse was an easy winner and scored in good position, but Grey had no more success than the others with his kick at goal. Another fine display of handling left Rosenfeld with another chance to dis- play his speed and he made no mistake, leaving Brookes and Jolley far in the rear. in the negr dation of this point. Again was the kick at goal a failure. Warring- ton now forced the pace in splendid fashion and praise- worthy efforts were made by the forwards. A desperate raid on the Yorkshire goal menaced Holland's charge considerably, and the custodian failed to stop one rush. The sphere was taken over, but the point was over-ruled by Mr Renton, notwithstanding the strong claims of the locals. The " Wirepullers " were not disheartened, and after Rushton had cross- kicked, the bail travelled to Brooks, who dashed over at the left-hand corner, with two Huddersfield men clinging tenaciously to him. This success seemed to inspire the Warringtonians to further exertions, and after Huddersfield had momentarily invaded the home quarters Mclntyre started a dribble, which again puzzled Wagstaffe and Holland. Skelhorne and Cox joined issue and Skelhorne had the satis- faction of scoring Warrington's second try. Like Huddersfield, Warrington had left their goal-kicking shoes at home. Thomas faring no better than Long. stall or Holland. For a time play was of an even nature, ' but near the close the superiority of the Huddersfield backs was again manifested and Oleesou was able to record the seventh try for the champions, there being no goal from the resultant kick. Result : Hudders- field, seven tries (21 points) ; Warrington, two tries (six points). A SHOCK AT WIDNES.

Hull Kingston Rovers were the visitors to Widnes on Saturday and played before 2,000 spectators. Early in the game Widnes got a lead through Daintith kicking a penalty goal. For some time neither side could claim any advantage and then some loose play on the part of the Widnes backs enabled Hicks to dribble over and score. Carmichael improved from a difficult position. Just before the interval Dean made a fine opening and Hicks added another try, and Carmichael f oaled. In the second half Widnes fell away greatly, and the Rovers did practically what they liked. Hicks added two more tries, and Dilcock, Stamm) and Mann also got over, Carmichael placing four goals. Lally and Reid scored tries for Widnes, and Jones placed a goal. Result :—Hull Kingston Rovers, 6 goals 7 tries (33 point) ; Widnes, 2 goals 2 tries (10 points). RUNCORN EASY VICTIMS.

There was only a moderate attendance at Chorley- road, Swinton, when these teams met. In defeating the men from Chekhire the home side did not unduly extend themselves. Playing with the elope in their favour the home side quickly ran up a score, leading at the interval hy 20 points to nothing, Bailey (2), Fair- hurst and Gartrell scoring. The concluding half saw the" Linnets " have more of the game, but several grand opportunities were thrown away owing to lack of finish. Moran, however, crossed with a splendid try, but this proved to he their only score. Moores and Parker each crossed the line on I ehalf of Swinton. Result :—Swinton 5 goals 6 tries (28 points), Runcorn 1 try (3 points). ST. HELENS BEAT THE CUP-HOLDERS.

This ruturn League fixture with Dewsbury attracted a crowd of 5,000 spectators to the St Helens ground. Belshaw marked in front of the Dewsbury posts, and ' Turtill opened the home score with a neat goal. Play was fought out at a fast rate, and from passing between Ware and Rhodes Flanagan intercepted and scored a somewhat easy try. Barton failed to improve. On the resumption, O'Neill, Price, Milner, Ware and Evans handled, the latter scoring, but Bradford failed to goal Immediately afterwards Rhodes and Milner passed and repassed. the latter scoring, Ware failing. Off-side against Dewsbury enabled Barton to kick a goal, the same player a few minutes later slipping Sharpies and scoring an unimproved try. Dewsbury again Opened out with beautiful back play and Sharpies scored, Ware failing. With a one point lead St Helens pot life into their movements, and in the last four minutes of the game first Manchester and then Belshaw crossed with good tries, Barton and Greenwood failing to augment. Results :—bt Helens 2 gals 4 tries (16 points), Dewsbury 3 tries (9 points).

div.head: Hu-ddersfleld Outclass Warrington.
div.p: Hu-ddersfleld Outclass Warrington.

Fortunately for Warrington, Saturday was a fine day, and a crowd of about 7,000 gr.thered at Wilderspool for the match with.fludderstleld, the League champions, the receipts being £147. There is probably no finer com- bination of footballers playing anywhere than the men wearing the Huddersfield jersey, and their brilliant expositions of the professional Rugby game have made them warm favourites wherever they go. Warrington were not considered to have any chance of stopping the successful career of the Fe.rtown men, but they had a good team in the field, Renwick being the only absentee. On the visiting side two prominent players were missing, Wrigley and Clark, but the substitutes were good enough to keep up the high standard of play. The teams were : Warrington—Jolley, back ; Brooks, Dickenson, Tranter and Mclntyre, threequarter-backs ; Nicholas and Rushton, half-backs ; Cheaters, G Thomas, Skelhorne, Fearnley. It Thomas and Cox, forwards. Huddersfield—Holland, back ; Rosenfeld, Gleeson, Wagstaff and Moorhouse, threequarter-baoks ; Davies and Grey, half-backs ; Chilcott, Cirenow, Higson, Long- staff, Swinden and Unsworth, forwards. Referee, Mr F Renton (Hunslet). Touch-judges, Messrs It Jones (Widnes) and E J Hannaford (St. , Helens). Warrington opened the play in the direction of the railway goal and the forwards were early prominent. The first movement of the visiting backs, however, gave a foretaste of what was in store. Play was carried to the home quarter, and here Grey, Davies and Wagstaffe handled brilliantly in the direction of the left wing. The Warrington men covered Moorhouse, but could not stop the progress of the ball. Back to Wagstaffe it went, and he throwing to Gleeson on the right, the latter made an easy opening for Davies to scOre, the defence being completely beaten by the cleverness of the movement. Longstaff failed at goal, but his side kept on the offensive. The ball was soon in the hands of the halves at midfield. Davies and Wagstaffe out- witted the home centres, and Moorhouse raced over at Ole corner with a hrilliant try. Again the goal was .missed, and Warrington showed both pluck and skill in a run to the other end. Rushton and Nicholas got the ball away cleverly, and fed Brooks. The latter raced down the touch-line and beat Holland finely, but was overhauled a yard from the line by Wagstaffe. Here Warrington scrumruaged grandly, and Rushton nipped round the pack with an opening for Brooks which the latter missed through dropping the pass on the line—a great disappointment to the crowd- For a short time longer Warrington held the opposi- tion. and Thomas bad a drop at goal, which was only a foot or two short. Dickenson and Tranter broke through on one occasion, but the speedy Fartown backs soon overhauled them. Play was in the visitors quarter when Davies cleverly broke away and fed Wagstaff's. The latter made a great run before handing to Gleeson, whose speed did the rest, and a third try was recorded. Keeping up the attack. the Huddersfield backs again handled with lightening rapidity, and Rosenfeld dashed over unopposed at the corner. Both goal kicks were wide of the mark. Again did the visitors get on the move, and Rosenfeld appeared a certain scorer, when Jolley came across with a rush and forced the Colonial over the corner flag, a tackle •

div.head: MONDAY'S MATCH.
div.p: MONDAY'S MATCH.

Warrington Fall Badly Against Wakefield. On Monday the postponed match with Wakefield Trinity was played at Warrington before a poor attend- ance. Neither side was at full strength, the whole of the home three-quarters 'crying off " with the excep- tion of franter. Thesubstitutes testified to the paucity of the club's reserve strength. Wakefield were similarly handicapped at half back and wing,and the tesms turned out as follows : Warrington : Jordan, full back ; Clare, Jolley, Tranter and Povey, three-quarters ; Rushton and Nicholas, half backs ; G Thomas, R Thomas, Cox, Fearnley, Skelhorine and Cheaters, forwards. Wakefield Trinity : Land, full back; Goodison, r Lynch, Poynton and Quarmhy, threequarters ; Kershaw and Smales, half backs: Walton, Burton, Johnson, 'Taylor, Beattie, and Crossland, forwards. Warrington kicked off against a fairly strong breeze, and aided by vigorous forward play they attacked strongly. Tranter took a pass from Rushton and brush- ing the visiting centres aside he threw to Povey. who missed the ball when nicely placed for sooring. Wake- field were penalised for off-side play and Thomas took a drop-kick at goal, which was near the mark. Kershaw eventually cleared, and a clever punt by Lynch found touch near the home line. The forwards soon changed the scene again with smart footwork, aided by a strong run from Clare. Play was at centre when Poynton took a good pass from Smales, and, bluffing Povey he cot inside and left the home team standing in a run behind the posts. Taylor goaled with ease. Warrington responded with good passing but Clare could not get beyond the Wakefield quarter. A mull by Jordan lost Warrington the advan- tage of ground and Wakefield strongly attacked near the home line. Kershaw secured, and made the defence look simple when he slipped over on Clare's wing. Eight points in arrears Warriogton made a desperate effort and Tranter again broke through with a single- hitnded effort and he threw to Thomas near the line, but the forward knocked on badly, and the chance was lost. Half-time: Wakefield 8 points, Warrington nil. On turning round, the locals made a flattering start Povey took play into the Wakefield quarter, and a fine effort by Treater resulted in a score. The centre beat Poynton and passed to Thomas, who bluffed the full back and gave Clare a walk-over near the posts Thomas hit the post with his shot at goal—a bit of hard luck that left Warrington still five points in arrears. Warrington seemed to deteriorate instead of improve. The forwards lost possession and the halves made blunder after blunder. It was not long before Wakefield settled the issue. Lynch and Poynton ran over half the length of the field and the latter seemed a certain scorer, when Skelhorne came up at top speed and downed the tall centre a yard from the line. There was some scrambling play in the home quarter, and the attempts to change the venue were feeble in the extreme. Eventually Tranter had a kick charged by Quarmby, who dashed over at the corner. No goal was kicked. Tranter next intercepted and ran clear away to the Wakefield goal, but was brought back for a knock-on. Final : Wakefield Trinity. 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points) ; Warrington,l try (3 points).

div.head: COMBINATION.
div.p: THE COMBINATION.

WARRINGTON "A " AT HITDDF.RgFIELD.—Warringon "A " team made their first visit to Yorkshire on Saturday and gave an excellent account of themselves against the champions' second string. There was an excellent attendance. Huddersfield were aggressive in the early stages, but directly the Warrington forwards became masters of the pack the game was opened out for Clare to score. Near the interval the visitors added another try through the medium of Critchley, but as was the case in the first ijastance, the goal shot was a failure.

In the second half the pace was hot throughout and whilst Warrington offered a stubborn defence they were unable to hold the" Tykes " out for Crowther went over for a try and a goal followed. Warrington's lead was thus reduced to a single point. Each side struggled hard and when it appeared likely that the honours would be carried off by Warrington, the home team were granted a try for obstruction 25 yards from tbe line. A goal followed, so that Huddersfield "A" won luckily by two goals and two tries (10 points) to Warrington " A " two tties (six points).

FIRST QUALIFYING ROUND. RYLANDS' RECREATION v SUTTONI Rylands men made a successful debut in the Northern Union Cup Competition on Saturday, when they con- quered the Sutton team at Sutton. The visitors had only a moderate back division, being without Floyd. Morris and A Horrocks, their planes being filled by Warren, F Horrocks and G Ogden. From the inception of the game against wind and slope, the visitors showed masterly still and scored two goals and one try. In the second stage the leaders appeared to be content with their advantage and never really forced matters seriously The winning forwards and hacks combined well and tries were scored by Leah, Warren (two) and Slater, Rylands' winning comfortably by 21 points to nil.

div.head: LATCHFORD V. OUGHTRTNGTON PARK.
div.p: LATCHFORD V. OUGHTRTNGTON PARK.

At Thelwall-lane, Latchford, on Saturday. Latchford at once pressed and troubled the visitors' defence. Smith, on the Latchford right, got away and put in a brilliant centre, but Burrows cleared his lines in good stile. Moss cleared and play was rapidly taken to the other end, where Birmingham brought off a flue clear- ance. Webb (Latchford) set his forwards going and Johnson and Taylor, on the left, put in some good work, a good effort being crowned by Johnson scoring a goal from fully 20 yards' range. Latchford were quite entitled to their lead. Half-time :—Latcliford, one ; Oughtrington Park, nil. Upon resumption, with the wind in their favour, the Park attacked and the home defence was hard pressed for ten minutes. A spell of midfield play followed. Smith, on the Latchford right, made a capital effort, Burrows just tipping his shot over the bar--a good shot and a clever save. The visitors now had a turn and from a perfect centre by Lord,W Thomason headed the equalizing goal.T he game was now strenuously con- tested, each side trying desperately to gain the lead. Both goals had narrow escapes. Having the advantage of the breeze, the Park had slightly the best of matters Robinson (Latchford) was penalized for an offence in the dreaded area. Thomason took the kick, but Birmingham saved his shot, but could not clear. The goal, however, was kept intact. A minute or so later the same player was again at fault. This time Thomas made no mistake and put his side ahead. A capitally contested game ended :—Owghtrington Park,two goals; Latchford, one goal. LYMIS V. ST. VINCENTS.

At Lymm. The visitors won the toss and elected to play against the wind and up hill. Even play marked the opening exchanges. Scarle cleared from Owen, whilst Pt the cther end Hinde easily repelled an effort by Mannion. From tho latter clearance Wilson obtained possession and getting away on his own scored a fine goal for the home team. Lymm now were having slightly the best of matters. With a capital long single shot Clare gave Searle no chance with a well-timed effort. At the interval Lymm led by two goals to nil. Going off with a rush Barber quickly added a third point for Lymm. This unexpected reverse thoroughly aroused the " Saints," and J Searle opened their account frcm a pass by Mannion. This was quickly augmented by a second point from the foot of Dudley. In the last few minutes the " Saints " claimed that the ball bad been through, but the ruling official thought otherwise, a good game ending : —Lymm, three goals ; St. Vincent's, two goals. The First Eleven lost to Stockport 4-1. Up to half time the home team did most of the attacking but the forwards are dead out of luck with their shooting just now. Pearson, however, scored a clever goal but Hull equalized for the visitors. Stockport were the best side in the second half and the three inside men, Bennett, Hull and Goodwin, scored goals, combining well throughout the game. For Stockport Hull (centre forward), Adams (centre half), Lowe (back), and the outside right, were the most prominent. For Latchford Knight played one of his best games and had the strongest wing to mark. Billingtoia and Wilkinson also did good defensive work. The forwards were good in midfield but could make little headway in the circle, although many of their passing movemeots were equally as good as those of the visitors but nothing came off. The Etscond Eleven proved that their defeat the previous week on a frosty turf was no criterion of their present form, because last week at Sale Cricket Ground where the couditions were in favour of proper hockey, and not hit and rush, they beat a vastly superior team to that of the previous week by 4-1. Bruhl at third full back had a large share in the victory and played a great. game. Dixon also did some strong hitting, and he and Bruhl cleared out the Sale forwards time after time. The first half was close, there being no score until near the interval, when Marsden shot a fine goal for Latch- ford. This was followed later by a couple from Minards. Than Sale opened their account with a well- deserved goal, but Colton completed a fast run on the left by scoring Latchford's fourth. Minards was good at centre forward, and Marsden and Colton were very successful on the left wing. The halves worked very hard, having a strong forward line to contend with, the hale outside left being particularly clever with hia stick.

CHESHIRE EDUCATION.

div.head: Shortage of Uncertificated Teachers.
div.p: Shortage of Uncertificated Teachers.

The Cheshire County Education Committee at Crewe on Monday, made a concrasion in favour of married women teachers, as the result of a dearth of uncertifl- nested teachers. The number of uncertificated teachers in the county area at the beginning of the year was 763, but the num- ber hal since been reduced,as district committees,finding difficulty in filling vacancies as they arose, had sanctioned the substitution of certificated teachers in a number of cases. The number of vacancies at present iS 95, and, it was said, was growing each month. There are now in Cheshire 105 certificated women being paid Sa uncertificated. It was decided to revise the commencing salaries of uncertified teachers, and in the Cabe of all women uncertified teachers the maximum salary is to be £6O a year. In view of the shortage, relaxations were made in the case of married women. While no appointment of married women teachers shall be made and approved, except with the special sanction of the Education Com- mittee, the restrictions hitherto-existing upon the per- manent employment of married women Ps assistant teachers shall be withdrawn from the end of the pres-nt Month, with these exceptions : (I) No appointment of a married woman as assistant teacher in the same department as that in a hich her husband is also employed as a teacher shall be allowed except with special sanction of the County Education Committee; (2) on the marriage of any woman teacher now on the staff, or henceforward to be appointed on the 'staff of any elementary school, her engagement shall be determined thereby, or at the expiration of one month's notice at the option of the managers, unless the administrative sub-committee gi% es sAaction for her retention on the staff of such school.

Ignorance of the Bill is the least charge that can be brought against the same reverend gentleman when he Fp aks of the 11-me Rule measure as " establishing a prieFtly regime in Ireland" and giving power to "enforce all the doctrines " of the Church of Rome. The true spirit of Non- conformity would make Ulster aspire to the position in Ireland for which her genius fits her, the leader- ship in every beneficent and progressive er terprise. At the bottom of all thes3 appoals to the p-ejudices of Nonconformists there is an absolute denial of the essential spirit of Norconfotmity. Ulster's outcry is that she will be in a minority. div.head: APPEAL TO NONCONFORMISTS.
div.p: THE APPEAL TO NONCONFORMISTS.
HOME RULE AND PERSECUTION
FOR RELIGION.
By Slr George Toulmln, M.P.

[Sir George Tou'in,n, M P., has represented Bury in the Liberal interest since 1902. A native ot Bolton, Sir George was educated at Preston Grammar School, and is now a newspaper pro- prietor,being managing director of the "Lancashire Daily Post " and " Preston Guardian." He has served as Chairman of the Select Committee of the House Of Commons on Publications and Debates. Sir George, who is a justice of the Peace for Lancashire and Preston, was knighted in 1911 Ile is a Fellow of the Institute of Journalists, sod is a well-known and popular figure in the newspaper world. Ile is also a prominent member of Ho

Weeleyan Connexion.] An appeal is made to Not:conformists by Unionists to resist Home Rule, vitalised by the assertion that under Home Rule Protestants would be deprived of their cherished civil and religious rights, liberties and privileges. If the appeal were well fcunded, its effect must be great, for only within a gencraticn have unjust laws ceased to penalise Nonconformity.. in England. "Things most offei sive, dieplaying most narrow-minded ignorance and bigotry, have been uttered against the Roman Catholic religion"- I use the words of Lord Edmund Talbot. But Nonconfor- mists cannot take such accusations on trust, and must ask, "Is persecution for conscience sake of Protest a' ts by an lush Parliament a ith a majoiity elected by Roman Catholics really to be feared ? " In my opini n it is mt. The appeel is at the bott m political, and it is not based upon Irish history, but is an appeal to prejudice, baseless where it is sinceie, sordid and con- temptible where it is a mere calculated d fence of an unjust ascendency. If it were well founded, no acetic n of British electors e ould more resolutely respond than Nonconformists. Their own struggles against laws past:ed by an over whelmiegly Protestant Parliament is too recent for None nformists to hesitate for a mon ent in speaking cut for religious freedom, should their firm belief in tie tolerance end wisdom of an Irish Parliament 1, gisia•ing f r the good of Ireland be deceived. Who are these Noeconformiets to whom Ulster Utionist politicians present themselves as helpless victims of certain oppression ? They are the local preachers who know the countryside and its his my r half a century, the deacons, church officers and class leadeis, Sunday school superintendents and teachers, or Band cf Hole Secretaries, ho have see!, succeeding generations pass from bumble igno at ce to a wider life which has enriched the nati at. It is not the leaders of Nonconf„rmity who in this matter are to be mainly considered. Gnat names can b quoted on both sides of tl e Ulste r controversy. hut the courage ani iedependence of thought of Nomad rmity have their root in the humbler ranks of plain ciizens. Will it be denied th it wl at they have won has been gained while they wet e a minority? Is it surprising that they cannot believe that Ulster even though in a minority, is afraid ? Nonconformists in England have achieved the right to worship God in their own fashion, without penalty. Hew can tl deem the safety of Ulster Protestants less secure thee their own, seeing that beyond the power of their own energy and intelliget cc in the two Irish Houses tie y have the supreme authority of the Imperial Parliament, where they will continue to have a voice ? For what they enjoy of equality and justice the Engl th Non- conformists had to struggle, and in many of their peaceful b ittles for civic rights denied ti kth, Roman Catholics were their allies. But in the main the relied upon themselves. Cannot Uts'er do the same.? Are any of the essentials of free ci izscship in d 'roger to Irish Protestantism because of religion ? At least, in Ulster, Protestants ave the franchi e • they are vocel, aid can speak in the proper ; lace. The generation still lives which saw the vote bestowed i England en the class amongst which " dissenters " are found. It was not until 1885 that the humbler rtion ot the country population we re made free ft om the serfdom of the voteless rnan. tlieter Protestant. have this free citizenship. 'They reed not fear, either, exclusion born public offices by religious testa ; their universities are not cl 'tied to them ; their ministers are not open to the enters of graduites of universities for a lack of culture and learniag, the oppertunity of which was denied. They will not have to bury their dead in silence, denied in a parish graveyard the ' ministrations of their chosen pastors. No cm-Tule ,ry Church rates will vex and penalise them. What is it really that Ulster Unionists ft ar ? Perhaps a racial memory of the wrongs inflicted by Protestants on Roman Catholics haunts them. They may reny.;mber that when a father died his children were handed over to a Protestant guardi in ; that an apostate yt linger son could co demn an elder brotht r to p .verty ; that it could be said, at one time, " the law d es not suppose any such person to exist as an Irish Roman Catholic." But even then it was rapacity, and not religion, that was the motive power actuating a Protestant Parliament. Whatever may be the cause of the Litter feeling in Ireland —racial, economic, agrarian— it is cot religion. Those who have suffered most for religion in Irelan' have been Roman Catholics •, and the bitter at suffer- ings of Irish Protestants have been inflicted by Protestant England. Every prosper us industry in Ireland ea& killed by English laws. Are the scathing words of Froude forgotten i " Pitiable and absui d story, on the face of which was wtitten madness! Industry delib, rarely ruined by the commercial jea'ou y of England ; the country abandoned to anarchy by the scandalous negligence of Eng'ish statesmen ; idle absectee magna'es forgettiog that duty had a meaning, and driving their tenants into rebellion and exile ; resident gentry wasting their substance in extravagance, and feeding their riot by wringing the means of it out of the sweat of the poor ; a Parliament led by patriots whose love of country meant but the art to embarrass Goverement, and wrench frcm it the spoils of office; Gove nment escaping from i;a difficulties by lavishing gold which destroyed the self-resptct and wrecked the character of those who st•.oped ti take it; the working members of the community, and the worthiest part of it, flying f (ma soil where some fatal enchantment condemned to failure every effort made for its redemption—such was the fair condition cf the Protestant cobt,. y planted in better days to show the Irish thp fruits of a noble' belief than their own, and the indutti ill virtues of a nobler race! Who can wonder that .English rule in Ireland has become a byeword ? " No c untiy was ever so misgoverced as Ireland, so oppress-d, so betrayal. And even when the frank selfishness of England died of shame, its goodwill was ever poisoned by some failure of intuition. But causes of ft iction in Ireland have been ameliorated the alien Church, the alien landlord, the alien system of local government The University question is no longer 'mute, Genera'ities will rot avail, and in detail Unionists have signally failscl to trove cat the intt rests of. religion are at stake. Indeed, it is scarcely too much to say that the dread shadow of penal legis- lation, called up by pictures of blood shed for religion, was proved to be without substance by debete on the floor cf the House. In respect of the charges and imputations ageinst the Irish Roman Catholics I must express my opinion that the accused are not guil:y, and the accusers not innocent Where a Protestant maj wity in Leland has its way unless they are belied by figures, Protestatite use their prsition to secure ascendency mere rigorously and intolerantly than his used where Roman Catholic are in a majority. If the reign of terror were a reality it would be seen in the South and West. But, do these people who appeal to Nonconformists in the name of religion really desire the same things that we desite—an extended franchise and the e-quality of man and man, independent of his religious views; an I equitable education system, under which our children will net suffer; the equality of all religions before the law? Is government by consent of the governed only to apply to Protestants? Is the creed of freedom which they preach only a variation of Pharieaism freedom, if we belong to the majority. What is the record if the Unionists who Claim the right to a permanent majori y over their fellow- countrymen? Upholders of ascendency in Ireland, they have upheld Plural Voting in England ; in the name of safety for religious rights they fastened on the village Nonconformi ts of England the Education Act of 19(.12 ; in the cause of freedom they opposed an amendment to that Act securing the right of 1 arente to repiesentation in School Management Committees, an effort to secure justice for religious minorities,

The I ancasbire Insuracce Committee met at Prrston on Monday afternoon, Alderman J T Travis-Clegg presiding. The Sanatoria Sub-Cvmmitiee reported that they had had a list of 61 applications from insured persona for sanitorium benefit, together with it report on each ease by the county medical officer of health. Two of the' applications had since been withdrawn, and 40 of the remnining cases %ere approved fir treatment. In regard to two c sea domiciliary treatment was granted pending removal to a sanatorium. div.head: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE.
div.p: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE.
Non-Commissioned Officers' bless.

A most intererting lecture wns given on Monday laet the 9111, at the above lisadquarters at Rose and Crown- street, by Colour-Sergeont Woodbridge, entitled "The working of a newrpoper." Colour-Sergeant Woonnurnon spoke upon the wonderful organisation which made it poesible for us to read at our breakfast ,ables bappenini..,s which perhaps only occu•red any six tp ors previously. He described a day and a night in a large newepr per officer, of all mentioning the editoriol staff, divided in to three sections r—lst, the editor and his personal assist- ants; 2nd, the news editor (or chief reporter) and his reporting corps; and 3rd, the sub-editor, lie then passed on to the mechanical s:de describing the linotype machine and the Leviathan-(douhle octuple) printing presses, which printed, folded, cut, and counted in d zone, newspapers cf eight pages, at the rate of 220,000 per hour, or 3,666 per minute. He then dwelt upon the Stereotype foundry, with its Photographic Der artmett, and described ard explained the work.ng of the " tape" on which the results of the various races tto , were obtained. He stated, as an instance of the speed e ith which the news was received from all quarters of the globe, that the official news of the death of President McKinley travelled frAn Amsrica to the office of the " Daily Post," in the ' almost incredible rime of 15 minute., and compered this with the time it, took to transmit tie news of the death of King George the Fourth from London to Edinburgh, in ISIO, namely, two and a half days. The lecture was most warmly received, and , attentively listened to, and in propnsing a vote of ' thanks to Colour-Sergeant Woodbrldgr, Sergeant- Bugler Goodwin stated that not only had the lecture been most interacting, but also very instructive, and they all thanked the lecturer for the able manner i r which it, had boeo de livered.

div.head: SUNDAY CONCERTS
div.p: SUNDAY CONCERTS
Legh Council's Divided Views.

At the I eigh Town Council on Tuesday a long and heated discussion took place upon the recommendetion of the Watch Committee to prohibit Sunday concerts in Leigh. There was a very large attendance of the general public. Councillor Gregory moved that the minute be referred back for further consideration. Ile strongly condemned the Leigh Free Church Council, vitro were behind the movement for abolishing Sunday conceits. Councillor Ashworth, president of the Leigh Free Church Council, said the Sabbath ‘8 81 given for rest and WOralip. COMLBCICiaii33I was 8 huge octopus that WIIIB thrusting ugly tentacles on the Christian Sabbath. All the music hall artistes were against working seven eaye a week, and that was what Sunday concerts were tend- ing tosiards. Alderman Fairclough raid there were a great many bandsmen in Leigh and district who only had the opportunity col Sunday of hearing good brass bands. Alderman Boydell, chairman of the Watch Committee agreed to take back the minutes for further discussion without a division.

div.head: WOODROW WILSON.
div.p: WOODROW WILSON.

here stands a Southener, Scots-Irish by descent, a Probbyterian, till lately a Professor and University President, lithe, barely more than blight in figure stern- eyed, with a long, rtrorg, lean face which is wrinkled both by laughter and by Lis fifty-six years. Ho has already taught and written history and political has understood the academic dialect, end has met with men of affairs. Above all, he has been learning quite rapidly of late ; but in his vigorous school of statesmanship he is still both just and obstinate, as undergraduates at Princeton University,"rearly twenty years ago, always knew him to be. Some of Ds will never forget that pottentious wagging of Lis forefinger es be talked of government as well as of liberty ; though we frankly marvelled at the simple diction which made confusion clear, and showed us that character was no mere ques- tion of report, but a matter of fact.—From the "Contemporary Review."

div.head: BIG SEWERAGE SCHEME.
div.p: BIG SEWERAGE SCHEME.
MORE OPPOSITION AT GRAPPENHALL INQUIRY.
Latchford's Plea for Exclusion.
"AN IDEAL GARDEN SUBURB."

The opposition to the Runcorn Rural District Council's £18,500 sewerage scheme for the townships of Grappenhall, Latchfoid Without and Thelwall, found further expression on Tuesday at the adjourned public inquiry conduced in the Large Room, Grappenhall, by Mr. F. o.. Stanford, A.M Inst., C.E. Each of the parishes concerned has offered strong objection to the scheme which, apirt from the annual cost of maintenance, would involve an expenditure as follows : _ _
- - Atse.sable Ap'tionm't Rate in £ Value. of cost. p'r annum. s. d. Grappenball Latchford Without 5,450 ... 4,068 ... 10 Thelma( . . .

At the first hearing the Inspector heard the statement of the case on behalf of the Runcorn Rural District Council, and the opposition of the parishes of Thelwall and Grappenhall and several companies who have works in the urea involved. The!wall pleaded for total exclusion from the scheme and Grappenhall submitted alternative proposals for the separate treat- ment of its own sewage. When the proceedings were resumed, Mr R T Fairclougb, chairman of the Latchford Without Parish Council, said tie opposition of that body was in the first place directed against the expense which they thought was too heavy. Further they contended that no such scheme was rrquired for the jurist). Before the Ship Canal was made, all the sewage us«l to go through Latchford Within, the outfall heing below the weir at Warrington into the Mersey. Under the Ship Canal Act, Latchford was divided into two parishes, Latchford Within continuing to discharge its sewage into the Mersey, while Latchford Without hi:d its out- fall into the Ship C Ina]. Both waterways were tidal— in fact, it was a race as to whether the tide first reached Latchford Locks or Howley Weir. Ile held that Latchford Without was in a better frisition than Latchford Within which bad its outfall into the river. There was no land in Latchford Without whne sewage could be treated ; it was practically all built upon. It would be manifestly unf jr for the Local Government Board to adopt tte separate scheme for Grappenhall, without taking in Latchford Without. At the present time some of the sewers in Latc hford were draining sewage friim one portion of Grappenhall. A clause of the Ship Canal Act allowed sewage to be turned into the Canal.

Mr W Roberta, vice-chairman of the Latchford Parish Council, said opposiiion to the scheme in that pirish was universd. lie had not met o:.e person who was in favour of it. The ratepayt rs bad had an,oppor- tunity of considering the scheme in public meetirg and he ventured to say that if their representatives on the Parish Council had taken an cpposite vie v they would all be turned out of °Mee whin the time of re-election arrived—(laughter)—not that they would regret it, but it would be an actual fact. Their little parish was quite diflorent from Thelwall in one respect. The introduction of the tramways from Warrington ten years ago had ben the making of the place. It had made it possible for the man with a moderate income—anything from £lOO to £3OO a year —to live out in the suburbs. The class of property which had been built averaged from £3OO to £550 yer house—the larger portion Lbuut £l.O. Those houses bad to a very lage extent been purchased by clerks and small tradesmen for their own use, and they had looked upon lyttchford Without as

Mr William Thro:sell said that if the scheme were adopted he would lose tenants or have to reduce rents. Mr 0 F Ashton (clerk to the Rural District Council) said he was afraid Mr W Roberts might unwittingly have misled the Inspector by his statement that the scheme had not been disclosed by the District Council Ile would like to ask whether Mr Roberts was present at a joint meeting of Parish Councils in February last, when the full scheme was explained by the engineer ? Mr Roberts : I may at once say " Yes," but I am speaking of prior to last February. Mr Ashton, how- ever, knows that not a single representative of the three parishes who was present at tbe joint me3tiog supported the scheme. Mr Ashton : That was not my questi. n. I only wanted to show that the District Council had explained the scheme. _ _

Mr Hatt Cook, who has represented the interests of Grapprnhall at the inquiry, said it would be found that the alternative scheme proposed by that parish took into account the rights of Latchford Without under the Ship Canal Act. He was not sure whether those who represented Latchford Without were unanimous in their recommendations. Some seemed to favour j Aning the borough of Warrington, others a. emed to favour no scheme at all, and some an isolated scheme. Lord Barrymore and Mr Charlton Parr wonld have no objec- tion to be joined with Lstchford Without, if the alternative scheme commended itself to the people of Latchford in conjunction with the inhabitants of Grappenhall. Mr Lister Kaye, chairman of the Grappenhall Parish , Council, said some suggestions that a sewerage scheme was contemplated were circulated in that parish four cr five years an. Although at almost every succeeding meeting of the Parish Council inquiries had been made as to what was being done they could get no information whatever. However, about three years ago the District Council told them a scheme was being prepared to cost about £ll,OOO. That project fell through, and they heard nothing more until eighteen months agowhen they were told that a scheme was being prepared for the three parishes at a cost of £20,000. Ile wrote protesting against such a heavy expenditure, asking for the substitution of a more moderate hut equally efficient scheme, and suggesting that p:izes should be offered to induce competition for the work. lied the scheme to he paid for as a private venture he was convinced that, none of the gentlemen a h;had approved it would have appointed an engineer with a free hand. At great trouble and expense Grappeuhall had sketched out a modified but efficient scheme, and he be hoped the Board would consider it from that parish's point of view. Mr Kershaw, on behalf the Manchester Ship Canal Company, said they had entered into an agreement under which their lands and works would be amply pro- tected in the event of the scheme going through. The company had presented a memorial against the scheme by which their interests would be largely affected, as they were the owners of 65 acres of land in Grappenhall and 12 acres in Thelwall, on the north side of the canal' They also owned additional land en the south side. These lands were suitable and were intended to be developed for industrial purposes—in fact they were acquired for that object. In order to develop the lands.

_ LOW RATES WERE ESSENTIAL; _____ otherwise manufacturers would not be attracted to the district. Works were gradually being erected on the banks of the canaliand he need only point out, as an example, to those of the Partington Iron and Steel
The Examiner, Saturday, December 14, 1912.

Company. The lands on the north side of the canal were not intersected by public roads and in the event of their development for works, the District Council would not be required to incur special expenses on lighting &c. The present scheme could not affect the land on the north side of the canal, which was absolutely cut off from the rest of the area, and what the company asked was the same as the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Go.,and the Warrington Tube Co.—that their land on the north side should be excluded from the snlieme. They were perfectly willing to pay their proportion in respect of their land on the south side. Mr Harold Smith had applied for the exclusion of Thelwall from the scheme and the company were quite willing that that should be done. They were the largest ratepayers and they considered that the points mentioned by Mr Smith in favour of exclusion were reasonable and that there was no necessity for Thelwall to be included. One statement that Mr Smith made—that there were 2 persons per acre in Thelwall—needed correction. There were actually 23 acres for every person. (Loughter.) With regard to the objections of Grappenhell, the company had no wish that more money than was necessary should be expended and they were willing to fall in with the smaller scheme, if the Inspector was satisfied that it was adequate and practicable. The clause in the Ship Canal Act, to which reference had been made, applied only to Lord Birry. more's land and not to the whole of Latchford and Grappeehall. It had reference to the system of drain- age in force at. the time the Act was passed and he contended that the company had fulfilled their obliga- tions under that head and that the section was therefore at an end. It had been suggested that because the Canal Company were regarded as the original cause of all the trouble, they ought not to press for exclusion, but he would point out that they paid for their land and compenstted the parties concerned tweety-flve years ago. The area on the North side of the canal could not be called a small one, as it embrac3d 600 acres.

_ Mr Dunlop, the Canal Company's agent, pointed out that in IRO the Runcorn District Council came to the company for a site for outfall works. A site was offered and it was then agreed that the company's land on the North side of the canal should be excluded from the scheme. It WB9 subsequently found that the si'e was 103 near dwelling-boosts in ThelevAll, so an alternative site WW3 select* d. It was only bccause the Council were not buying the company's land that they now refused to exempt their lai d on the north side. Mr Ashton : I think, as a condition of ktting the Council have any land at that point, you stipulated that your land on the north side should be exempted from the scheme?

Mr Dunlop : It eas not only our condition, but it was accepted by the District Council. Mr Westbrook, on behalf of Messrs William Long and Son, the owners of two tanneries in the neighbour- hood, said that, with regard to the Cliff-lane tannery, they had an agreement with the District Council to take their r ifinlnt int) their sewer. As to the thappenhstl or village tannery, part of the }up, sed eerier would run in trout of the prem sea a..d the firm wished t.,) b 3 assured that, who' they called upon the Council for the facilities which the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act conferred upon ttem as manufacturer., they would not be met with the utj ction that the sewers were only sufficient for the r. quirt meats of their own district. Mr As ttal real Le wai as.ured twit the engineer had bad retard to tbe poseible requirements of traders for the di: p. a lof their r flt.ent. He also promi:ed to put in a copy of the agreement with regard to the Cliff. lane tanney. MR. ASHTON'S REPLY FOR THE COUNCIL. ENGINEER'S CRITICISM OF THE ALTERNATIVE SCHEME.

Bef ,re replying on b. half of the Ceuecil, Mr Ashton read a leeg letter from Mr Diggle, the engineer, who was revented by incisposition from attending the adjourned impiiry. Mr Diegle pointed out that the alternative scheme for Grappenhall was sprung upon them for the first time at the impiry and such methods were contrary to the general pra, tice. On Thursday last, he called at the office of Mr Mountain, the engineer for the suggested alternative scheme, and asked to ree his drawings. Mr Mounta'n told him he had not prepared anything beyond a six-inch ordnance map showing the alternative site, and that he had not prepared any scheme, but simply suggested the adoption of a separate site for Grappenhall, for whom only he was only acting. He had simply copied his (Mr Diggle's) plans of sewers in Grappenhall, and adopted them, and also the prices, which he thought were fair, but had made provision for the manholes being further apart,snd prepared a reduced estimate for sewage disposal works for Grappenhall only. On a previous inspection of the plans, Mr Mountain admitted that the combined scheme was an excellent one and could not be improved in one single detail if one complete and comprehensive scheme was to be adopted. The es imate of £B,OOO for the alternative scheme was ABSURDLY INADEQUATE for complete works, and altogether misleading. The alternative proposal had only ripened in a few days before the inquiry, and great efforts bad been made to induce an owner to give two acres of land to form a foundation for that scheme. Mr Diggle pointed out that more land would be required, and after going into details of the cost, he estimated that the total amount for a separate scheme for Gr Typenhall would amount to £12,715. Thus from Grappenball's point of view there was a saving of £930 in favour of the joint scheme, irrespective of the fact that the placing of sewage works so near to habitable dwellings and build- ing land would be nothing short of vandalism. Lord Barryraore, knowing the whole facts, would never have been wiliing to oiler assistance to such a ruthless I scheme of spoliation of a pretty district. The cost of constructing a separate scheme for Thelwall would be quite out of the question, as it %mild be £3,000 more than under a combined scheme. The opposition engineered against the combined scheme at the last moment had not originated in any desire to provide the best scheme for the district. When he (Mr !Jiggle) had been in the district, he bad been assured on all sides that his scheme was regarded as the best one ; the only objection which had been raised was that they wanted to keep back the scheme, entirely on account of the cost, and by opposition they could at least create delay. Mr Ashton said it had been stated by Mr Harold Smith, on behalf of Thelwall,lhat Admiral Jones Parry, the representative of the parish on the District Coun- cil, had opposed the scheme foe a long period. Admiral Jones Parry ceased to represent Thelwall in March 1910. He did not now reside in Thelwall and he had entered into a provisional agreement to sell to the Dis- trict Council the land required for purification works. Mr Smith further suggested that because Grappenhall was three times as large as Thel wall, the burden on the latter parish would to three times as heavy. He had apparently overlooked the fact that the cost was not being ((pally divided amongst the three parishes, but was being apportioned according to population. While the cost to Thelwall was estimated at 10d. in the £, Grappenhall would have to pay Is. fid. in the £. Mr Ashton went on to say that the maintenance cost of the combined scheme would be £2OO per annum. The scheme was to provide for 5,000 people, but it, was not intended to construct all the works in the first instanc3. It was confliently estimated that the actual cost in the first instance would not exceed £15,000. That would albw the maintenance charges to be added to the estimate and the amount of rates on the three parishes would not be increased beyond the figures given at the opening of the inquiry. It had been suggested by opponents that no alternative site had been considered by the engineer That was entirely wrong, as Mr Diggle carefully examined the whole area of the three parishes before deciding upon the present site. Upon the question of the necessity of including Theism!' and Latchford Without he should simply rely upon the inspector's visit to the area of the irquiry. As to the plea for the exclusion of the lands on the north side of the canal, he admitted that the owners ore that side would not derive any immediate benefit from the scheme. They would, h motor, have tiro &citrates which would accrue from the works on the south side by the development of the area, the natural increase of assessable value which would follow, and the greater ability of the south side to assist in the development of the north side. The site suggested for the alterna- tive Grappenhall scheme was situated in the heart of building land and the scheme would prove ruinous to property belonging chiefly to small owners in the vicinity. There had not been in the whole of the opposition any criticism of the estimates or the engineering details of the Rural Council's scheme. The opposition had been confined to the cost and the necessity of works. It was therefore assumed that the Council's seheme was unassailable from an engineering point of view. The alternative scheme would be against the interests of the district and would be a curse to one of the most rapidly growing parish ce in the Council's area. The Council said that their scheme was was the only practicable solution and the most economical one, and one giving the best finality of any scheme which could be devised. The inquiry then closed.

div.head: AN _IDEAL GARDEN SUBURB
div.p: AN _IDEAL GARDEN SUBURB

Their rates already were very much higher than those of thelw-all or Grappenhall. They stood at 53. 2d. in the ,C and anything approaching an addition of Is. which they were advised the scheme would mean, would absolutely and entirely stop any further building speculation. (Hear, hear). It had bean rumoured for some twelve months that a scheme was looming before them in the imrneditte future, but whenever inquiries had been made they had been unable to obtain any definite information from anybody. (Hear, bear). they had a worthy and respected representative on the District Council but, with all respect, it appeared to them that the authority bad not gone the right way about the work. (Hear, hear). They in their wisdom had thought fit to engage a man whom they all admitted was an eminent engineer, but they gave Mr Diggle carte b!anclie to prepare a scheme. There had been no attempt on the part of the Rural District Council to criticise it or to try and reduce the cest in any way. They simply said: "We have appointed this man. We have absolute confidence in him and we are simply going to try And carry out what he advises." It sounded common sense that any man, given a co.nmission of that kind, would make as gocd and as big a scheme as he possibly could If the Rural District Council had paid due considera- tion to the representations of th 3 three parishes con- cerned, they would at least have said to Mr. Diggle "We really think this scheme is far too costly for these three small parishes and you must modify it—cut it down one half." If they had met the parishes in that spirit they would not have been faced with such strong opposition. The people of Latchford Without main- iained that their present drainage was quite sufficient for the requirements of the parish for the next ten years. During the whole of the ten years he had been a member of the Parish Council he had not heard a single complaint from a resident as to any nuisance in the parish. They bad practically no cesspools—there migt.t be three or four, but they were in connection with large detached houses which he might call mansions, and they were so looked after that no nuisance could arise. Since it became known in the parish that such a costly scheme was contemplated, not one new house had been commenced. It another ls or Is 3i were adied to the present rate of 53 23, young fellsws in receipt of £l5O a year or £2OO a year who had by thrifty and temperate habits been able to take houses in that suburb would find it impossible to remain there and would have to go back to the town. The tendency of the Local Government Board was to er courage the opening out of suburbs for the benefit of the toiling masses. Latchford Without had doubled itself, with a population of a most desirable class, during the past ten years and they wanted to encourage that development. A ve,y much more modified scheme would be ample for the requirements of the parish for the next twenty years.

Mr Arthur Browne, as a ritepayer, owner and occupier in Latchford Without, pointed out that that parish was in the Parliamentary borough of Warrington and rather than that such a wild cat, or as he preferred to call it, Utopian scheme should be brought into operation ho would prefer ABSORPTION BY WARRINGTON

for municipal purposes. The rates of Warrington were only is 10d. Assuming that the new :acme would cost ls 6 d in the £, it would raise the rates of Latchford Without to 6s Bd. They had not, however, the same advantages with regard to streets and roads as the rate- payers of Warrington possessed and they wese charged 6d per I,COO feet extra for their gas because they were outside the borough boundary. There was already a main sewer in Latchford Without, and they had not been told whether it would be used in the new scheme. One side of the road in which he lived was in Latchford Without and the other side was in Grappenhall. There could be no shadow of a doubt that the Inspector had decided that Thelwall should be dirmissed from the scheme, and he (Mr Browne) contended that it was impossible to have a separate scheme dividing Gropenhall and Latchford Without. Ile contended that under the rights conferred upon Lord Barrymore and his derivative vendees under the Manchester Ship Canal Act, of 1885, the inhabitants of Latchford With- out were entitled to turn their see age into the Ship Canal. The company had never dared to interfere with that right and, as long as that advantage prevailed, what necessity was there for a big new scheme ? Latch- ford Without might at any moment be taken over by the Corporation of Warrington and, if the present scheme passed, he should favour that course. Mr Joseph Twiss,on behalf of the Warringtan Estates Company, said Latchford Without did not require a sewerage scheme, as its drainage was perfect and would stand examination by any engineer in the country. The adoption of the scheme would make further develop- ment of the district impossible. Councillor John Pemberton said he was the owner of seven houses and 16 acres of land, assessed at about .£l5O a year, in Latchford Without. He objected to the scheme on the same grounds as the previous speakers. Ile had had considerable experience of public life and he considered that in a scheme of that magnitude there

OUGHT TO BF. COSH'ETITIONI. Human nature was human nature. lie did not mean to say that an engineer wculd deliberately end with premeditation make a scheme as expensive as possible but when there was no check npoa him, he would no dcubt provide for the best scheme he could think of. If there had been competition for a scheme which would adequately sewer the neighbourhood with a stricter regard to the cost, he believed a very different scheme would have been brought before them. Latch- ford originally belonged to Warrington, but when the Ship Canal was constructed an enhance took place, part of Stockten Heath being inc'uded in the Borough, while Latchford Without was excluded. Hitherto the interests of Latchford had been safeguarded by the cause in the Ship Canal Act that its sw.inge should be turned into the Ship Canal which tad a greater volume of water than the Me Bey. Surely if Warrington with over 11,000 houses was allowed to discbarge its sewage into the river, Latchford with 150 houses could not be doing wrong in using the Ship Canal fc,r that purpose. Latchford had developed very rapidly in the last ten years but the present tcheme would put an end to that progress. It would be unfair to impose upon the parish the burden of a schmue which was not required. With the exception of four houses,the whole of the district was provided for by the existing sewers
which, at the present rate of progress, would be ample for twenty years. Before that period expired Latch- ford would ur.der the Town Planning Act, have been absorbed by Warrington, and as

div.head: WARRINGTON WOULD HAVE TO PROVIDE A SCHEME
div.p: WARRINGTON WOULD HAVE TO PROVIDE A SCHEME

OF ITS OWN some day, it would be a pity to put the inhabitants of a small district to the enormous cost of a big scheme. If the Local Government Board declined to recognize the efforts of land and property owners in providing adequate drainage, it would mean that they would decline to go to such expense in the future. He under- stood that the object of the Board was to encourage good drainage and healthy housing conditions. He would he the last to object to the scheme solely on the question of cost, if it were necessary for the health of the district. He would not care if it cost 23. Gd. in the £ ; it would be money well.spent. Under the pre- sent conditions,however, he contended that the scheme was totally unnecessary and there was no need to spend a penny on it. Mr t4' W Wright. on behalf of several large rate- payers, raised similar objections. Tbe scheme, he said, would entail great hardship on those who had already borne a proportion of the cost of providing the exist- ing drains. He asked for Latchford Without to be struck out of the scheme.

Councillor It Ilenshall, as a " very unfortunate " owner of land in Latchford Without, said the price he paid for the land was based on the assumption that there would be no need for a sewerage rate because ample provision bad already been made. Ile had spent a considerable sum on drainage. They all knew the extraordinary elasticity of rates—outwardly, be meant, for he had never known them to contract. (Laughter.) Even 10d in the .£ on the present rate would mean 20 per cent, and would be practically prohibitive. Mr William Tinsley made a point of the fact that much of the land in Latchford Without was nat avail- able for building purposes and the rate would fall very heavily upon the inhabitants.

GRAND DUKE MICHAEL ALEXANDROVITCH. It is reported from St. Petersburg that the Gland Puke Michael, brother of the Tzar, has renounced his rights to the succession to the throne, refusing t) annul his morganatic marriage. His wife recently gave birth to a son. He was married secretly nearly three years ago to Mme. Mamontoff, the divorced wife of a Moscow millionaire.

div.head: IMPORTANT SALE OF GROUND RENTS.
div.p: IMPORTANT SALE OF GROUND RENTS.

An advertisement on our front page gives part i culars of an important sale of ground rents in Warrington and Olford, which will take place at the B!ue Pell Inn, lloreemarket-street, on Wednesday next at 5 pm, Mr John Mainwaring being the auctioneer. The ground rents amount to .4:968 per year and include the works in Folly-lane of the Longford Wire Co., Ltd., and the Lynton Wheel and Tyre Syndicate Ltd., and a large number of houses in the borough and in Orford. .+ Full particulars, plan, and conditions of sale may be had from the Auctioneer, from Messrs Mrs White and Co, Bold-street, or Messrs Henry Gre3nall and Co., solicitors, Winwick- street.
Dr. William James Howarth, medical °Meer of health for Kent, has been appointed medical officer of health for the City of London.
The cruiser Medea leaves Malta on the 19th inst. for Crete and Beirut, to relieve the cruiser Promethus, which will proceed to England to pay off.

An impressive ceremony took place at the Parish Church en Thursday afternoon, when the Rev W J Stanton, of Greenfield, Thelwall, laid the foundation stone of the new choir vestry. There was a large gathering of parishioner; The choir, clergy and church officers proceeded to the site singing the hymn " Blessed city, heavenly Salem as a processional. A short form of service was conducted by the Rectar who afterwards requested the Rev W J Stanton to lay the stone. 'rho architect (Nfr Segar Owen) presented the rev gentleman with a silver trowel. In the course of a short address Mr Stanton pointed out that in old churches little provision was made for the vesting of the clergy, tha reason prob tbly being that there were so many churches connected with monastic institutions. The clergy prepared themselves there and came into the churches to conduct the services. Now it was different. They needed more vestry accommodation than had previously been the case. He commented upon the beautiful character of the Parish Church services, and said he had known the church from boyhood. Ila•ing laid the stone, the rev gentleman said : " I declare this chief stone of the new vestry of the Parish Church to be well and truly laid. In the name of the 10,ther and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen." During the singing of the hymm " 0 Lord of hosts " a collection was made on behalf of the building fund for hich .Cl5O is required. After further prayers and the blessing, the choir, clergy ant officers returned to the church, singing the hymn "Now tank ye all our God."
