div.p: Christ Church, Latchford.

£9l was the sum re-dizod by the annual sale of work in aid of the parochial organiz Along of Christ Church, Latchford, whish took place in the Parish Room, Grappenhall-road, on Saturday afternoon. The stalls, which were laden with a great variEty of wares, were presidf d over by the following Plain-work stall : Mrs Briggs, and the members of the Church Workers' Association. Fancy Work stall : Mrs G Dakin, Misses Massy and J Fairclough. Toy s'all : Mrs Venn, Misses Atkinson, Skinner and Tuns tall. Flower stall : Mrs and the Misses Broadbent. Refreshment stall : Messrs Fairclough, Harrison, Deacon and others.

The opening ceremony was performed by Miss Tinsley, of Penketh, end the chair was occupied by the Vicar, ths Rev G C Briggs. Among others on the talalform were the Rev \V Handy Cock and Mr J Fairclough. The Chairman said there were many organizations in the parish, all of which asked for grznts from the Church Workers' Association, which also supported any big schemes which they had on hand in the parish. A large grant was made when the church was decorated, and they had also looked to that sale to help them in the endowment fund,and in past yearifit must have given several hundred pounds to that obj,ct. (Applause.) During the last year or two the sale bad also assisted him to pay off a loan from Qleen Anne's Bounty for the enlargement of the Vicarage, and he was grateful to the Church Worker's Association for their help in that matter. (Applause). Miss TINSLEY said it was pleasant to see the church helpers working so harmoniously together, and with such good results. The present was not [Aim when they could flag in their efforts to support their old Church. She wished them every success. (Applause). A vote of thanks was accorded to Miss Tinsley on the proposition of Mr J FAIRCLOUGII, seconded by the Rev W MINDY COCK.

div.head: Kitchen Paradise.
div.p: The Kitchen Paradise.

We are not romancing. The kitchen paradise (writes the Bev A M Mitchell in the Burtonwood Parish Magazine) is a great possibility in every home that is a home, a present fact in many a house; a kit chen paradise leads to a heavenly home, there is but a step between the two—from Paradise to Heaven ! The evolution of diet is bringing in a most delightful kitchen revolution. Evolution, at its best and highest effects the truest, the most enduring revolution. Gradually all things that offend are being excluded Irons " that hidden somewhere" below stairs, or, in the back premises, whence issue forth savoury odours and toothsome dishes which constitute the daily menu, whence, too, is supplied, the weekly, yearly round of cooked provision which at least, does satisfy tho appetite, if it does not comfort the stomach of the eater and gladden the heart of the consumer. The kitchen, as we have known it, has been the recep Uncle and repository of many kinds of disgusting "eat- ables," " high " carcises, blood oozing joints, slimy fish,tneasley pork,and other favourite" tasty " eatables, sickening to look at, revolting to the tocch. Ugh ! What dirty work we may make and enforce to provide an English meal! Thanks to the evolution of diet, this unhappy, degrading serve of things is passing, the old barbaric kitchen order is changing, giving place to the new, for diet, like God who gives it, fulfils itself in many ways and flesh p3ts must not defile tho home nor corrupt the world. The reformed diet itself an evolution, is working a great transformation in the English kitchen ; that Augean stable is beiog cleansed, purified, arid transformed into a paradise, a place of pleasure, and delight, of culture, and refine- ment. From every kitchen should be banished all that is. coarse, offensive, disgusting, barbarous, cruel ; nothing should b 3 tolerated there which the most refined and sensitive ladies cannot touck and handle without repugnance. Why should not a house- keeper and her maids be as proud of the kitchen as the scientist of his laboratory, as the artist of his studio ? Science and art are not out of place in the kitchen ; the evolution of diet is the work of science, the application of the knowledge to practice is an art—the cooking art. The true cook will be as enthusiastic about table dishes as we find the artist ahcut his pictures, the musician about his pieses. Scientists and artists are wanted everywhere, they are wanted to further and promote the kitchen paradise. The Christmas reason, above all others, sees the kitchen at its worst. Christmas " good cheer" defiles and degrades our cooks. Christmas cooking means kitchen barbarism run riot. The Advent of the Prince of Peace is celebrated by the letting of blood in torrential streams, by the wholesale, wanton slaughter of inoffensive, sentient creatures, to provide flesh meats for pot, spit or or en, to the degradation of the worker and, may be, the injury of the eater, Does it ever occur to the ordinary flesheater in general, and the Christmas feaster in particular to ask,—how is God honoured by this wanton slaughter, how is the body bettered by the flesh of slain beasts, by the carcases of dead birds ? How has all this carnivorousness come about, from whence has it sprung ? Christmas slaughter is demanded from want of thought, more than want of heart, it is the demand of an old pagan tradition, a mild form of cannibalisro, which is indeed loosing its grip but it is difficult to shake off. But the evolution of diet is on its way, the new order of cooking is at hand, the kitchen paradise is nigh-! A happy Christmas to all cooks who live and move in the kitchen paradise !

div.head: Wycliffe P.S A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S A. Society.

There was a large gathering at the open meeting on Sunday, presided over by Councillor Peter Peacockevho spoke of the possibilities and splendid opportunities given to the Brotherhood. It was not held down by either sectarian or political parties, but its work was broad and evangelical. Their opportunity was to help in purifying the town in every possible way, improving the slum dwellings,removing the acknowledged offences of the town. They could set a good example of purity of speech and brighten the lives of all around them, thus assisting good government in the town. They must not merely ho sympathisers, but must help the Watch Committee in every endeavour to improve the town both on week-days and Sundays. The Rev L Gascoigne, of Manchester, gave the address on " The back doors." lie said he found in his experience amongst the people that they would liv3 at the back, on the darker side of the house. Ile gave some amus- ing stories of "back-door people." He plintel out that in life people kept their front door closed to the influence towards a Godly life. Christ cane to the front door of their hearts, lie wanted to come in to make their hearts clean bright and happy, but people got to their backs and would not open the front door to let Christ in. They treated Him like the poor minister or club collector,and often said "bother him for calling now. We are too busy. We are at the back and cannot be traubled."—The Salvation Army Band played selections, which were greatly appreciated, and also led in the hymn. The:president read the lesson and the speaker led the prayer. One new member was welcomed. A vote of sympathy was sent to Mr Hewitt of Manchester-road, in the death of his father, Mr Walter Hewitt. The president announced that the Rev T T James, M.A., of Sheffield, had accepted "the call" to Wycliffe Church.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Guild.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Guild.

The members of the above- society had a delightful evening at their weekly meeting last Monday, when 11, paper was read by 'Mr R Mungall on ' Edwin Waugh.' The Lancashire Dialect Writer and Poet." First of all the speaker gave a short and interesting account of Waugh's career, his charming personality and love of not 'TO, especially the moors, and then proceeding to read selections from his poetry and prose writings.— The selections were most enjoyable and the humourous ones were given with such zest that the speaker had somotiraes difficulty in proceeding, owing ,to the keen enjoyment of the mirth-provoking incidents. There was a g attendance over which Mr B Williamson, presided.

div.head: S. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: S. John's Presbyterian Church.

Sunday was obterved as Foreign Missions Day, the hymns, prayers and sermons harmonizing with the occasion. The morning discourse by the Rev W Reid from the words " Ask of me and I will give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost, parts of the earth for thy possession," was of God's purpose and methods in Christ concerning the heathen. In the evening the preacher gave a sketch of the life of Livingstone, touching on his ancestry and the nature of his home-training—in no small way resp-msiblo for the character of the missionary. Next to his sympathetic power over men was his determination, seen right from the days when big book wos placed on the spinning-jenny to the days when he sought the cure for African fever, opposed the Boer system of enforced labour, and strenuously fought against, and befriended the victims of, the slave traffic. He did not send home statist;cs of converts made, but pioneered the vast work of saving Africa's millions, by his comprehensive attitude towards its condition. Among his greatest discoveries he placed that of finding the common denomination of white and black.

Wycliffe Congregational Church. The Rev J G anscoigne, of Stockport-road Congre- gatior,al Church, Manchester, occupied the pulpit' morning and ev, cling in Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday, and in the af ernoon in his cipacity of PreEident. of the Llncashire P.S.A. Federation he delivered an address at an open meeting of the P S.A. society. Addressing the children at the morning service he took for his theme the following lines : These things shall be : a nobler rsce Than ere the world has seen shall rise With flame of freedom in their souls And light of knowledge in their eyes. He pointed out that those who had the flame of free- dom in their souls and the light of knowledge in their eyes, must p( ssess faith, hope and love. His sermon was based on the text"! have planted, Apollos watered but God gave the increase," (I Cor. iii. 6.) It was helpful to remember he said, that God needed men to help Him. When the worker realised that he was co-operating with God even when performing the ordinary transactions of life he would engage in it with more heart and spirit. Work bezame a burden when we regarded it as a task. The danger of our present day civilination seemed to be a desire to escape work. Paul's heart was in his work and the text was really an exult- ant note of triumph. A hireling simply worked for the money he was going to get at the end of the day, but the real worker put his heart into his work and realised that he was ca-operating with God in making a bettor world.

The evenings discourse had reference to Paul" commendation of Phebe as "a servant of the church.'e (Romans 16c Iv). In answering the question Why serve the church ? The preacher gave three nations (I) because it existed to promote and inspire worship (2) because it had a gospel to proclaim and bear wltness_to (3) because it was essential as a barrier against encroach- ing worldliness. The preacher enlarged upon these reasons with deep insight and gave many illustrations in their support. Worship, he said, was really ones' sary to our life because it was an essential part of human naturelt was important that the soul should be awakened to reverence, wonder, awe and love, and th 3 church that exibted to do that was contributing a large amount of good to the world. A letter of great interest to the members of the church and congregation was read from the Rev T T James, M.A , of Wycliffe Chapel, Sheffield, in which be accepted the call to the pastorate at Warrington.

div.head: Roman Catholic Progress In Lancashire. Archbishop Whiteside's Remarkable Statistics.
div.p: Roman Catholic Progress In Lancashire. Archbishop Whiteside's Remarkable Statistics.

A psatoral letter from Archbishop Whiteside wa S read on Sunday in all the churohes of his archdiocese in connection with an appeal on behalf of the Liver- pool Diocesan Mission Fund. Ws Grace says, in refer- ence to the spread of Eucharistic practices and devo- tion:—

It has been said that when the history of the Catholic Church in later ages comes to be written, It is likelY that the twentieth century will be called the century of the Blessed Sacramrnt. 13e this as it may, it 15 certain that when we look around us and see the wonderful renewal of the spiritual life that has already in so short a time resulted from the two Decrees of tha Holy See—the one 0° frequent Communion, the " other on the first Communion of children—we ara disposed to honey° that we are on th 3 eve of a great and f sr-reaching increase in God's Church of devotion to the Blessed Sacrament. As far as our own diocese is concerned, w° are thankful to eay that the practices incalculated by these two D:tcrees have taken deep root amongst the faithful. This is due in a great measere to the zeal of our clergy. They have given a ready obedience to the repeated injunction of the Holy See that " parish-priestt. confessors and preachers have frequently and witn zest to exhort the faithful to this devout and salutory prao tine of frequent and daily Communion; " and the fait' ful on their side have given a ready response. in like manner, in their watchful care of the school children,t° which they have been seconded by the hearty co-operli- Lion of tha teachers, they have seen that the little one° at the dawn of reason were suitably prepared for the reception of the Blessed Eucharist;so that now very few in our schools reach the age of eight without having mads their first Communion. Hence as a result of the fir" Decree the number of Communicants, made in the diocese has risen by leaps and bounds, from ab°°,.. 1 900,000 made annually four years ago to over 4,000,00 u made during the past year. In consequence of P..° second Decree, in the year following its-promulgat'° the Easter Communions in the diocese rose from about 198,000 to about 221,000, an increase of 23,000 in o°_, year, due in the main to the number of little Children who for the first time fulfilled the Easter preceP,t Not only do the children approach the Holy Table ;_`:, large numbers, but from all sides there comes ,tuf same gratifying account of the wonderful faith, an°4 the recollection almost beyond their years, with vrol't the little ones receive Our Lord. The silent work tin is now going on in the souls of all, both young and through early and frequent Communion, is a great 000 solation to pastors of souls, and inspires great b°Pse for the future.
LETTERS OF A SLENDEg SCHOOL CHUM To HER DUMPY FRIEND.
Second Letter.—DISPUTINg. THE OLD-FASHIONED BELT"' THAT OVER-STOUTNESS RUNS IN FAMILIES.

My dear Sallie, First, in answer to your imperative question, I rlici not subject myself to any alteration in my regular diet during the time that Marmola Prescription Tablet° were converting me from an over-fat frump into al: present slim and comely self. Elinor Jameson called this morning bringing her eldest stepson, a youth of about eighteen. Beall!, one couldn't help being sorry for him, for he is 50 frightfully fat that it is a wonder how he manages to keep awake even as well as he does. an ri Elinor met me last week at Dentwood. 8, to-day's call was made on purpose to ask me how on earth I had managed to bring myself down to MY present proportions. . Of course I told her about Marmola Prescription Tablets, and advised her to get a trial bottle from her chemist's, or send 2/9 to the Marmola Co, DePt-* 123 i, 86, Clerkenwell-road, London, E C., asking for. a bottle to be posted to her. She expressed hereelt perfectly willing to buy a ton. I told her that 000 tablet taken after each meal would complete the cure' in a few months. What has been most trcubling Elinor is the feat that, sooner or later, the lad must suffer from corpulency because his mcther and grandmother were, both " feather-bed-tied-in-the-middle " sort of people' But I reassured her by telling her that my father; weighed nineteen stone while my grandfather was, s believe, enormous. Do write soon and tell all the news to Your .loving MARGARET;
The Examiner, Saturday, December 14 1912.

The peaceful relations with other countries which had prevailed since Liberals succeded to power had enabled the Government to take up such social legislation as old age pensions, labour exchanges, and national insurance and the Children's Act. There was no political question affecting the men of the country but which inalrectly affected the women and children, but the women's point of view was apt to be kept in the background and they did not receive the attention they could demand if they were in a stronger electoral position. (Applause). However, the women's political organizations had given an impetus to such bodies as the Co-operative Guild and women's trade unions which had been formed to deal with their own home subjects. An instance of the influence which could be exercised by the women was the increase of the old age pension to married women from 2s 6d per week, as originally proposed, to ss. Sbe claimed that that was achieved through the efforts of the ‘Votnen's Liberal organize- along and if that was the only work they had done, they had justified their existence. (Applause.) Mrs Barton also commended the prominent part which the Liberal women of Warrington took in supporting the measure for the SUPPRESSION OF THE WHITE SLAVE TRAFEIC.

The women bad given the impetus to that reform and it was to satisfy their demand that the Bill had been passed. She was glad that the flogging amendment had been retained—(applause)—because those who did not want to be flogged need not engage in that vile traffic. (Applause.) By helping to keep a Liberal Government in office the Liberal women were assisting in evading war, in giving to the people better means of living and in using the wealth of the country for better purposes than destroying their fellow-creatures. Not only did war devastate the corquered country but it impoverished us at home The Government was doing what it could. little by little, to ease taxation of the masses and to spread it on the shoulders best able to bear it. The Sugar Convention would no longer throttle us, because the Government had decided to withdraw from it, and then they would he able to remove that tax and also the impost on ten. Alluding to national insurance Mrs Barton pointel out that very shortly the people would begin to feel the benefits of it. They would wonder why they bad ever objected to being compelled to contribute, especially when they considered the enormous amount of money at present paid away in poor rates and subscriptions to hospitals Sm. One of the best things in the Act was that the thriftless who had never striven to do anything for themselves and who had drifted into poverty, would now have to show why they were not working, or pay to insure themselves against the day when sickn es would make help necessary. The medical benefits would be a great boon to the people because they would not be so apt to allow themselves to slip into thoroughly had health before consulting a doctor. In some respects the women were not being as well treated as the men but they hoped the women's organizations would steadily keep their requirements before the public. Housing and land reform were promised in the near future hot they hoped that before those measures became law women would have sufficient power to say "We must have this or that." (Applause). Mrs. CROSFIELD, In proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Bartou, said everyone in the room would agree that politics touched women just as much as the men. She imuressed upon the workers of the association the necessity for reading literature on political questions. Mr Lloyd George was going to bring in TWO MAGNIFICENT REFORMS _

in the stripe of housing and an alteration of the land system which lay at the root of so much of the trouble England. Although at the present time we were experiencing a great boom in trade, there were no end of evils eating at the heart of England, which called for redress. The two great reforms she had mentioned would be one of the royal roads to a better condition of thins. (Applause). Mrs PEMBERTON seconded and the vote was heartily accorded. _ .

Mrs BARTON, in returning thanks, expressed the hope that at the next election the Liberal women would do their utmost to see that Warrington returned Mr Drosileld. (Applause). Their opponents knew that the legislation of the present Government would so redound to its credit that it would be a very difficult thing to persuade the electors to return a Tory administration. They were working might and main and leaving no stone unturned to influence the people. The Duke of Westminster and other wealthy Tories were putting down their money because they knew that the continuance in office of a Liberal Govern- ment would mean that the wealth in which they bad entrenched themselves would have to be better distributed.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.

WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION N.A. CENTRE. Last week end was a blank. We heard of about three members who thought of paying the Gowy a visit but they discarded the idea when the time drew near, after consulting several Gowy fishers who say December is the worst menth in the season for results from the stream. Anglers at present are patiently waiting the time when the stone I ait are in full swing. AS the Gowy is recognised as the best stream for miles around Warrington for this kind of angling, the results on the set board testify to this. SPECIAL GENERAL MERTIN(.. The meeting at headquarters on monnny night last Was not attended as was expected. Of course, if the nature of the business had been known to all members, there would have been a greater gathering of members' It was decided to ask Mr James Reynolds, of Liverpool to give a lecture. The secretary went through the correspondence concerning the taking of the Gowy and it was seen by all members present that the result has been brought about with no little trouble. Remarks were made on the different centres interested besides Warrington, Chester coming in for great praise for the way in Which they have fallen in with the scheme and the generosity of their delegate in proposing that they (Chester) will find all that is necessary fo,r protecting the water. Our delegate then read out his report on the general Meeting of the Northern Anglers. Members were interested in this report from the commencement until the finish. He commenced with the Executive Council Meeting which was held previous to the general meeting. At this meeting four delegates Of the Freshwater Reservation League were given a good bearing and it was decided to consider a ninety days close season. It was also decided at this meeting that the Northern anglers lake over the fishing rights of the Gowy owned by Lord Shrewsbury from January Ist, 1013, on the same Breement as they lease other streams and canals. Everyone present seemed delighted with their officials Who have had this in hand for the manner in which they have added another water to those already possessed, and the little expense it will cost the society. At the N.A.A. general meeting, the main topic was the election of officers, there being no less than three beminated for the presidency, and after a rather 'uncomfortable ten minutes on collecting the votes it Ws. declared that Councillor It 0 Atherton of Wigan Ivaci elected president for 1913. Mr Brown of Crewe 'wee elected vice-chairman. All the other officials !Rend as before. A vote of thanks to the pit officers 'brought the meeting toa close.

div.head: LIBERAL WOMEN.
div.p: LIBERAL WOMEN.
SUCCESSFUL YEAR'S WORK REVIEWED.
Mrs. A. H. Crosfield at the Annual Meeting,

Au eminently successful year's work was under review at the annual meeting of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association which was held at the Liberal Club on Wednesday afternoon. The large attendance testified to the loyalty and enthusiasm of the members who have during the past twelve months rallied to the support of the association in a most encouraging manner. Mrs A H Crosfield presided and among others present were :—Miss Crosfield, Mrs Dodds, Mrs Ztba Armitage, Miss Bessie Dutton. Mrs Walker (treasurer), Mrs Osborne (secretary) and Mrs Barton of Manchester. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

Miss BESSIE DUTTON proposed the re-election of Mrs A H Crostield as president,remarking that the members appreciated how very willingly and well she had dis- charged the duties of the office. Mrs ARMITAoR seconded and the proposition was carried with acclamation. The following additional officers were elected : Vice-Presidents, Mrs Z Armitage, Mrs Pierpoint, Mrs Walker, Mrs James Dodds, Miss Crosfleld, Miss Bessie Dutton and Mrs Henry Roberts; hou treasurer, Mrs Walker; bon secretary, Mrs Osborne; executive com- mittee, Mrs A H CroAeld, Mrs Dodds, Mrs Walker, Miss Crosfield, Mrs Pemberton, Mrs Osborne ; General Committfre and District Captains, Bewsey Ward, Mrs 'J.' Pemberton ; Fairfield, Mrs Osborne; Howley, Mrs Hill; Latchforf, Mrs Walker; Orford, Mrs lialitwell ; St John's, Mrs Roberts ;St Austin's, Mrs E V Walker; Whitecross, Mrs Delaney; Town Hall, Mrs Lindley ; Latchford Without, Miss Walker ; Stockton Heath, Mrs O'Brien ; Padgate, Miss Short; Penketh and Sankey Bridges, Miss Dodds: additional members of general committee, Mrs J T Locker, Mrs Hassall, Mrs T Locker, Mrs J Hawthorn. Mrs Bunch.
THE YEAR'S WORE.

Mrs. OSBORNE-, in presenting the 21st annual report, said the year just ended had been an eventful one, and much had been accomplished. The committee had taken a keen interest in their duties, and the members had supported their efforts with commendable spirit. Altogether they ought to feel gratified at the success of the association, and it should give them encourage- ment to enter upon the new year with great ambitions. (Applause.) They regretted to have to record the death of Mrs Garnett, a vice-president. Mrs Dutton had to resign the position of captain of St. John's Ward, owing to ill-health, but bad consented to remain a member of the general committee. Reference was made to the success of the sewing class and to the pleasant day at Colwyn Bay which the members spent at the invitation of Mrs John Crosfield. The fancy dress ball and carnaval which took place on ,February. .Ist was most successful—probably no prettier spectacle had been seen at the Parr Hall. Another happy innovation took the form of a bowling main for the committee and auxiliaries, forty prizes being competed for. The annual picnic proved to be a most enjoyable allair and might be added to the long series of successes promoted by the association. There was a touch of novelty about it, for it took the form of a sail along the Manchester Ship Canal to Eastham Gardens. But the time of the members and committee was not altogether spent in pleasure. Edecational work was undertaken and accomplished. Delegates from the association attended the annual Council meetings of the Women's Liberal Federation in the Queen's Hall, London, the spring conference of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union at Blackburn, and the annual Council meeting of the Union at Liverpool when Mr a Osborne was elected on the Executive Com- mittee. Miss Crosfield addressed the meetings on women's suffrage. A public reeeting on the National Insurance Bill was held in Bold-street schoolroom, when Miss Potter gave a flue exposition of the work that great measure would accomplish. Seven very successful and enthusiastic ward tea meetings had been held and addresses were given by Mr and Mrs Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Miss Bessie Dutton and local speakers. Thanks were due to the captains and auxiliaries for their valuable services. Resolutions had been sent from the association to Sir Edward Grey and Mr Lloyd George thanking them for their support of women's suffrage. Whilst the committee had no desire to take credit for the town's meeting which was held in the Parr Hall recently on the subject of the White Slave Traffic, yet it was through the initiative of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association that the matter was taken in hand and it as particularly gratifying to know that their efforts were so successful. (Applause.) The report also referred to the successful meeting held at the invitation of Mrs P H Brown at her house at Orford and to the election of Mrs Lindley as a representative of the association on the General Committee of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Women's Liberal Associations.

div.head: FINANCES.
div.p: THE FINANCES.
Mrs WALKER reported that the association was in a very healthy state financially, there being a substantial balance at the bank. (Applause). MRS. CROSFIELD AND _WOMEN'S INTE RESTS

_ IN POLITICS. Mrs CROSFIELD said the reports of the hon. secretary and hon. treasurer were very satisfactory and proved that the association was healthy and thriving. (Applause.) Women in Warrington—and indeed throughout the country—were beginning to realize what a very important part they could take in the politics of the country, (Hear, hear.) In certain directions they could help even more efficiently than the men. They had no self-interest to serve and their efforts were entirely unselfish. They had no special ambition of their own to achieve but were simply working for the cause of Liberalism, and that was the spirit in which the best work was done. (Applause.) Women had certain qualities which enabled them to canvass and to persuade the electors more effectively than the men. A woman could far more easily introduce herself into a home by charm of manner and grace of personality, and could obtain a hearing in many cases where the door would be closed in they face of a man. Having warmly commended the work of the ward captains and auxiliaries, Mrs Crosileld pleaded for greater diligence in ward visitation. The more they considered Liberalism, the more they must feel how closely it was linked up with the welfare of the home. Whether it he Free Trade, Education, the Children's Act, or the Insurance Act, women were very directly affected by modern political issues and it was therefore only right that so much political work should be done by them. They must not be satisfied and content with the good work of the past, for where there was no progress there could only he retrogression. They could not afford to stand still, but roust go forward as rapidly as possible. One thing which impeded progress was over- confidence. They had suffered from that in this town, in times past, and she would warn Liberal women against allowing that feeling to predominate. They must work hard in their own districts and show women the necessity of political knowledge. A great many women unfortunately imagined that politics and the government of the country did not concern them at all—in fact they prided themselves on knowing nothing of such matters, which they considered to be only men's affairs. It was, however, their business to take an intelligent interest in what was going on in the conntry. She was looking forward to another pleasant year of office, but her work would not be nearly so agreeable if it were not for the efficient and willing help she received from Mrs Osborne, Mrs Walker, Miss Cro,field and the other members of the committee. (Applause.) WHY WOMEN SHOULD SUPPORT THE GOVERNMENT. _ _

_ Mrs Barton then gave an interesting address, con- gratulating the association on having attained its majority. Dealing with the rise of Women's Liberal organizations, she pointed out that they came into being soon after the extension of the franchise to the agricultural labourers in 1884 made evident the awful amount of illiteracy which existed in the country. When an election came round it was necessary to go through the country teaching the men who were newly enfranchised how to mark their ballot papers lectures being given with the aid of a blackboard and a' lantern. Women's associations found that a great educational work confronted them for, at the very first election after the agricultural labourer had been enfranchised,a Tory Government was returned to power. The Conservatives at once recognised that the people must be got hold of, so they instituted all kinds of amusements. Lord Salisbury on one occasion declared that what the people wanted was a circus; they did not rEquire the vote. (Laughter.) The Liberal party was appalled at the amount of ignorance that was brought to light through their demand that the people should be allowed to vote. At that time, comparing our nation with Russia and Italy, and even with Turkey, we were much behind them in the matter of education. We had a great deal of leeway yet to make up before we could arrive at the excellence of the German nation or even of Russia in that respect. Mrs Buton then passed in review the great work of the women's organizations in educating the electorate on Home Rule, Temperance Reform, Disestablishment and other questions which, despite their ponderous sound, could be grappled with by women. Dealing with the long spell of Tory domination from 1895 to 1909. she showed that war Invi resulted in increased food taxation while the Sugar Convention into which the Tories entered, had the effect of doubling the price of sugar.

div.head: ACROSS-COUNTRY.
div.p: ACROSS-COUNTRY.
Warrington's Way.
[By THE OUTPOST].

Loyalty and enthusiasm in club life can be shown in various ways, sometimes it is eAly discerned, at other times a careful search might be necessary. When you approach the precincts of the Warrington Athletic Club, and you sight the club's headquarters you see a lasting memorial of the loyalty and energy of its members. I wonder how many of the harriers or athletic clubs in England own their own premises; quite a small number lam sure. I still further wonder how many can claim the credit of having built their own club-houses ; personally I only know of one, and that is the Warrington A.C. A better example of devotion and determination in amateur athletic club life in England I do not know, consequently I have the greatest pleasure in recording the fact. It appears that some two seasons ago the officials were notified that their headquarters, the hostelry of a patron, was to be demolished and fresh quarters must be secured. Harriers are not profitable clients to any hotel proprietor, and it is not always convenient for the latter to accommodate them. This was the prime consideration in the committee's mind when they resolved to become builders in the literal sense—they are well known to all as team builders of repute. The second consideration was the means whereby. Being practical men they decided to become their own archi- tects, masons, plumbers, and labourers. The outcome of their united efforts is a structure of ample propor • dons, good appearance, homely, and if not exactly palatial. well, a building that has the merit of answer- ing all the requirements of an athletic club which demands modern facilities by which the members may obtain the best results from their training labours.

div.head: MODERN .M_ETHODS.
div.p: MODERN .M_ETHODS.

Exactly how long the building took to erect is not known, nor are the time-sheets of the artisans available. Those men who could afford the time in the evening after their ordinary labours were ended gave a few hours to the " pavilion,"others did the same in the early hours of the morning, while Saturday afternoon was a time for all to be occupied. The building is mainly composed of wood and glass on a wood founda- tion. The frontage is about GO feet long by about 30 feet deep. There is a front entrance which opens into a spacious apartment set ',part for dressing and massage. The back portion is smelly divided into two departments, one used as a committee room and the other as a bathroom, wil h hot and celd water. There are no electric light fittings, but there are oil lamps. Water pipes are not laid on from the main. The water that falls on the roof is collected in a number of water tubs, and then trans- ferred into the pavilion as required. No club in the country could hope for better train- ing quarters, and if thm et are any who would like to emulate the deeds of Warrington and become possessors of their own premises at a roughly estimated cost of £lO. they had better write direct to Mr Charles Berry, the bon. secretary. The rent is a nominal one, and is payable to the Warrington Football Club, an organisa- tion that is obviously inspired with a kind desire to help along this enthusiastic band af workers. Imroediatsly outside the pavilion the men can com- mence their running on a rough field which is suitable for winter work. In the summer time the enclosure of the football field, situated immediately in front of the pavilion, is planed at the disposal of the members on payment of a small charge for the season. Thus we find the members of the Warrington A.C. properly and comfortably housed, and with all the modern simple means made available by their own united efforts.

div.head: LOOKING AHEAD.
div.p: LOOKING AHEAD.

Having dealt wit7h-i.lie-P-renilSei;".or quarters, I must now devote space to the doings of the active members. I find the list is growing; it now reaches something in the region of 150, and of this number somewhere about 50 per cent play an active part in the barrier work. A few of the remainder are summer birds, and perform only on the track. Everything is methodically managed. A useful list of fixtures is arranged, which includes inter-team races, kandicaps, &c , and when at home there are several recognised courses where the men may race. I saw one of these on Saturday with about thirty members having a scamper. Racing plays a foremost part in the programme, and every encouragement is given to a man who wishes to reach a high plane in the racing world.

With so much attention to racing matters it naturally follows that there should be a desire to constantly be on the look out for young and raw material. I saw quite a thriving batch on Saturday, several of whom I should imagine will be prominent in the West Lanca- shire C.C. Association's novices' championship, which is due to take place in Warrington next Saturday. With regard to the team that ran second to Hallam- shire in the Natiom.l and Northern Championships last year,. all are available again. At present C Vose is showing splendid form; better I think than when he won the "Northern" two seasons ago. His colleagues ii Holbrook, W Bolton. A Siddall, Antrobus, T Turton, and F Antrobus, are a formidable crew, all keen on the game and anxious to beat their past perform- Qsietly, and in their own fashion, they are striving to reach that state of fitness that will enable them to race Hallamshire on something more like level terms than hitherto. 1 hope

div.head: Sam N. Green, SPOTFI:4IOmP, PiRKET,
div.p: Sam N. Green, SPOTFI:4IOmP, PiRKET,

they will succeed. They are good sportsmen all ; we bave seen enough in recent years to prove that and in their desire they will have the good wishes of their strongest opponents. We all hope to see a better class of Athletes grew up in Great Britain. Some of us are confident of the future, and in this our belief is strengthened by the fact tnat there are clubs like Warringson A.C.. and their truly bard-working sincere helpers, who unselfishly devote their time and labour to bring about the desired result. To mention names would be invidious. I just record the fact that after the run on Saturday turned in at the pavilion to find all the men had bad a hot bath ; and a number of masseurs, members and supporters of the club were busily engaged massaging the runners. Every man was dealt with in turn. It was a hive of industry for half an hour, and left an impression that there is little wrong with the Warrington Athletic Club.—From the At News. (By PEno.) A pack of 30 ran a number of laps on the fields adjoin- ing Wilderspool Causaway. Of the seniors who ran about six miles Chris Vose, II Holbrook and T Turton were most prominent, and the brothers Antrobus did splendidly when the small amount of training they have been able to do is considered. W Bolton, J Parsonage, and A SiddalOwere notable absentees ; of Juniors, A Gregson and J Li vesey showed promise, and the novice moved exceptionally well with J Hanson J Nurse, W Walters and J Watson the most noticeable.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Genuine burlesque comedy, quaint humour, up-to- date witticisms and really rollicking situations are included in the now famous sketches "Bloomsbury Burglars" and "My Pal Jerry" which have been pre- sented at the Hippodrome by Lew Lake and Co., this week. The large "houses" which have assembled nightly have been convulsed with the eccentricities of Lew Lake and Bob Morris as Nobler and Jerry respectively. Exception might be taken to some of the boisterous accompaniments of the acting, but thia can be overlooked in the general effectiveness of the sketches. A clever cycling turn is provided by 'The Minerva Troup including Eddie Hughes, ex-Amateur Champion. Mounted on cycles the quartette play an exciting game of " football " using the front and back wheels as a means of forcing the " leather " through the narrow posts which serve as goals. It is really marvellous how, rushing round within the small area of the stage, the cyclists avert disaster, hut it is rarely any of them have to dis- mount,and after concluding such hairraising evolutions the troupe are accorded round upon round of applause. Monty Walker is a clever dialect comedian and scores a decided hit with his two songs, particularly "I do like my lodgings" The Six Buster Browns, described as the real rag timers, are a combination of clever artists, and whether in singing 'or in dancing they soon distinguish themselves, the turn being far above the average. Edie Vern), a dainty comedienne, is at once a favourite with her distinctive style in two popular numbers. Irving and Jasmine are smart drawing room entertainers and their voices blend exquisitively in an Irish love song. Other artists who contribute to a capital programme are Fred Wright the flippy comic, Emily Millard, comedienne, and Ethel Stephenson, who uses a splendid voice to decided advantage in vocal tit-bita at the piano.

div.p: THE CONSCRIPTIONISI AGITATION. We are beginning to feel grateful to Lord Roberts for the speeches he has made of late in favour of compulsory military service—" the fancy name for Con- scription, just as Tariff Reform is the fancy name for Protection" (vide Daily News) People were inclined to be apathetic on the question—both schools of thought complain equally on this point—but the veteran soldier has at last aroused the country by scare headlines and an attack on the Territorials The result is admirable from our point Of view. Newspapers and public men all over the country are beginning to take the con- scriptionists seriously, and there is a growing volume of protest against such an anti- British proposal. The Tory party is coquetting with the question in the spirit of desperation which impels men to catch at straws, and nothing is more certain than that the straw will break and cast the party into the depths of oblivion. As a contemporary points out: "It is only in recent years that the conscriptionist movement has captured the reactionary Press and the reactionary money. Such coincidences are not accidental. In a very sinister sense Tories want conscription for the " education " of the democracy." We are going to pin our faith on the democracy. Thelconscriptionists can go hang! In another column Mr. G. Dale writes in defence of Lord Roberts. With that defence we are not concerned. But our correspondent touches on another point which it would be neither fair to him, nor wise of us, to ignore. He makes some rather strong reflections on the patriotism of gonconformists as expressed hi official circles. They carry their anti- militarism, so he says, to the length of deprecating service in the Territorials. A Methodist class teacher has told his young men that if any of them join—e-d the Terri- torials he would be ashamed of them. Are we to take this as a fair expression of the Nonconformist conscience on the question of National defence? We hope not. If it were -so we should regret, as Mr Dale seems inclined to do, our Nonconformity. We have
I

report of the Bureau of Statistics of Labour and Industries, ninety-seven strikes which occurred in the State during the year ended September 30th last resulted in a wage loss of 1,004,635 days. Not only did the " protected " American workmen of New Jersey find it necessary to strike for better pay, but more than half the strikes failed. This, remPmber, is in only one State out of forty-six. The best comment on this condition of things fell from the lips of the new President of this Protectionist country, when he said the other day: "I want the men out of a job to know that there are fewer jobs in America because of the tariff, because the great combinations limit the output, limit the productions, limit the number of those who produce, and, therefore, there are hundreds of thousards of poor fellows out of employment on account of this very thing."

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, December 14, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 14, 1912.

The electors of Newton Division will note that Lord Wolmer is continuing his extra- ordinary course in opposing the Trade Unions Bill. The other day he made what Mr. Ramsay Macdonald called an insulting suggestion when he brought forward an amendment to secure the accurate counting of votes at trade unions ballots. This could only mean, as Mr. Macdonald pointed out, that in Lord Wolmer's opinion these votes were habitually miscounted. Lord 'Wollner also suggested that the ballot should take place under the supervision of some person appointed by the Registrar of Friendly Societies. This amendment, which was rejected, seemed, said Mr. Clement Edwards, to be based on the idea that all trade unionists were scoundrels, ard this, indeed, seems Lord Wolmer's view and the view of the Tory members who support him. Lord Wolmer is evidently out to destroy trade unionism. The spirit of the noble lord may be further observed in a question that he addressed to Mr. Churchill, which was meant to insinuate that Mr. Churchill paid for his dinner to the Oxfordshire Hussars out of public monies. Mr. Churchill was able to sh3w that nothing was further from the truth and added that it was extraordinary that ;he suggestion should have been made.

Beech House School. The annual performance by rupils attending the above school at Stockton Heath took place on Wednes- day, when a writ enjoyable evening was spent by those invitcd by the Misses Westbrook to witness it. The fairy play selected, was " Sleeping Beauty" and the different characters were well acted by the pupils, the clear enuneination king a great feature, showing careful elocutionary trait,ing. The solos and choruses were beautifully rendered. Tableaux, which were much admired, brought a most successful evening to a close.

Picturedrome. "The Grandfather " is the star picture for Monday and Tuesday. It shows how a woman treated her father-in-law and how she regretted it afterwards. On Wednesday and Thursday, " Wittsotne but wise" in which a young woman captures a notorious bandit will be shown. "The finger of scorn " will be the chief attraction on Friday and 6aturday; this is a fine story of a woman whom the villacze disliked. There is a special picture on Thursday, Friday and Saturday, entitled "The Badminton Hunt." It depicts some splendid horsemanship and is well worth seeing. Promotion for Mr. J. S. Place. We are pleased to announce that Mr. John Spencer Place (eldest son of Mr Elijah Place, chief markets inspector, Warrington', has been promoted f tom the post of staff paymaster to that of fleet paymaster. Mr Place, who is 37 years of age, has been in the service 21 years. He was educated at the Boteler Grammar ty:chool, Warrington. It is interesting to recall that when the Victoria was rammed by the Camperdown, Mr Place was one of her commissioned officers. He was, however, invalided home at the time of the catastrophe, and the officer who took his place was drowned. The Children's Teeth. The Education Committee made an interesting departure ,on Thursday evening, when the school dental officer (Mr Hedley H Taylor) gave an address to parents, in the Silver-street school, on " The care of the children's teeth." Last year the school medical officer examined 5,106 school children, and fund that no fewer than 3,919 had defective teeth. In order to assist the parents in temedying this state of things, the Education Committe have established a dental clinic. Mr Holman Kingdon (chairman of the medical Inspection sub-committee) presided at the lecture, which was fairly well attended. The subject was made more interesting by lantern illustrations.

A. sale of work arranged by the Ladies' Working Society of Wycliffe Congregational Church, in aid of the Church funds, was held on Thursday afterp.oon in the Memorial Hal. There was no formal opening ceremony, hut during the afternoon the newly- appointed minister (the Rev T T James), accompanied by hia wife, took the opportunity of making the acquaintance of the Church workers. They received a hearty welcome on their visit to the sale. Stalls were presided over by the following ladies :—Mesdames Ziba Armitage, Slack, J Walker, Winskill, nekton, Ball, Sutherclen, Knowles, Edelsten, Thomas, Jeffery, Joseph Hawthorn, Podmore, Atkinson, Wackerell, Misses Ellison, Harristm and Rathbone. Refreshments were provided during the afternoon and evening.
FOR MODERN FIREPLACES and Cooking Ranges corn bining economy with simplicity try J. S. GARLAND Ironmonge2 Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. St. John's Church.

A cake and candy sale in aid of the Church Build- ing fund of St. John's Presbyterian Church was held yesterday afternoon. Mrs Thomas Locker performed the opening ceremony, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to her on the proposition of Mr Lewsey, seconded by Mr P H Brown.- The Rev W Reid, who presided, stated that for the upkeep of its ordinary ministrations the Presbyterian Church looked to its own members, but appealed to outside friends for aid in church extension for which, in the way of class- rooms, &c., there was an increasing need. An effort on a larger scale would be made next year. The stalls were presided over by Mesdames Reid, Wrench, Miller, Prentice, Lewsey, Leiper, Hodgkiss, Brown and Marshall, Misses Smith, Bennett and others.—ln the evening a Christmas tree was a great attraction to the youngsters, Santa Claus bring impersonated by Mr W Russell.

Literary and Philosophical Society. Before the members of this society at the Masonic Hall on Tuesday evening, Mrs Ridgway gave a delight- ful paper on "Philip Bourke Marston and his pcems." She pointed out that the poet was the son of a dramatist and poet, Dr Westland Marston, who was a lineal descendant of John Marston, the play-writer of the IGth century. Philip was sightless and his poems and sonnets were so full of pathetic yearning. His inner life was written in his poems. He was not ashamed to lay bare his soul and his aching quivering heart in so vivid a fashion that beholders must weep sympathy. Again and again he had to mourn the passing over of his nearest and dearest, and in his poems the personal note sounded sharply and sincerely with a simplicity often heart-rending. The blind poet brought to light his own individuality; he discovered to the world his personal experience, and the result was truth and beauty.

Licensing Transfers. At the Borough Police Court on Monday the follow• tug transfers were graut-d: —John Cheadle, Smiths Arms ; John Wrii Pliuston, Hawthorn Inn; Thomas Bolrerts, Bay Horse; off licence, 73, Battersbrlane, Frederick Thos. Lashford.

The Warrington Chess Club. Last week-end the Club was visited by the President Mr Coates, and the Secretary, :Mr Beckwith, of the Cheshire Chess Association. The President, four times Cou,ty Champion, played Eleven simultaneous games with varying success and gave a most interesting exhibitiou, s int.ing the majority of the finished games The meeting was well attended and very much erjoyed by the members.

Warrington Boy for the Navy. The Admiralty have itAimated to the Local Educa- tion Committee that tejr Nominee (Louis C Leigh, of 2, Baxter-street, an ex-Secundary School pupil) has succeeded in obtaining the twenty-sixth place in the country in the recent examination of candidates recom- mended by certain Education Authorities for admission into 11.11. Navy as Artificers. This result reflects great credit upon the boy (who will proceed to one of JIM Dockyards almost immediately to enter upon his training as a Boy Artificer) and also upon his old school and the town.
