The members of the p-ung Men's Bible Class con- nected with the Ellesmere-street Wesleyan Sunday school promoted a tea and social gathering on Thursday evening of last week, when a large number assembled. The proceeds are to be devoted to the ;unday school prize fund. The proceedings were presided over by Mr Joseph Finch. A pleasant feature of the evening was the visit of Mr Charles Drinkwater from Failsworth (a former teacher and worker in the Mission up to the time of leaving the town), who was accompanied by a friend who con- tributed one or two items in the evenings enjoyment. After tea the evening was spent in a miscellaneous programme and several game ,i were also introduced. The leader of the class is Mr E Howard. Musical Successes.

The following pupil § of Miss Maud Jennings, Diploruee of the VILLE and prize-winner of the L.C.M. passed very successfully at the recent examination held in Manchester, namely Flossie Merris, 4, Museum-street, who has been awarded the Bronze medal for theory of music, having gained the maximum number of marks (100) ; Miss Lily Taylor 14. Enville-street, senior grade piano, 85 marks, first class vviiti honours ; Master Sylvester Hall, 133, Sankey-street, SI marks, first class with honours ; Miss May Mather, 2, Church-street, intermediate grade, 81 marks, first class with honours; Miss Ellen Miller, 11, Nora-street. primary grade, 90 marks ; first class with honours. Master Hill now has five honours certificates, and is only 12 years of age. At the recent examination held at Manchester by Victoria College of Music, Miss Margaret Halton passed the Junior Grade in singing, with honours. Mr FH West passed in pianoforte playing., Ask for Whitbread's Famous Ales and Stouts in
screw-bottles.—Sole agent, PETER. LEIGH, HOCER-
market st.—Advt.

The Late Mrs Mather. The remains of the late Mrs Martha Mather were interred at the Warrington Cemetery on Monday afternoon in the presence of a large number of relatives and friends. A very impressive service was held in the Legh Street Primitive Methodist Church by the Rev W Cooper who also conducted the service at the graveside. Mr W H Ward presided at the organ. Wreaths and other floral tributes were received from " Charlie," " Mary," " Lizzie," "Martha Ann and Walter, and family," "Harry and family" (Canada), "Lily Tom and Roily," "Vin, Ernest and family," " Albert and Katie, Alice and Rodger," "Bertha and Harry," " Ada and Jessie," "Jim and Ted," "Lucy and Alfred," "Martha and Leonard," " Vinnie and Leo" (London) Boscows, Mrs Howard (Southport) Mr and Mrs Baker, Mr and Mrs Foulkes. Mr and Mrs Pugh, Mr and Mrs Wakeman, (Wolverhampton), Mr and Mis Rodgers, (Grappen- hall), and Mrs A Cook Burtonwood). Ask for Whitbread's Famous Ales and Stouts in
screw-bottles.—Sole agent, PETER LEIGH, Horse- market st.—Advt.

Warrington Photographic S3ciety. In consequence of the arrangement decided on at the beginning of this session that some of the meetings should be on a Thursday, two lectures have been provided for this week's fare. Tuesday evening was filled very instructively with a talk and demonstration in the Bromoil process by Mr J B Potts of the Everton Camera Club. If the resulting sea-piece as shown by Mr Potts is one of the " First Steps in Bromoil," to give the lecture its proper title, some of us are a long way from the first steps, and will be very pleased when we can toddle. Mr F V L Mathias presided over a fair audience. On Thursday, Mr G H Walker who knows Dublin and Wicklow so well, gave a very interesting lecture on the beauty spots of those two counties. He gave many details as to the folk-lore and the legends of Glendalough and the vale of Avoca. The slides were by Mr Sykes who has travelled the same routes, and many were excellent, especially those showing Bray, Arklow, and the Sowerscourt estate. Both contributors to the evening's pleasure were heartily thanked by those present, numbering between 20 and 30.
CUTLERY.—Joseph Rodgers & Sons' celebrated Knives and Forks, &c.—Agent, J. S. GARLAND, Bridge st., Warrington.--Adst.

Sunday School Teacher Honoured. A. very interesting gathering took place the other evenit g at the Methodist Free Church, Buckley-street, when Mr William Roberts, who has been one of their Sunday school,teachers for 35 years, was the recipient of a handsome clock, the gift of the past and present scholars and members of the Church. Mr IEI Woolley, sen, made the presentation on behalf of the donors. and alluded to the long and valuable service rendered by Mr Roberts to the Sunday school and his acquaint- ance with ttie old chapel in Dallam-lane in 1871. Mr A Taylor (superintendent) and Mr W Shaw also referred in complimentary terms to Mr Roberts' valu- able work in the school, after which Mr Woolley handed the handsome clock to Mr Roberts. The recipient, in accepting the present, thanked all the scholars and old associates and said he would prize the gift for the feeling u hich he knew had prompted it. He had worked many years as a Sunday school teacher and hoped to be spared for many more to continue his labour. LAMPS, Oil Stoves, Coke Stoves.—J.S. GARLAND Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Sale of Work at Friars'Ameen. In connection with Friars'-green Church, a social evening and sale of work took place on Thursday night. The sale was organised by the ladies of the church. It was opened by Mrs John Strange, of Grappenhall, who was introduced by Mr James Hudson, the president of the church. In a graceful speech she feelingly alluded to the former connection of herself, her parents and grandparents with Friars'- green Church. Referring to the object of the sale namely the extinction Of the debt, she said that a debt on a place of worship was not an altogether unmixed evil, as it had the effect of uniting the people in work. In conclusion she hoped the sale would be a success. A vote of thanks, moved by Mr Alderman Burton,and seconded by Mr Aquila Cook, having been heartily endorsed by the gathering, the sale commenced. A varety of side shows including an art gallery, shoot- ing gallery, fish pond, hoop-la, Sic., were provided and were well patronised. The stall were presided over by Mrs S Dale, Mrs Burn, Mrs Wright,the Misses Burton, Miss Grirnshaw, Mr Findley Dale and Miss Freda White. A sum of .#:3O was realised.
ANTHRACITE STOVES, clean, cheerful, smokeless, no fnmes.—Agent, J. S. GARLAND. 51, Bridge St. Warrington.—Advt.

Warriiigtonian's Gift to a Church. A peal of new bells and a new clock, the gifts of Mr and Mrs Colin Maclver (formerley of Warrington) were dedicated at the Church of St Michael and All Angels, Blaiedon by the Lord Bishop of the Diocese (Dr E C Sumner, Gibson) on Tuesday afternoon. November "26th. To record the generosity of Mr and Mrs Maclver, a hand- some bronze plate has been affixed to a wall of the church. This was executed by the West Bromwich Crafts Guild, and the central panel bears the following inscription: "To the glory of God, and in memory of her parents, Peter and Isabella Stub., of Blaisdon Ball, the tower was repaired and the figs,. existing bells recast, and a new one added, by M .iy E ten Maclver in 1912. At the seme time the tower clock was put in by Colin Maclver. Rector, Gilbert Ensor, M.A. ; Wardens, C Maclver and J S Bate." On the sides of the panel are two texts, that to the left being " The souls of the righteous are in the hands of the Lord," and that to the right, " Whatst ever thou doest do it as unto the Lord." It was during the lifetime of Mr and. Mrs Peter Stubs, who were also long and honourably associated with Warrington,that the church restoration movement was initiated, and ly making these memorials Mr and Mrs Maclver are carrying out their wishes.

the warmest admiration for the young men who voluntarily enter the Territorial force, and to decry their aims and enthusiasm is not the duty of any Christian whether he be Churchman or Nonconformist. The Territorial force is an admirable institution, capable of fulfilling all the requirements of home defence, and we agree with Mr. Dale that "if the number of men asked for by Lord Haldane could be obtaineo and adequate training given, even the ideal which the N.S.L. have in view would be almost realised.' 'At any rate we should have heard the last of conscription. More power to the Territorials!
Anyone who gives REAL POLITICS. careful and impartial

- consideration to the speeches of Mr. A. H. Crosfield cannot fail to be impressed by the striking contrast between , his thoughtful and well-considered treatment of the great issues of the day and the frothy, superficial utterances to which Mr. Harold Smith treats his supporters. Mr. Crosfield's methods are those of the serious politician,bu t the borough member never condescends to real argument—his policy is to divert attention from a hopelessly poor case by sneers and gibes at his opponents, and high falutin Ulsteria about the streets of Londonderry " running with blood." It is a relief to turn from Mr. Smith's unedifying perform- ances to the honest concern for industrial betterment which is evidenced in Mr. Crosfield's important speech to the Trades and Labour Council on Thursday evening. Without trenching upon politics Mr. Crosfield dealt with some of the most urgent problems which confront those who are anxious to civilize the conditions of employment throughout the labour world,and his position as a British representative on the Inter- national Association for Labour Legislation enabled him to speak from first-hand inform- ation of world-wide movements fraught with vast possibilities of benefit to the toiling multitudes. It was evident from the close attention with which the trade unionists followed Mr. Crosfield's address, that it proxided much food for reflection, and not least signiicant was the comparison which he drew between the lot of the worker in England and the less humane conditions which obtain on the Continent and in America. Earlier in the evening Mr Crosfield had attended another of , the highly successful series of ward ' meetings promoted by the Women's Liberal Association. The recent unimpressive visit of " King " Carson furnished him with a topic which he turned to good account and he made a decidedly convincing point in call- ing attention to Canada's recent magnificent proof of loyalty to the Empire as a refutation of Sir Edward's woeful pronostications of the disaffection and unrest which he wishes us to believe are the inevitable outcome of the right of self-government.

After a long series of THE TRIUMPH OF notable trade returns, FREE TRADE, that for last November which we summarize this morning, is the most striking of all (says the" Daily News" of Monday.) On a total volume of trade amounting to £124,000,000 the increases, as compared with the "boom " figures of November, 1911, are just under £2,372,000 in British exports and in imports well over £5,500,000. The importance of this last figure lies in its promise of a continuance of prosperty, for nearly all the increase is under the head of raw materials, of which cotton is infinitely the most conspicuous. It is clear that among the two bad winters on which Mr. Bonar Law counts for the conversion of Lancashire to Protection that of 1912 is not going to be included. Of course, Mr. Chamberlain's test is exports, and whether we take the figures of the month or of the eleven months Free Trade comes out triumphantly. But there is no need to argue the point any longer, when the evidences of prosperity have become so palpable that even the ranks of Tuscany are driven for decency's sake to cheer. There was a time when the Unionist Press either condensed or suppressed the testimony of the trade return. Now we find them announcing the activity of all our industries from the housetops.
In one State alone of UNEMPLOYMENT IN ths United States of TARIFF LAND. America there were

nearly a hundred strikes in the twelve months ended Septem- ber 30th last. That is quite sufficient to show that Protected America is not a land of content. It illustrates also the words of the new President, Woodrow Wilson, who said that under the Protective tariff "prices climb faster than we can push our earnings up." Wilson said also, "the labourer finds that his wages d,p not rise with the manipu- lation of tariff duties. He sees that those duties build up wealth in private coffers, but his share is hard to get at." Most grievously has this fact been learned in the State of New Jersey, where, according to the annual

div.head: LNOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: LNOTES AND NOTIONS.

Mr. Harold Smith's rude simile with regard to Crosfield on Carson—" a fly on a barracks "—has been well capped this week by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield who wittily likens Mr. Smith to a mosquito on a bull, the bull being the Borough of Warrington. The mosquito is a disagreeable intruder addicted to pin-pricks, and we must say the applica- tion to Mr. Smith seems very apt.
. . "Of course, our whole tariff policy has its object to raise prices."—Dr. Delbrueck, Imperial Secretary of the German Home Office, in the Reichstag debate, Nov., 1912.

What he called "a -simple question" was asked by the prospective Unionist candidate for the Loughboro' Division (Mr. N. W. Smith-Carrington). It was this: "Could anyone tell him a single country which had tried Protection and wanted to give it up?" —(" Leicester Chronicle," Nov. 23). The answer is easy. This country tried it and gave it up; and millions of voters in America and Germany have shown this year that they, too, want to give it up. * *

* - The highly creditable success of a War- rington boy in the national competition for positions as naval artificers suggests another answer to the ever-pressing problem : " What to do with our boys." Hitherto the Education Committee has experienced some difficulty in finding candidates, but the fact that a Warringtonian has secured a good place in the list, should direct attention to these promising openings for smart boys, and stimulate a laudable ambition in the minds of local students to equip themselves for the appointments.

Chancellor Thomas Espin, whose death occurred at Walsingham, near Bishop Auck- land, on Thursday of last week, was well known to the Church officers of Warrington and district, for he had frequently held Courts, for the admission to office of Church- wardens and sidesmen, at the Warrington Parish Church. He had reached the advanced age of eighty-eight and was one of the greatest authorities in England upon ecclesi- astical law, not one of his decisions having been reversed. He was a moderate High Churchmen and approached all controversial subjects with the charity becoming a Christian gentleman. *

The question of the architectural work for the new Council schools in Parr-street and Oliver-street, which gave rise to such a stormy scene at the last meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday, is likely to occupy further attention. Councillor Pemberton objects—with some reason—to the work being given, without competition, to a local firm who have already designed one Council School to the satisfaction of the authority. He has now given notice of his intention to move at the next meetings of the Education Com- mittee and Town Council, that the decision confirmed by the Council last week be rescinded, * * *

There is no more active and progressive boey in the town than the Women's Liberal Association which, in many respects, can give points to the men's organisation. It has a paying membership of something like 2,000 and always contrives to finish a year's work with a balance at the bank. The annual meeting has been held this week and the report of the hon. secretary embraces a pro- gramme of achievements of which any society might well be proud. Mrs Crosfield makes an active and enthusiastic president, who fully appreciates the incalculable value of women's work on the right lines in the affairs of the nation. "The more they considered Liberalism" she said, "and the more they must feel how closely it was linked up with the welfare of the home." Women to-day are looking far beyond the home, but the crux of all questions for them still remains within the boundaries of house and family. *

The inquiry into the big sewerage scheme for the townships of Grappenhall, Latchford Without, and Thelwall, has ended with little satisfaction for the ratepayers. It seems to be the general opinion that the Rural Council's £1.8,500 scheme will receive the approval of the Local Government Board, which usually shows a preference for estimates and figures of full, round dimin- sions. An active opposition to the scheme has been engineered by the parishes con- cerned, and no one has done more for the pecuniary interest of the ratepayers than Mr. A. Lister Kaye, who endeavoured to get a modified scheme for Grappenhall adopted. There is no doubt that in this township the imposition of an additional rate of is. 3d. in 'the £ will be a hardship on property-owners and residents, while the advantages of the scheme are mbre imaginary than real in many parts of the district. It is one of the reflections on present-day local Government that the " will of the people" has so little chance of prevailing in matters which concern them so closely as does the project under , notice.

* Consternation has been aroused among the more thoughtful Tories by the withdrawal of the Referendum pledge by which it was hoped to capture the vote of Lancashire for the reactionary party. They see that this cynical repudiation of Mr. Balfour's pledge can mean nothing but the revolt of the Unionist Free Traders, with the same disas- trous results as in 1906. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, in his speech to the Liberal Women's Assoc- iation on Thursday evening, called attention to the very significant protest of the " Liver- ' pool Courier." Says this paper : No single item of Uilionist policy should be allowed to jeopardize Unionist success at the General Election. Yet that is precisely what Tariff Reform will do, unless Lord Lansdowne rehews the Referendum pledge. Without that Pledge we cannot succeed in Lancashire and Yorkshire. Without Lancashire and Yorkshire we cannot secure a working majority. ' This is plain speaking, and it is not from al Free Trade but from a most vigorous Tory Protectionist organ that it proceeds. Tariff Reformers are indeed in a sad plight !

div.head: MR. GROSFIELD AND LABOUR. ADDRESS TO TRADE UNIONISTS. THE EIGHT !WIRD' DAY.
div.p: MR. GROSFIELD AND LABOUR. ADDRESS TO TRADE UNIONISTS. THE EIGHT !WIRD' DAY.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield was present at a social held under the auspices of the Warrington Trades ard Labour Council at Atkinson's Cafe on Thurethiy evening and, in addition to contributing to tho musical programme, gave an imp.etant address ch industrial topics. Mr S H Smith presided over a gof attendance, and the proceedings proved highly successful. Songs were artistically rendered by Booth and Mr McArthur, and the clever humorole sketches and concertina so/os by Mr S Aelland were reativ appreciated. Mr AEI Crosfield played several pianoforte solos with a taste and skill which called forth general admiration. Mr A. E Trow was an fficient accompanist. Mr C DUKES (secretary of the Council) gave art address, in which he said the present unrest in the labour world was the fesult of men being deprived of that which they actually produced. The strikes which were constantly occurring were not merely incidents, but were the culminating point of many grievances; Mr HALEY, who was introduced as the father of the Trades and Labour Council, proposed a vote of thanks to the artistes. He referred to the great interest which. Mr Crosfield was taking in one important phase of the. Labour question—the eight hours' day,about which. more was _likely to be heard in. the. near future.

Mr A H CROSFIELD, in returning thanks, said that although in a misguided moment Warrington dispensed with his services some little time since-(laughter)-he still had a great many irons in the fire and life in these modern times was so complex that there were many important issues demanding attention. With regard to the move- ment to which Mr Haley had alluded, he had given a great deal of time to it, both in England and on the Continent, and he was happy to say that considerable headway had been made. Mr Crosileld next touched upon the work of the International Association for Labour Legislation, which, he said, aimed at

CIVILIZING THE CONDITIONS OF INDUSTRY. Wherever there were poisonous processes which wrecked the health of the men or women workers.in any country, the association sought to get rid of them. It was also bringing about a reduction of excessively long hours of labour and concerning itself with the principle of the minimum wage. No doubt Mr Dukes would say that the associa- tion did not go the whole hog, ores far as he wished it to go, but he (Mr Crosfleld) could only say that he honestly believed that the association had not only done work of incalculable benefit to tens of thousands of workers in Europe, but was destined to achieve reforms of a much wider value in the immediate future. (Applause.) In England we bad made a start with the system of Trade Boards—he admitted on a small scale, and there ought to be an immediate extension. (Hear, bear.) He himself had approached the Board of Trade with that object in view, and he was informed that the Board intended to equip themselves for an exteusion but that they required expert knowledge to be accumulated by their staff to enable them to cope with it. Of course, Government depart- ments were apt to be slow. (Laughter.) Having touched upon the beneficial results of the introduction of the Trade Boards Act into four indus tries, Mr Crosfield said there was an overwhelming mei for the application of that measure, as the Bishop of Oxford had said, to the agricultural labourers and he (Mr Crosfleld) held, equally to the town labourers of England. (Applause.) In some respects be would differ from those present. He was not prepared to see anything iike a sweeping, reckless extension of the Trade Boards system where they got above a certain line. He would be content to begin with those instances of low-paid unskilled labour, where he felt that not only was there a strong case, but that they would have to work through Parliament to get that evil in the industrial world removed. (Applause.) Another reference to the information gleaned by the International Association for Labour Legislation led Mr Crosfield to call attention to the fact that the con- ditions of employment in the United States were in many respects one of the biggest

DISGRACES TO MODERN INDUSTRY. Moreover, their Co stitution had been so fashioned an almost to block the way to industrial reform. It was largely through the efforts of the International Associa- tion that the abolition of the use of white phosphorus had been carried in America by means of a tax upon that poisonous industry which had, in fact, taxed it out of existence. (Applause.) When at the Lugano Conference, the question of the limitation of the hours of work for women was discussed,a ten hours day ands 60 hours week were suggested as a maximum. He (Mr Crosfield) said that, in his view, a 55 hours week erred on the side of excessiveness for women but

if that were persisted in, they should at. least make it a 53. nays' week. He was not the only one who pressed for that and it naturally brought beforo the Continental deleptes the cognate questi.,n of the weekly half-holiday before the Sunday day of rest. Although at the Lugano meeting tbey found that

_ CONTINENTAL IDEAS WERE A LONG WAY BEHIND he was glad to say that when the second biennial con- ference was held at Zurich, opinion bad, in the mean- time, made considerable advance on that question and was fast ripening all along the line. At the next spring International Convention a sixty hours' week would be probably adopted as the limit for women. Although that was too long, it was a step in advance, and only showed how infamous many of the hours of work must have been vs hen it became necessary to pass an international law of that kind. Mr Crosfield proceeded to argue that the enactment of more unmans conditions on the Continent would make industrial , reforms easier of accomplishment in England. He did I not say that employers of labour ought not to be ready to make sacrifices to bring about such a reform as the introduction of the eight hours day which had already effected such a vast change in England. After careful consideration they felt that the best way to drive the eight hours' question ahead was to concentrate their efforts on selected industries, instead of fighting for a broad principle and losing themselves in attempt- ing something which would not be manageable. Having regard to the million and a quarter workers in the

IRON AND STEEL TRADES of Europe and America, they decided to put that industry in the very forefront of the eight hours' movement. His work in that direction brought him into touch with several trade union manufacturers in that trade in England, and he never listened to more graphic accounts than they gave of the total difference in social and physical condition which they found in those parts of the country where the eight hours' system in the blast furnaces had been introduced, as compared with those districts where the barbarous twelve hours' shift was still in vogue. He held that it was true patriotism for employers to make some sacrifice to help to brinz about a civilized condition of industry. (Applause.) Touching upon the question of " SPEEDING tr," _ _ _

Air Erosfield. after referring to his own Com- mercial experience, said his idea of the goal they must aim at—whetber for brain or manual workers—was first to get rid of the excessively long hours and then to ensure brisk, alert work during the time a man was employed. There was no justification for continual " speeding up," and employers ought to be on their guard against it. An extraordinary degree of ignorance still pervaded the industrial communities of Europe and America on these vital questions. He knew perfectly well that there were cases in which costs would go up considerably with the shorter hours, and that was where the International Association came in. They did rot esk for any branch of industry to be checked or crippled in THE WORLDS COMPETITION, .

and on that ground they sent invitations to all the Governments concerned, with a view to international action. He had been putting a little pressure on the Home Office to get the iron and steel trades dealt with. Last Tuesday Mr IlodgA, who had rendered him great assistance, Came to lunch with him and, along with the very able secretary of the British section, they discussed their plans with a view to getting the question up to scratch within a reasonable time. He was hoping that they would have an International Convention called by the end of next summer with a view to the introduction of the eight hours day on the Continent and in England. Whether they succeeded in that or not, he was very hopeful that that part of their work would be accom- plished in the course of a few years. (Applause.) He was not there to brag about the conditions in England —he knew how much necessity there was for improve- ment—but, at any rate, they were not as retrograde as he found things on the Continent. There were already branches of trade in Britain where the eight hours day was in full swing, to the satisfaction of employers and employed; it had particularly swept South Wales. (Applause.) In Germany there were 193,000 workers in the iron and ;steel trade at the last enumera- tion, and not two per cent of them had the eight hours shift. In America—and he called it an absolute disgrace to the American employer—forty-three per cent of those engaged in the iron and steel trade were working twelve hours shifts and seven days a week. (" Shame.") Yes, it was monstrous and scandalous. " I do not talk like this" added Mr Crostleld " merely because I am addressing you whose interests are chiefly with the workers. I talk in exactly the same way on questions of this kind when I meet employers." (Applause.) Continuing Mr Crosfield said it was encouraging to find 100 representa- tives of many nationalities notwithstanding the serious differences which might be expected to divide them, united with the common object of trying to check the cruelty of circumstance, the worser part of natural law which was at the bottom of the undeserved suffering and hardship which existed throughout the mighty industrial world of Europe and America. He was glad to say that some of the leading Socialists in Europe were working on the International Associa- tion. While Radicals and Liberals were represented, they had also not a few enlightened Conservatives co-operating with them, and he did not think it was a bad thing that it should be possible for men, of what- ever party, to show a little unselfishness and an honest desire for human progress which might be facilitated by that association in which, on the advice of Sir Charles Dilke, he began to interest himself sOnae years. ago. (Loud applause.)

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, December 14, 1912.

church ceased to be a National Church it had no right to keep the National funds," says Miss Cros- field. Personally, I do not see why any church, whether National or not, should keep National funds, except on the ground that such funds were presumably given as a gift to be retained. But the church has not ceased to be National. And she possesses no National funds. Large sums were given to Dissenters by the nation in times past and up to the year 1831. Are they right in keep- ing them? "In no instance Miss Crosfield says, 1" would endowments by private persons be touched, the title deeds of which went back about 300 years." It is not clear what she means by this. It is true that the funds given to the church since 1662 will not be taken away. But funds given to her cen- turies before that date by private persons will be diverted from her use. Such is the modern method. It has always been understood that the longer one has held possession the stronger becomes the title. Miss Crosfield's friends now say that the longer the possession the weaker the title. "If Noncon- formists could support their own religion, why not church people? " asks Miss Crosfield. The answer is, that church people do support their own ,religion and these very endowments are visible evidence of of it. Because of them, churchmen are able to divert much of their benevolence, and certainly to a far greater extent than Nonconformists, to such really " undenominational " objects as hospitals and other necessitous causes, which are certain to suffer if the church is disendowed.—Yours, &c., H. J. WESTBROOK.

;OME.

Sir,-1 am afraid that the Rector has made a mistake. lam not quite so youthful as he would lead your readers to suppose; especially in these day's, when oven the poor curate is by some accounted " too old at forty." To the Rector's hope that as I grow older I may "learn wisdom, and grow in knowledge and humility," I sincerely and fervently say" Amen !" I have great respect for the age of the Rector, and for his activity and zeal, but even his advanced years do not give him the right to attempt to be sarcastic at the expense of a younger minister who, despite his youthfulness, has already had eleven years of active Christian service in London, Aldershot and Warrington. Now, as to the Rector's criticisms, I did not say that I doubt the validity of Anglican Orders ; I simply tried to make-it clear that Rome refuses to recognise them, as was proved eighteen months ago by the correspondence which passed between Canon Willis himself and the Rev Father Whittle, as to the renunciation by Rome of her claims to supremacy. An "intelligent study of history," past and present, will convince any impartial student that such hopes will never be entertained by the Papal Church. To close, I again say that, while the Rector wishes f, r Re-union with Rome, I wish, and work for-a return to Reformation principles, but I trust that, while attacking systems and principles opposed to Protestantism, I still treat thrse gentlemen opposed to my teaching with the courtesy due to them, whether they be youthful or otherwise.—l am, Sir, yours LS:c
WILLIAM T. JAYE.

div.head: Emmanuel (Reformed Episcopal) Church, Bold-street, December 116, 1912.
div.p: Emmanuel (Reformed Episcopal) Church, Bold-street, December 116, 1912.

Dear Sir,—ln the letter of Canon Willis, published in last Saturday's " Examiner," there is a para- graph which, with your permission, I will discuss. It is that "Anglican orders do not need the recog- nition of Rome." As Roman orders however they do need such recognition, and I will go further and say that to be a member of the Eternal Priest- hood established by Christ needs also that recog- nition.

It may be interesting to Canon Willis, and to " Examiner " readers generally, to know that about fifteen years ago there was a petition to Rome from the Anglican clergy to inquire and ascertain if their orders were valid or otherwise, and they were pronounced otherwise. How is it that Canon Willis, as an Anglican clergyman, does not know this? And if he does know, why does he ignore it; and if Rome's approval does not matter, why was she appealed to? And finally, if our reverend friend was against appealing to Rome, it is only another sign of the disunity and discord which domi- nates the Church of England. However, Canon Willis is quite right in one respect. The position of the Anglican ministry does not need authorita- tive pronouncement from Rome, as we all recognise what it is. It is that body of men who do the work of the Church of England which was founded by Henry VII. That church, which was started as a protest, as its name implies, and which name it will bear until its dissolution, which is apparently closely pending. It was established by means of murder and pillage. Covetousness and hate were the chief inspirations of Henry and his satellites. The present body of clergy are they who have succeeded to and are enjoying the estates and revenues confiscated from the Catholic church. They are subject to the King and Parlidment. They preach without authority, and when they do, it is to people who are at liberty to qualify what they hear, and interpret as they choose, as they claim to have the right to use their private judgment on matters of doctrine. Have they? Whence did such a privilege originate? Protestantism has been a decaying force since its inception, and judging by the present trend of circumstances, and the events of the past few years, is in a galloping consumption. The figures given in your Notes and Notions column last Saturday bear eloquent testimony to this, wherein it is stated that since 1902, 1,500 schools which are, or nearly all are Church schools, have been handed over to authorities under which other than Church of Eng- land doctrine is now taught. Surely if her doctrines are worth anything, the retention of the right of teaching them to her children at day school is worth fighting for, as such is the only place the vast majority can learn them. But no. They are being given up without scarcely a struggle. The irrevocable and inevitable decay has set in. This church which began with plunder, has been contemporary with privilege. With the end of privilege, i.e., the end of the power of the House of Lords as established by themselves, her ignominious end is approaching. What could otherwise be expected of an institution pretending to have Divine authority, but really established by man, and established by such means? That Canon Willis will have the grace to see the light, and the courage to embrace it, is the sincere -wish of—Yours truly, JOHN RICHARDSON. 86 Buttermarket-street, Warrington. _ December •12th, 1912. -- MISS CROSFIELD AND DISESTABLISHMENT.

Sir,—" It was calculated" said Miss Crosfield, "that Nonconformists paid two-thirds of the up- keep of the Established Church. This was chiefly on account of tithes." Calculated by whom? Surely by no one acquainted with the facts. Tithes, or to he correct, rent charges in lieu of tithes, are not payable by the tenants but by the landlords, who, according to our Liberationist friends, are church- men. Tithe rent charge is payable because of the ownership of land on which it has been charged, just as a ground rent or any other charge, and the payer is not concerned with the destination of the payment beyond seeing that he pays to the right person and gets a proper' receipt.. " Tithes," con- tinued Miss Crosfield, " brought in a little history," which she proceeds to give. "They were originally granted by the State for the use of the National Church." Who told Miss Crosfield this? Can she name the date and the title of the statute by which such grant was made? "The Established Church," she says "was set up in Wales by the Normans in 1115 but the Christian Church in Wales. was far more ancient." Neglecting her differentiation be- tween the Established and the Christian Church, will Miss Crosfield give some authority for her statement? I have always understood that though the Normans brought the Church in Wales, and in England also, more definitely into line with the Western Church, and were rather heavy handed in doing it, yet there was no new church " set up " in Wales any more than in England. "The Welsh Church did not become a new institution, it was still the old church but with a new spirit developing its dormant strength." " The idea that there was a sudden break at this epoch with the past history of the church and that a new line of bishops began which had no connection with the old Celtic bishops, is entirely modern and would have seemed to Urban himself, as it does to any sober and unprejudiced student of facts, nothing less than a ridiculous fan- tasy." As regards the Welsh bishops being English- men, it should be remembered, as Mr. Gladstone pointed out, that "there are four Sees in Wales, and yet between the reign of Henry VIII. and the Revolution no less than 44 Welshmen were appointed to fill them." It is doubtless true that from the beginning of the Hanoverian period a large number of Englishmen were appointed. This was owing to lack of endowments, the Reforma- ' tion having left the church in Wales so poor that it was necessary to appoint men who at the same time held office in England. But what has this got to do with the church in Wales of to-day? Is Miss Crosfield, or am I, to be condemned to-day for the doings of our ancestors or even for our own shortcomings in the past? Does Miss Crosfield know the origin of Welsh dissent? How that in its origin it was more English than Welsh, and was propagated by soldiery? Does she know that even to-day Welsh dissent has its seats of authority in England? If Miss Crosfield will read b"Thveiartioser and decline of Welsh Nonconformity," y Cambrensis (himself, I believe, a Dissenter) she will learn something to her advantage. "The moment a

div.head: MEDICAL TREATMENT OF SCHOOL
div.p: MEDICAL TREATMENT OF SCHOOL
CHILDREN.
Sir,—An important judgment was given the other day at the Court of Session in Edinburgh by Lord Dunedin.

l'he Court held that the Glasgow School Board was entitled to provide medical examination and super- vision of school children but not treatment, even where parents through poverty or ill-health were unable to secure the treatment required. This judgment will prevent the Scottish Education Department from providing treatment, and one wonders whether the English Board is similarly affected or whether it has special powers provided for by legislation for the medical treatment of school children found physically defective. —Yours etc., SCRUZATOR.

div.head: COMPULSORY SERVICE. Nonconformist Patriotism Questioned.
div.p: COMPULSORY SERVICE. Nonconformist Patriotism Questioned.

Sir,—As was anticipated, the more thoughtful section of the Conservative party is thoroughly dis- gusted with the low simile which Mr Harold Smith, M.P., recently applied to Mr A H Crosfield. And there are quite a number of Liberals who are equally disgusted with the unseemly allusion to Lord Roberts contained in the letter of Mr Massingham, which having originally appeared in the "Daily News' was reproduced in your issue of December 7th. When he characterises Lord Robert's speeches as " devilish," classes him with General von Bernhardi and expresses the opinion that if he and General Bernhardi with "their supporting scribblers" were marooned for a time all would be well, he not only betrays a want of delicacy and good taste, but also supplies by the vehemence of his invective a ready means of measuring the poverty of his argument. If the " devilishness ' of Lord Roberts' speeches is thi ught by Mr Massingham to be due to some analogy between those speeches and General Bernhardi's recent book we think he must be labouring uuler a misapprehension, as many who have read both are unable to discover such points of analogy. If space would allow, a few quotations frOm the book in question would prove the absolute unfairness of the comparison. I have sympathy with Mr Massingham's desire to give the Territorials a fair chance, and as a Free Churchman, who while admiring very much in Non- conformity, has never been able to understand its attitude to the question of home defence, I respectfully suggest that as Mr Massingham urges "the present government and the Liberal party to take the Territorial force in hand and give it all it wants to make it a good, set vicable, well-kept,eflicient body, the campaign of re-invigoration be inaugurated" in NonconfQrmist quarters. If Colonel Seely or General Bethune could attend the conferences, synods and district meetings of those churches and place the facts before them, especially the important one that in the event of an invasion the Nonconformists would have to be defended by Churchmen, some good might be accomplished. In the December number of the "Independent Methodist " we are informed that a Free Church deputation waited recently upon Colonel Seely to protest against Sunday shooting by Territorials, and that he took occasion to reproach the Free Churches for their lack of patriotism in not supplying their share of the country's defenders. " Free Churchmen" says the writer, " have chosen other ways of serving their country, and it is well for England that they have done so. They are anti- militarist for the most part and we rejoice in the fact." It would be difficult to exaggerate the inconsistency of the average Nonconformist on this question. If accused of lack of patriotism he is insulted. In fact, if these shores are threatened he says he will go forth to meet the invader. But, if we ask him to learn some little of the art of war, he indignantly assures us that " his kingdom is not of this world." When urged to support National Service he is strongly opposed to compulsion in any form and will only tolerate voluntary methods, yet he refuses to volunteer. A few months ago the teacher of a large class of young men in one of our Methodist Sunday schools publicly stated that if any of the members of his class were to join the Territorials he would be ashamed of them. Surely the Nonconformist conscience in these matters is a very incomprehensible quantity, We certainly agree with Mr Massingham that the Territorial force could be improved, and if the number originally asked for by Lord Haldane could be obtained and adequate training given, even the ideal which the N.S.L. have in view would be almost realized. But if this government and the Liberal r arty can obtain practically no support from the Free Churches, which are the mainstay of Liberalism, the problem that disturbs Mr Massingham and many others will be no nearer solution. Yours truly, G. DALE.

THE RIGHTS OF ANIMALS. Sir,—May I draw your readers' attention to the following illuminating sentence in Dr. Manson's letter? —" The Royal Commission on Tuberculosis decided, so far as this country was concerned, that a large amount of tuberculous disease in children was directly due to tuberculous milk." Kcch decided that "so far as Germany was concerned" this was an impossi- bility, and yet tuberculous cows exist in both countries, and the inhabitants of both, drink germ- infested milk. While such differences of opinion exist, arising from identical experiments on animals, I contend that better results would accrue from a distinction between sick cows and healthy cows than from one between germ-containing milk and non- germ-containing milk. It is possible to look so long and earnestly through a microscope that you cannot see an elephant at your elbow. Dr. Maueon thinks that Anti-Vivisectionists have a function to perform, and it is that of "making the orthodox examine the grounds of their beliefs and prove their contentions." He has furnished us with a laudable ambition, but, alas! it is his own party who frustrate it. For the Research Defence Society is conspicuous for making assertions without proving them, and the more we controvert their obvious errors,' with the greater alacrity do they run away to fresh assertions and leave the grounds of the old ones unexamined. This can easily be proved in the pub- lished controversies between Dr Hadwen and Mr Stephen Paget which I shall be happy to supply to any enquirer. To suppose that milk is dangerous in which the tubercle bacillus is so sparsely distributed (if, indeed, it be there at all) that it cannot be detected under the aiicroseope shows an attitude of mind to which Florence Nightingale alluded in the words, " The disease germ fetish and the witchciaft fetish are the products of the same mental condition." In Jersey, where tuberculosis in cattle is practically unknown— so much so, indeed, tnat cattle from the island can be I imported into the United States without having under- gone the tuberculin test—the percentage of tuberculosis in human beings is as high as it is in this 1 country. In conclusion, may I protest against Dr. Manson's charge of "misrepresentation " OD account of a sentence from Sir Frederick Treves which is. quoted i by Anti-vivisectionists to prove exactly what t says and nothing else? It is a sentence absolutely independent of context. It is not a quotation of opinion but of fact —natuely, that Sir Frederick Troves was gravely misled on his own confession, by experi- ments on animals.—Yours etc., BEATRICE E. KIDD. Secretary British Union for the Abolition of Vivisection.

div.head: WYCLIFFE PASTORATE.
div.p: WYCLIFFE PASTORATE.
ACCEPTANCE BY THE REV. T. T. JAMES, M.A.

The members of Wycliffe Church and congr.gation are to be congratulated upon having, with the least possible delay, secured a successor to the Rev. John Yonge, who retired from the pastorate in June last, after a long and honoured ministry, extending over thirty-six years. A fortnight ago a call was extended to the Rev T T James, M.A. of Wycliffe Chapel, Sheffield, and on Sunday the gratifying news was received from Mr James that the invitation had been accepted. Mr James hopes to begin his ministry in Warrington in February next, and a cordial invitation is extended to all Wycliffe friends, old and new, to co-operate in making this 'new era in the history of the church a happy and prosperous one. Mr James comes to Warrington with an excellent record. Intellectually strong, he is an eloquent preacher and rarely uses a note in the pulpit. He is a hard worker in all kinds of religious activity. His Institutional Church work in Sheffield has been very successful. He is also a great favourite with the young people, and his talks with the little ones are much enjoy ed. Mr. James is 36 years of age, and is the third son of the Rev. Alfred James, who was for 29 years minister of the Humberstone-road Congregational Church, Leicester, and is at the present time Nonconformist Chaplain at the Leicester Royal Infirmary. His early education was received at the school for the sons of Congregational Ministers at Catenharn, Surrey, and at the Wyggeston school, Leicester.
In 1894 he entered the Lancashire Independent College, Manchester, winning the Woodward scholar- ship. Four years Liter he graduated at the Victoria University at Manchester in the Honours School of
History. In 1900 he passed the examination of the Theological Senatus, being placed second in the first division.

Leaving College, he filled with great acceptance for five years the position of warden for the Lancashire College settlement at Hulme, and in January 1907 he commenced his ministry at Sheffield. In addition to his pastoral duties Mr James has for some years held the position of Examiher in Religious knowledge to the Sheffield Education Committee. He is also Hon. Secretary and President elect of the Sheffield and District Brotherhood Federation, member of Sheffield district Executive of Yorkshire Congrega- tional Union, member of Lancashire College Com- mittee, and Hon. Secretary of Lancashire College Old Students' Association.

Mr James has been greatly assisted in his work by his wife, to whom he was mar 'ed in January, 1907. Mrs James is the second dau ter of the late Rev 3 Horatio Johnes, an alumnu of Lancashire College, and minister for some years of the Congregational Church, Haslingden. Mr and Mrs James have one little daughter, three years of age. —. . . . .

The acceptance of he paatorate was made known at each service on Sunday, when the Secretary of the church (Mr. C. Eccles) read the following letter (which gave great satisfaction), to the congregation : Wycliffe Church, Sheffield, December 7th, 1912 Dear Mr. Eccles,—The invitation to the pastorate of the Wycliffe Church, Warrington, has had my earnest and deliberate consideration. 1 have felt horn the first that it demanded that both by reason of its unanimity, and of the steps which led the church to a decision. It has not been easy for me to find the answer, for my work and my church in Sheffield have become deeply imbedded in my life, and I have learned to love my people here. But, after much thought and prayer, I have come to feel that your invitation constitutes a call whi,cli I dare not disregard, and I accept it very heartily in the con- viction that this is the Divine will. I shall come to you in that assurance. I trust that God may grant us as minister and people a happy fellowship in the Gospel, and that we may discover, as time passes, an increasing joy in the service of Jesus Christ. I have not yet had the opportunity of conferring either with you or with my friends here as to arrangements in the immediate future, but I would suggest provisionally that my ministry should begin at Warrington on the first Sunday in February. With kindest regards yours very sincerely, t. T. JAMES." .The "Sheffield Telegraph" and the "Sheffield Independent " make the following references to the Rev T T James' departure. • LEAVING FOIL WARRINGTON.

The Rev T T James, M.A., who for six years has carried on a most successful ministry at the Wycliffe Congregational Church, Langsett-road, is leaving for Warrington. People and pastor have got on well together, and the church has prospered under his care. The " call " to Warrington, however, has left him no alternative. He will leave Sheffield at the end of January. Great regret is felt here at the prospect of his removal.
THE REV T T JAMES RESIGNS HIS SHEFFIELD CHARGE.

The Rev T T James, M A., of Sheffield, has announced his intention of accepting the pastorate of the Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington. Speaking to his Wycliffe Chapel congregation on Sunday the Rev. gentleman said it had been an exceedingly diffi .ult question for him to decide, but after long and tarefui consideration he had been led to feel that this was the right thing for him to do. He had to thank all his friends at Wycliffe for their unbroken love and loyalty. The relationship between minister and people in that church was of a par- ticularly happy nature. To his deacons he owed a deep debt of gratitude. It had been a hard task to contemplate the severance of such ties, and it would be a real wrench to lay down his work there, but he would do so in the belief that whatever success had been given them during their years together, there were still greater things before the church in the future. He expected to close his ministry in Sheffield at the end of January.
REV. T. T. JAMES, M.A.

div.head: TED MILK
div.p: TED MILK
LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
DEBATE ON WOMENS' SUFFRAGE.

Thursday evening's meeting at the Parliamentary Debating Society was devoted to a discussion on '• Womens Suffrage" introduced by Miss Withering- ton. There NiBS a gcod sprinkling of the fair sex pre- sent and the debate was thrown open to members of the public. After a lengthy hearing of the pros and COOS of this much vexed question a vote vies taken and the SPEAKER (Mr Jas /Sall) declared the resolution carried.

In opening the debate Miss Witherington proposed the resolution " That the time had arrived when the Government must grant the franchise to women on the same terms as it is now cr may be in the future granted to men." She said opponents of the great. reform rarely attacked the principles which underlay it, but contented themselves by settling up imaginary difficulties, and prognosticating grievances and dinste, in the event of their just demands being conceded. The principle was justice and equal human rights and t'lere were many people, who did not understand what those demands really stood for. In the law cf divorce there was one standard for the men and another for the women. For one false step a man could obtain a divorce, but for a life of immorality a woman could not obtain a divorce unless the immorality was coupled with cruelty. Our legislators had not yet realised that the worst kind of cruelty was that which touched the human spirit and crushed the human s)ul. A Royal Commission bad reported on this matter, and ere long, legislation would be put into force to give woman equal rights in the matter of divorce. Was it right, fair, or just that the question should be settled without the women in the country having the power to use their direct influence. Their opponents would go into ecstasies about the indirect influence of woman, but when it came to using influence of a direct kind every- thing was then quite different. If the indirect influence was good, how much better would be the direct influence ! It WAS often said by anti-suffragists that WOMBIA place was the home ; but it was when they came to define what was home, that she parted company with her anti-suffragist friends. (Hear, hear). Home was ry spiritual idea ; the foundation was respect and the edifice love. Wherever there was suffering to be relieved and sorrow to be assuaged, there woman was at home in the work which was dear to every womans heart. Legislation had entered into their homes and it did not unsex women to pay rates and taxes, but when it came to calling the tune it was awful. (Laughter.) They were ready to use the women to do the drudgery of the world, yet when it came to having an effective say, she was debarred.
Mr F A JENKINS (Postmaster General) seconded the resolution.

Mr P DavaarrouT (President of the Board of Trade) moved the rejection of the resolution and endeavoured to explain the far-reaching effects of the enfranchise- ment of women The present electorate wag something like seven millions and if they passed adult suffrage they would increase the number to 20 or 22 millions. He agreed with the statement of Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman who in 1307 when speaking on Mr Dickinson's Bill said the measure would enfranchise only a small minority of propertied well-to-do single women and would not touch in any degree the mass of working women. In his opinion there was no right to vote. It was a duty, obligation and responsibility which had been put upon men who were qualified to undertake the duties attached to the obligation. He contended that women were physically unfit to carry out the duties which were imposed upon men by the vote. The interest of the great Empire would not be safeguarded by granting the vote to women. Miss STEVENSON who addressed the House from the public benches in favour of the resolution, said it was , not merely a question of votes for women but it meant it was a great human question.lf it were only a question of benefiting women they would not find the great women of the country fighting the battle. Great altera- tion had taken place in the industrial movement. It wag stated that woman's place was the home, but they must. remember that legislation had taken the industries out of the homes into the workshops of the world, and women had followed them there. It was ,the duty of the nation to bring up the legislation to the times in which they lived. It was in the interest of the men to give women the vote. At the present time there was a Bill before the Imperial House to grant adult suffrage. For such a measure there had been no demand on the part of the men, they were simply climbing in on the shoulders of the women. Objections had been made to the granting of the suffrage because of the militant , action, but she held that those people who only gave lip service and cheap sympathy were responsible for the militant tactics., Mr N NEILD (president of the Local Government Hoard) seconded the rejection of the resolution. He contended that the majority of the women did not really want the vote and the question to his mihd was only one of expediency. The outlook of the two sexes on industrialism Was absolutelY different. With woman work was only a temporary necessity, her hope was centred on marriage, but la the case of a man it was altogether different. The State looked to every man to aupport a family. Miss F DAVEY also spoke in favour of the resolution. She contended that women had been forced into the industrial world not on equal footing but as rivals of men. They desired labour to be paid for as labour, Irrespective of the question of sex and they demanded the vote on the same ground. If it were a duty andel obligation they were perfectly willing to share it the least the men could do was to let them share their burdens. It was only by grantiog the vote to women that they could expect to raise the wages of women workers Mr E A WHITE (Prime Minister), although opnegi" the resolution, said if it had been moved in a mere, modified form, he was not at all sure that he would pc": have supported it. He was a Conservative in 11". methods, and if a change was to be tried he preferred 11, gradual one. He deplored the militant tactics, to'" believed that if women as a whole wanted the vote Oa would get it. The reason tho subject was not moo: seriously considered was because the great majority et women did not want the vote. He agreed that them was a minority, a section of ;single women and wailer° who considered they were entitled to the vote. Wile: it came to giving women the franchise on the sail.);'. footing as men, there was a strong argument againgt , He believed it was a fact that there were more worae" than men in the country, and if adult suffrage he passed the whole force amuld be in the hands of 'id women because they were in the majority, and well be able to out-vote the men on all questions. vote Mr CHAMBERLAIN (Soc.), remarked that if the as was to be granted on the property qualification heicv_ he opposed to it, but if placed on a democratic baft:a.,,e, would support it. He was of the opinion that II 1",,,3 women who were so eager for the cause turned na of their energies into the industrial field, the emagc

potion of women would soon he brought about. Mr lirtousF (Nat, Dublin Harbour), was not in favour.of granting the franchise because he thought would take the women from the very place they thollght' she was more powerful in—the home. said Mr J JARMAN (Lib , Leader of the Oppositiofl). the argument had been raised that women if they oa. the vote would be swayed by sent'ment whilst men °ler governed by sheer logic. He thought it was more like that men would be governed by sheer beer. (Cries o " All ale." He believed if women as a wh°,le„ had the vote they would get the temperance (Pesti; settled in a more satisfactory manner than it was like to be at the present time. As far as the wages q and equal rights were concerned,there was something w be said for the man who had a home to keep together; because his responsibilities were larger than those °.!'„ single men and women. As to the unfitness of WOrrIll" in the realm of high (Mance he disagreed, believing that women were quite as capable as men from mathematical point of view. in winding up the debate Miss WITITERINGTON uestic!ri the fact that a member of the House could call a gr,"," spiritual movement like theirs foolish, was onq„ token of arrested development. Under the resoltlici,oo; if the vote were granted there would be ii" beir women enfranchised and for the benefit of t Socialist friends she would like to state that eight,"
per cent. would be working women. On a vote being taken the SPEAKER declared thet the . .

div.head: WARRINGTON NONCONFORMITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON NONCONFORMITY.
ITS 230th ANNIVERSARY

div.head: SUPPLEMENTARY CHAPTERS. An Episode of 1673.
div.p: SUPPLEMENTARY CHAPTERS. An Episode of 1673.

The various extracts given in our last two chapters from papers which belong to our local Nonconformity go to show that the Conventicle Act,though a severe measure, did not, in the early years of its operation, inflict much suffering upon Warrington Noncon- formists. Though ; a national measure for the extermination of Dissent it depended for its administration upon the justices and con- stables, and, as we have already written, neither the clergy nor the justices of Lancashire were disposed towards severity. Not so the loyal Sir Roger Bradsbaigh, Justice of the Peace, and pillar of the Royal cause. Did the Lord Lieutenant show himself apathetic? Then Sir Roger could provide zeal enough for two. Did the local constables frequent conventicles and screen the law breakers? Sir Roger had energy enough to track down both the transgressors and their abettors. When this famous Royalist died in 1684 (though it is much too soon in the story to anticipate his death) Samuel Shaw, the afterwards Rector of Warrington, wrote of him: Whats the surprise, whence is this mourning bred? Alas! the great, the good Sir Roger's dead. In loyall veins if 105,311 blood e'er ran, This was the man. And had the Virgin Church a true bred son, Then this was one. Tell not the loyall party this, lest they, Losing so strorg a fort, should fear betray, Conceal this mournfull seoce from just men's sight Lest feebled justice take a second flight. Yet even so untiring and resourceful a Justice as Sir Roger must often have felt lonely at his task of suppression. For the Nonconformists besides being people of uncommon courage, showed con- siderable ingenuity in evading the Con- venticle Act. Here is one little prescription that was duly reported by William Haggett to Sir P. Musgrave. (It will be remembered that the Act of 1664 made it an offence punishable by fine or transportation for five people besides the family to meet for worship.) They chase a convenient house where other houses are p-sty rancked on both sides and ye other side of ye streete pretty neare, there being noe more but four besides the speaker, they open there kasements on b-.th sides and on ye other sides of ye streete. And so hears him out from ye window. The constable who came to investigate and found himself getting the advantage of a sermon that echoed from a window along the alley would probably have endorsed the modern sentiment that a coach and four can be driven through any Act of Parliament. There was little need, however, for War- rington Nonconformists to study subterfuge. Did not Richard Radcliffe and Thomas Hall, two of the constables, come to Conventicle themselves, and did not Richard Nicholls with a house full of worshippers tell the lieu- tenant that he cared for neither him nor his warrant? But the day came when Sir Roger found a powerful ally in Warrington. An angry Rector joined with the Justice and a much less-happy period began. Of the cause of the Rector's our readers must form their own conclusions from a document we are about to quote. It appears to have broken forth not in the early years of the Conventicle Act but upon the withdrawal of King Charles' Declaration of Indulgence. The course of local events may be stated briefly. Driven from the town by the Five Mile Act Robert Yates returned in 1672 under the shelter of King Charles' Indulgence. His own house in Church-street was licensed for preaching and hp himself took out a license as preacher. But Rector Ward did not like to have the late Rector so close to him, even though the services were placed at different hours from those of the Parish Church. Out of regard for his wishes the Court House was licensed and the Nonconformists began to meet there, still avoiding the hours of the Rector's services. But Rector Ward complains yet again and changes his time of worship so as to make it simultaneous with that of the Court House. There is evidently strained feeling and when the Declaration is withdrawn smart persecution of Dissenters begins. We have no narrative to help us and all that can be done at this distant date is to collect the various fragments that have survived in court records and manuscripts. A very valuable side-light comes from a letter written in 1673 by Roger Kenyon, Clerk of the Peace. It will be remembered that when the Indulgence of 1672 was withdrawn, Dissenting meetings became illegal and the Conventicle Act again operated. Taking advantage of this the Rector and his friends begin an active campaign of persecution against the Nonconformists. We gather from the letter that a conviction has been made against the l'conventicklers," and fines have been imposed Upon them and also upon the owner of the barn in which the unlawful meeting was held. But the owner of the barn has died, and the clerk suggests that the £2O fine imposed on him might be raised by spending the amount over the other convicted ones. Here is the letter : The Clerk of the Peace to Sir R Bradshaigh con- cerning Conventicles at Warrington. Honoured Sir Roger The Bearer bath beene with mee for the warrants about Conventicklers at Warrington, which I have sent you by him Flee tells !nee the man who is Fyned as owner of the Berne was but a Poore man and is since his conviccion dead. Sir, as hee was a poore man you might assesse and Impose his Fine amongst the other that wears present soe as none of them exceed £2O; and this warrant goeing out as of the 20th of January, his being dead need not be taken notice off. He therettre (the Bearer) desires me to propose to you that that £2O which is for the owner of the Barns may be by Reason of his Poverty (for the conventicle of the 18th of Jan.) imposed upon Thomas Rizley of Woolston-cum Poulton, gen. £5 This gentleman (as the Bearer tells) is one that saith they will not desist Joshua Abraham, grocer £5 Samnell Leech, woolen draper £5 These 2 gave security to the owner of the Barna to save him harmless Richard Richardson, Ironmonger £2 10s. This is a rich man and the Clerke at tire Barns Richard Radcliffe, Innkeeper £2 103 He frequented the Barne all the while he was constable. For the Conventiokle the 28th December : John Marsh of Bolton, £5 This is a young attorney, son of the old Post Mr. of Preston. Henry Higginbotham of Salford, £5 A young rich man; his Father an ould sequestrator, £2 103. Richard Richardson (their Clerks), £2 10a. • Richard Radcliffe, Innkeeper, £2 10s. Robert Holbroke of Orford, ..-C2 10s. John Dunbabin of Great Sankey, £2 103. Sir,—lf you think fitt theose be thus put in I shall if 1 receive such direccion' make the warrant anew and send them and draw up the Reccord accordingly.—Sir your humble servant, ROGER KENYON. Peele, Feb. 13th, 1073-4,

For the Right Worp,ll Sir Roger Bradshaigh at Haigh, These present. The comments of the clerk upon the con- victed Nonconformists and their ability to pay the fine arevery interesting, especially the note upon Richard Radcliffe who "frequented the barne all the while he was constable. " The next thing revealed in the correspondence is that be was not the only constable with Nonconformist sympathies. When the fines were levied two out of the four constables declined to seize the goods of the Dissenters. Of course there was a dead- lock, as the two willing constables declined by themselves to execute the warrants. This drew from the Rector,Joseph Ward, an angry letter, of which the careful knight preserved a copy in his letter book. The Rector of Warington to Sir Roger Bradsbaigh. Honoured Sir, Leiutenant Grimsditch brought the warrants to distraine upon our Con- venticlers' goods sign'd and seal'd by your self, Mr Houghton and Mr Banister. These Two Constables are Ready and Willinge to Execute them according to order. But inasmuch as there be Two of there Brethern that hide thenselves, to Prevent (as they think) themselves from being concern'd. It is theirs Humble Request to your Worship that they may have a Warrant to cause them to come out to ther assistance or to direct them to some Course which they may be assisted Sir, the Insolencie of the dissenters in such that they Threaten highly and much contemne all the Authority that 13e5 in any or all Justices of Peace, so that, Sir, without some speedy Course they will bee growce to that Height that it will prove dangerous and difficulte to suppress them. Wherefore, I pray, favour us so farr as is tyme to grant as your ayd tux' direction, whereby yen will doe I-oth God and his Church and our couutrey respectable service,and oblige all honest hearts and him to pray for you who is, Hozored Sir, your mo3t affect friend and very humble servant,

div.head: JOSEFII WARD.
div.p: JOSEFII WARD.
Feb. 22nd, 1673. To this Sir Roger gives answer two days later:

Castleton, Feb. 24th, 1673. Sir, Beeing heare with Mr. Holt when I received yours I acquaint( d him therewith and it is both our Admiraciona that s e much Insolence should yet remaine after see much Clemency, especially by a person cf so much Judgment and Moderation as I tock Mr. Peake to be. But one may Geus the Rest by it. It is not proper to send a Warrant for the Two absconded Constables till you who Procured the Warrant have brought it to them or left it at their houses; which they doe not Execute it with the other then you may take it againe and deliver it to These two who are to Execute it at theire Perills, and the other Two Constables may be prosecuted for their Neglect by an Indictment at the next Sessions. And These Constables are to make a returne what distress they have taken and what the cannot Come at without breakeing open of doores, and then have a Warrant for that. In the meantime take notice of everie Conventicle that bath been since, that wee may Run them up to the 2nd 3rd or 4th offence and consequent), to the utmost Penalty of the Law; which I am sure the Lawe will justify° both the Justices, Informers and Constables in the Execution of. But praye also take notic3 of that part of the Act to goe to the Constables, Churchwarden or Overseer of the Poore, when you can truly Informe them of a Conventicle; and then if they doe not take notice of it and come to the next Justice for a Warrant against them, they Bunn another penalty. In the.meane tyme of this Post I shall Write to Coll. Kirkby, &c. er.d (have) this obstinate Insolence f thei a presented to the House of Commons,who no doubt will owne that noe Licence Can Protect them ; end I doe not doubt Lut (if they continue soe peremtory dangerous as to defie Govern- ment) t) have some of them sent for by a messenger to owne by what authority they do these things, for the House would be glad to find cut such promoters to eeditien. And I doubt not but such an Example as this will begett a more severe Lawe and suply of any defect in this, which they may thanke themselves and theire Brethren may thanke them for. Mr Hoult and others heare will Heartily Joyne with me, being sensible such proceedings pretend a Confidence they have of another Warr to defend them. This is all I have to say at present till a further , opertunity, wherein you may Command for the ' preservation of Peace in Church and State. IL B.
One other document from Sir Roger's book remains to copied. This is of the greatest interest and will give material for yet another chapter. (To be continued.) .
A.M. • A WOMAN'S LUCKY FIND.

A short time ago she would probably have laughed at the idea that she was on the eve of a lucky discovery which was to affect her whole future. She was the victim of the most agonising pains in the back and sides, and used to experience a dreadful hearing down feeling impcssible of description. div.head: Local Teachers and Headships.
div.p: Local Teachers and Headships.

A general meeting of the Warrington and District Teacher's Association was held on Saturday morning , in the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings, Mr F J Emson ' presiding over a large attendance of members. The Secretary (Mr F Longshaw) reported that the replies received from the various loral candidates for muni- cipal honours at the last election had, with one excep- tion, been satisfactory. The question asked was, "Are you in favour of restricting headships in Warrington schools tO local teachers ? " Mr J Arm- strong gave a report of the proceedings of the last meeting of the Lancashire County Association of Teachers. It was decided to supput the candidature of Mr W B Steer, of Derby, for the c ffice of vice- president of the NUT., and of Messrs Pearson (Liverpool), Sharpies (Manchester), Alcott (Great Harwood), Hudson (Salford), and Miss Wood (Man- chester) for the executive, Lancashire district. The following were appointed to represent the association at the annual conference next Easter at Weston- super-Mare : Messrs J Upson, F II Longsbew, A Malcolm, J Cann, G Newburn, and the Misses Orton and Upson. Nine new members were proposed, and the association is now very strong indeed numerically.

MR. URE AND WIDNES LIBERALS. The progressive Young Liberal League of the Widnes Division has been fortunate to procure Mr Alexander Ure, K.C., M.P., Lord Advocate of Scotland, as president for next year. The learned gentleman has notified his acceptance by letter, also stating that he will address a meeting of Liberals in Widnes during the coming year.

SPOHR'S "LAST JUDGMENT."

From Monday's strange mixture of rabid Soc ialism and music to Thursday's night's oratorio at the Parish Church is because of the musical associations an easy transition enough. I have heard the "Last Judgment" annually for the last twenty years or ro, and I am glad to think that, notwithstanding the sneers of superior persons who have apparently no further use for either Spohr and Mendelssohn, the work is growing in popular favour. In matters of musical taste and art in general, we continue to make steaiy progress; as to these things, indeed, many of our Nonconformist churches are breaking awayfrom the bad old traditions handed down from a spiritual ancestry that, with all its excellences, did protest too much. I rejoice, therefore, in the more widespread recognition of the function of music in the service of the church. Surely it is well 1 to employ everything that art can cffer in order to make the worship of God as perfect and imprrssive and as striking to the ear and eye, as it possibly can be. As long as these externals do not really come between the worshipper and the object cf supreme adoration, one is bound to employ all the gifts with which he is endowed in making his act as perfect and beautiful as may be. I heard a clergyman make this claim at a performance of the " LastlJudgment " only on Sunday last, and I for ore cheerfully concede it. Nhether many readers of this paper will agree with it, I know not; but I am a free lance, and editorial acquiescence is not here involved —what I mean i that the opinions expressed in this column are my own simply and that nobody else is in any way answerable for them.
