div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
NEGLECTED REGISTERS.

The cccurrence of the phrase "crumbling volumes" in " A.M.'s "latest contribution respecting Warrington Nonconformity reminded me of an experience of my own while compiling a local history. I had reason to examine the parish registers very minutely, and I found them so dilapidated that hardly two consecutive leaves bung together, and even single pages were torn. They were most interesting and valuable records, but those responsible for their preservation did not seem to realise this, so I ventured to call public atten- tion to the scandal with the result that the books were placed in the bands of an expert and skilfully and , very substantially repaired. I mention the matter heie in view of the possibility of local parallel. If any reader happens to know of a similar instance hereabout, he would :ender good service by reporting it with the object of speedy remedy. Permanent and irreparable injury has been caused in the past by the carelessness and ignorance of persons having charge of parish registers. THE DISTRICT NURSES.

Surely Councillor 11. Roberts' " ambition " to see £2,000 invested on behalf of the Warrington District Nursing Association is not of the "vaulting " kind which "o'er-leaps itself." I think that for co populous a centre it is very modest indeed, and it ,‘ mild be a grave reflection up-'n the place to suggest

that the estimate were an unrealistic dream. In oue corner of a West Riding district in which I formerly worked there is a small borough of 25,000 inhabitants where a nursing institution has been recently estab- lished, and the committee have cal!ed for a capital sum of £2,500, and already appear to be in a fair way of obtaining it. Come, Warrington, play up ! The heal Association has abundantly justified its exist- ence ; it is economically managed, and the excellent work of the admirable nurses must by this time be " known and read of all men " hereabout. THE OLD MISTAKEN WAY.

May I for a moment revert to the current articles on Warrington Dissenters in the bygones? Last week the writer told how the Bishop used to deal with Sabbath breakers. I have in my possession a copy cf a justices warrant against such an offender who, in default of paying the fine imposed was actually sent to gaol for a month for refusing to attend service at his parish church ! This occurred well within living memory, for the document is dated 1810! One need not go very much farther back in ecclesiastical history for reliable records of shameful public penance imposed upon women convicted of certain violations of moral law. TOO LITERAL.

Last week's story in the "Children's Corner "I brought to my mind one or two othlrs which I lately had at first hand fr.( m the teachers in whose classes they originated. The ycung ladies in question are in charge of five-year-old children—one at Haslingden and the other in the " Holy Name" school in Man- chester. As the former put it to me, in such cir- cumstances one has to resort to various devices to secure the youngsters' attention, and lately, having to give a nature lesson, she produced some srecitnens of the horse chestnut, and solemnly assuied the children that if they were quite still and listeced intently, these would speak to them would " say all kinds of things to them, and tell them such beautiful stories." Having distributed the specimens, she pro- ceeded in simple language to give the botanical lesson—in short, to interpret the horse chestnut's beautiful sterT. The order in that class was wonder- ful for a while ; then a little fellow rose in his place and in evident distress exclaimed : " Please, teacher, mine's not talking to me !" Naturally, she was inwardly convulsed ; but controlling her features with a supreme effort, she told the aggrieved kiddie it must have been " because he wasn't listening." Though plainly unconvinced, he had no alternative but to sit down again. Thenceforward, however, the dis- appointed young sceptic eyed his chestnut with evident misgiving not unn.ingled with disgust; and there is reason to fear that his teacher's" fairy tales" do not now appeal with quite the old force to this particular juvenile. A LITTLE DIVERSION.

In the other case, the perplexed teacher, well-nigh at her wits' end for some means of momentary relief, asked her restless class if one of them could sing a song or part of a song, adding that any such might forthwith stand up and proceed with the contribution, the prize for the best being either an apple or some " cboes," Some pretty keen competition ensued. After a couple of other "turns," one little chap who had seemed very eager to get his chance, jumped up and startled his teacher by piping out—
" If a man kisses another man's wife, And goes and tells his brother, He ought to have his tonsils cut, He ought to have his tonsils cut, He ought to have his tonsils cut Before he kisses another!"

Of course the teacher was shocked by the more than questionable morality of these sentiments from so small a boy. At the same lime, the peculiar mode of punishment proposed to be inflicted upon one who is unable to keep his own counsel respecting his doubtful osculatory exercises appealed irresistibly to her sense of humour, and she subsequently took the proud possessor of the precious fit-bit aside, and rescued it horn unmerited oblivion. " CAS EY."

- I am not a Socialist nor a labourist in the mcderb and restricted meanings of these much-abused terms, but I have always had a sort of sneAring admiration or ‘` Casey," who was at the Co-operative Hall on Monday. Many of his contributions to the weekly organ of the party under whose auspices he appeared in Warrington are written in lighter vein than the generality of the articles in that journal, and are genuinely humorous. And then there is his beloved violin. I write from memory, but I think it is Edwin Waugh who somewhere says that "a mon as plays a fiddle well should ne'er awse to den," and " Casey" undoubtedly plays that instrument very well in deed. Years have passed since I heard him, but I _have not

div.head: CASEY.
div.p: CASEY.
THE WANDERING MINSTREL OF SOCIALISM.

Who is Casey? The queAion would doubtless be asked by many Warringtonians who read that the possessor of that euphonious name would give his famous lecture and 1, iulin recital" in the Co-opera- tive Hall last Monday evening. An "Examiner " reporter sought out Casey before he faced his audience at d found him quite willing to chat about himself and his mission in life. In the first place "Casey" is a pseudonym. Its owner's real name in this case is Walter Hampson and he describes himself as the wandering minstrel of Socialism. "I all a dealer in concord, not in discard" he remaiked, and those who have fallen under the spell of his music testify that the saying is true. Casey is a homely, companionable type of man ; in his face are blended the dreaminess of the artist and the shrewdness of one who has rubbed shoulders with some cf the hardest phases of life. Be is steeped in music; his violin is his greatest treasure and he is never so happy as when playing the masterpieces of master minds for the edification of the common people. Casey plays only the best and—what is as surprising as it is encouraging - he finds that it is appreciated, even in these days of the light and trashy. He told our representative that he was brought up as a chimney sweep but, by dint of much dfort la his very limited lei •ure time, he gradually drifted into music as a profession. Ho also cultivated advanced democratic opinions which led him to "foist himself," as he put it, upon the Socialist movement. Since then he has striven incessantly to imbue the workers with a craving for the ideal and attistic and in his lectures he points out what, in his view, is the way to attain higher things. " Socialism " he said "does mean more beauty in life. We contend that the present system of over-work and machine-methods, slum dwellings and squalid conditions arc absolutely fatal to true art. People are divorced from the artistic by their trying conditions of toil and the multiplication of shoddy articles, which such men as William Morris so drastically condemned. Michael Balling, the new conductor of the Halle- concerts, recognizes that those who promote such high-class enterprises do not, in reality, reach the people, and be is trying to bring about a revolution, as far as Manchester is concerned." Vs

" And what is your object ? " queried the reporter. "I am out" said Casey "to give men, women and children a happy time. 'The wailings of politicians do not worry me at all. I don't say that they are not doing something that is absolutely necessary— I know the present system is bad—but I cannot do it myself. I am doing the work I like—that is, lam Socialising my music." Casey has known the grip of the " wander lust." He has played all over the world, from Bow and Bromley to Brazil, from Ireland to Iceland. Asked how he was generally received by the workers of the United Kingdom, he said he was welcomed everywhere, but he found the Welsh people particularly responsive. Casey is a writer as well as a musician. Next to playing the violin, he finds penning its praises the most congenial of occupations, and he is at present engageth on a volume of random recollections.

In his lecture on Monday evening Casey tald his audience that he is one of the "soundest " men in the Socialist movement, because sound is his economic basis. In a delightfully interesting way he traced the history of music from the old folk song to the modern composition,and showed the uplifting effect of music upon life in general. Treating art in its broadest sense, he argued that the artists of the past were the serfs of the rich, for even Shakespeare and other great writers of the time had to dedicate their most wondrous works to "my lord" and " my lady." The musicians of the past were also com- pelled to travel from court to court and castle to castle singing the praises of the aristocracy and of the quality known as chivalry. The consequence was that art was not entirely untrammelled. Men like &filet and Dickens had eliminated the element of patronage from art and literature by pictming and voicing the humble lot of the poor, and depicting life as it was actually lived by the masses. In music, t^o, we were in the midst of democracy, The majority of great musicians were brought up in poor surround- ings, and led lives of suffering and privation. Men like Verdi, the son of a baker, and Dvorak, the son of a butcher, had sprung from the ranks of the people and voiced their feelings and aspirations. The lesson of lecture was that no-one counted for anything who did not do something useful, whf ther with pen or pick. The idler should have no place in a community where every- body should be doing something for the world's good.

div.head: CRIPPLED GIRLS' FLORAL EXHIBITION.
div.p: CRIPPLED GIRLS' FLORAL EXHIBITION.
PRETTY SCENE AT THE PARR HALL.

In bleak December, when gardens are desolatd and denuded of flowers, it is as refreshing as it is novel to find oneself, cia entering the Parr Hall, surrounded by all manner of blooms in rich profusion. Roses, chrysanthemums, lilies, violets, primroses—in fact almost every variety of English fhwer that one could mention—make up a mass of beautifully harmonising colours which delight the eye. Only on close inspection does the visitor realize that he or she is not gazing upon Nature's actual handiwork. In every respect, save sweetness ofiscent, these flowers realize the charms of the original. How came they here ? They are the work of the poor blind and crippled gills who, but for the noble efforts of the John Groom Crippleage and Flower Girls' Mission, would have no definite pur- pose in life and would oft-times be a burden to poorly circumstanced parents. By training them to make artificial flowers, the mission enables the girls to play a useful part in the world's work and to become self-supporting. The skill and industry of these afflicted girls, once they have been instructed how to turn their talents to account, are remarkable. At the Parr Hall exhibition, which closes to-night, a contingent of deft-fingered workers is busily engaged in producing el:nice blooms and, watching them, one cannot but be impressed with the truly philanthropic motives inspiring the founders and helpers of this institution which gives the maimed and helpless a new outlook on life. The scheme of decoration is most picturesque—floral pyramids and arches, trellis work and banging briskets being arranged with perfect artistic (fleet.

There was a large and representative attendance at the opening of the exhibition by Mrs Henry Greenell on Monday afternoon. Mr Roger C Parr presided and there were also on the platform : Mr Alfred Groom, of London (son of Mr John A Groom, secretary and founder of the mission); Mr Alfred Trongbton (exhibi- tion manager), London ; the Revs E C e Carleton, James Collins, B Percival, J H 0 Hollingworth, H Ogden and W Reid, Alderman Smethurst, Mr James Whitley and Mr J B Starkey. The CHAIRMAN expressed his entire sympathy with the work of that old-established and well-deserving institution, which was founded in the year 1866 by the late Earl of Shaftesbury,and had since been ministering to the wants of the poor, blind and crippled, who were unable to take their position in the world like other girls. Unfortunately, when the; were afflicted in this sad way they might he considered a burden to their belongings, and it was then that this institution came forward and tried to render them self-supporting. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was sure they all greatly appreciated the energies of those who were devoting their lives to the betterment of the condi- tions of these poor girls. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. ALFRED GROOM then gave an interesting reaumd of the work of the mission, pointing out that it origin- ated in an effort to help the women and girls who were selling flowers and watercress in the streets of London. He referred to the interest of the late Earl of Shaftes- bury, who became the first president cf the mission and proved a real and valued friend to those whose welfare it sought to promote. That branch of the work was still being carried on, with greater success than ever In Loudon there were no fewer than six centres where these flower girls met from week to week, and where everything that was possible writs dme to make their lives 131I;ht and happy. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had an orph Image at Clacton-on- Sea, where they accommodated no little children, irrespective of creed, age or physical infirmity. No votes, payment or iufluence were necessary to secure admission ; the child whose need was the greatest had the first consideration. That was his father's rule. (App'ause.) They were kept until they were 15 years of age and the majority were provided with situations as domestic servants, and even after they had left tho institution an oversight was kept of them. Touching upon the work among the cripples, Mr Groom said every flower in that hall had been made in the Crippleage either by a blind or by a crippled girl, and these were gathered from all parts of the kingdom. He did not want people to imagine that the girls were waifs and strays. They came of most respectable parents who, however, were too poor to bear the burden of an idle child. The girls came to the homes helpless but as a result of their training they became self-supporting. (Applause.) There were many glorious institutions in the landwhich helped cripples to relieve the monotony of life, but this was the only institution which sought to help them permanently, and which I tried to make a business for them. Let it be clearly understood that theirs was not a sweated industry. Girls who had only one hand could make 103' ' 12s or 149 per week and he thought that was a proof that the rate of pay must be good. (Applause). One of the crippled girls then banded to Mrs Greenall a basket of beautiful artificial flowers.

MIS GREENALL said the institution; was one of the most far-reaching and humane which could possibly exist. These girls, who were handicapped in the race of life, were able to compete with their store fortunate sisters, thanks to the instruction which was given to them in the mission. It had been shown that all were welcome. There was no denominational difference, and every grade of society, as long as people were respectable, received a hearty welcome. The girls when they left could not fail to be brighter, more lively and more robust aryl most of them went away with a trade at their finger ends. Surely that was a great help 'to them ! (Hear hear, and applause). It spoke volumes for the manage- ment of the mission that hundreds of these girls were able to earn their own living instead of being dependent upon their parents who were probably unable to main- tain them and at the same time to provide then with the necessary medical assistance. The reason why they were taught to make flowers was because the work was elevating, light and interesting. She was sure they would all agree with her when she slid they gave a very hearty welcome to the girls on their visit to Warring- ton, and thanked the management for the good they were doing. She wished them the beet of luck in their efforts. (applause). On the motion of the Rev JAMES COLLINS, seconded by the Rev B PERCIVAL, Mrs Greenall and Mr Parr were warmly thanked for their services. div.head: CORNER, CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
div.p: CORNER, CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.
WILD ANIMALS AT PLAY,

It comes as anew idea to us to think that wild animals may turn out to play. They all seem so serious that the idea of them having play hours is curious to us. But in a lecture given in London by Mr E Setar Thompson I have just been reading some interesting things about the wild creatures of the fields and woods. _

Ask some old game-keeper said the lecturer. " Whether he has not seen the animals in the woods congregate for a regular play-time and he will tell you things worth knowing." It seems that the merry game of " King of the castle" is quite a passion among badgers. One gamekeeper told Mr 'Thompson how badgers used to gather every night round an old tree stump and one mounted to the top the others would snap at his tail or hind legs and pull him down. Then another would mount in his place and the game would be played for a long time without any ill- feeling. But foxes are not particularly sociable. however intellectual they may be. In winter nights they will meet when the moon is shining and just sit in a big circle look- ing at each other. It is a sort of Quakers' meeting, and when this begins to get , monotonous one gets up and walks with dignity into the centre, his tail stuck out behind and the fur round his throat puffed out importantly. At all these council meet- ings the same thing happens, Whoever has the ear of the house utters his message in sharp sentences—" chir-chir "—and retires to make room for another until closing time is

announced. But birds are more highly developed socially than animals and nothing pleases a grouse like the sound of a drum. Some birds reared by the lecturer used to begin a sort of cake-walk on a big tin tray under the stove whenever they felt happy. They simply loved to hear their little feet thump the tin, and if he drummed with his fingers on the furniture down would go their wee heads and up would go their wee tails and they would be at it like professionalso, He had also watched them make a ballroom of a small mound and keep up a giddy whirl for two hours. _ _
This love of the drum, says Mr. Thompson, goes right through nature. Every animal is infected with it.' _ _

But there is one thing that the learned lecturer could not make up his mind about. When as,dog hears music and puts his nose in the air to moan, he cannot tell whether tbe creature is pleased or sorrowful. No more can we. We gave that puzzle up long ago.

A COLONEL AND CHURCH SUBSCRIPTIONS. Colonel GI W Treble, C.M.G., commander of the 7th Battalion (Colne Valley) West Riding Regiment, opening a bazaar at All Saints', Micklehurat, Wesley, OD Saturday, said he thought church people should subactihe a little more to their churches. They paid annual subscriptions to their clubs without hesitation, but they did not pay annually to their church. The more wealthy among church people ought certainly to pay annual subscriptions to keep the church going, and the poorer people ought to pay weekly. Unless they got some system, they must raise the money by bazaars

The Examiner, Saturday, December 14, 1912
LAW. EitiflTl3 RICISSRVED.I
ME ROYAL HUNTER.
BY HUME NISBET,
Author ef "Ball lip," "The Swampers,' Thu Reverige of Valerie," "A Colonial Tramp," " Where Art Begins," 4ke.

lam a earisian by birth. Singularly modest, and truth-loving, yet brave, adventurous, and chivalrous, as the majority of my talented countrymen are. When young, I was considered one of the handsomest and most fascinating of Frenchmen. Need I add that being thus considered in -my own country gave me the right, without undue vanity, to challenge the world of connoisseurs in masculine beauty. lam old now, though still stately and well-preserved, therefore I dare de. scribe *self without fearing ridicule. Frenchmen have no need for that mock modesty which is so disgusting in Englishmen. We have proved our masterly qualities, in War, Art, Literature, and Fashion. We can fold air hands, twirl our moustaches, and smile Com- placently at all spiteful criticism. Ha! We have a hundred good reasons to be proud of the generous soil from which we have sprung. But this is digression, and what I have to re- late is so astonishing that you might well doubt its veracity, only for this personal assurance of my honourable nature. I have seen. I have ex- perienced. I have endured. Enough! Who doubts my relation after this must be prepared to exchange cards and cross blades with me.

Behold 'me this evening, my friends, at sixty- five years and four months. You say, "Not so had, old fellow. Stiff in the back, and upright; full-chested, and steady on the legs; a long way. from the foot of the hill yet." Just so, comrades. Now imagine what kind of fellow I wan at twenty-five. I desire you all to do so for a particular reason which you will know presently—a fatal reason. These charms, which Nature had gifted me with so lavishly, besides winning the devotions of a beautiful woman, re- vived a ruthless jealousy which had lain dormant for centuries. Please change my snowy tresses to the sable hue of the raven. Restore the lustre of my faded eyes. Reduce by twenty-five inches my waist, and brighten the complexion which has grown dull by forty years of regret and—de- votion to the table—and you may realise what I was when I first met my fate, the beautiful Ashtaroth. Alas! when a man has loved and lost, if he survives the cruel stroke, he becomes a gambler or a bon vivant. The green baize- covered table never attracted me, therefore I found suremse at the other.

_ I am not tall, as you can see. Tall men, like tall women, are ungraceful and stupid. The proper height for wit and perfection are five feet six inches in man, five feet four inches in woman. These were my inches exactly. Enough! Now let us proceed.

Endow' ed with a EtiElciency of fortune to make me independent of drudgery', I devoted my energies and leisure to the study of dead races. Egypt; and Assyria enthralled me, and I became an expert in archeology. I left France and wandered among the ruins of Egypt and Assyria, ending more pleasure in deciphering the hieroglyphics of the Pharoahs and the cuni- form characters of the Babylonians than I have done since over the choicest masterpiece of our Parisian. chefs.

- When i-Wiurned after four years' travel,, I brought with me many relies to adorn the walls of my room, after I had given my contribu- tions to the museums. One piece of bas-relief I kept to myself, and had inserted into the wall above my dining- room mantel. I did this partly for its intrinsic qualities, for it was a beautiful example of Assyrian carving, which I had managed to con- vey intact to Europe; and, what was rarer, the colouring still remained fairly fresh upon it. But my chief reason for retaining it with me lay in the fact that while I 'flati managed to read the bulk of the inscriptions, one word alone puzzled me. That single word stood apart from the other characters, and was more deeply cut and most peculiar in its formation. This fascinated me, and kept my curiosity on tiro quji. vive.

It represented a royal hunting scene, with two figures in it, these of the king and hia charioteer. The king stood bow in hand, as lie had discharged his arrow. Three arrows still re- mained in the quiver at his shoulder. The charioteer stood on the ground, holding the heads of the horses. It was an exquisite piece of work, and as I had unearthed it from an underground chamber never before exposed to the light of day or the atmosphere, the in- cisions were sharply defined, and the colouring marvellously fresh. The painted eyes of the king were vivid, and the gold, purple, and blue tints on hie robe singularly brilliant. It gave mo an exquisite pleasure to sit and watch the picture. At times also it seemed to enthral me in a curious fashion. That deep, sombre eye looked at me and ap- peared to follow me with a slumberous, haughty staro wherever I sat. The charioteer also was a sinister personage, who seemed to have turned his head and fixed me with his watchful

I had at this time begun my great work, not yet quite finished. The manual labour disgusted me, therefore I advertised for an assi‘stant who had some knowledge in this particular line of research. ^. My test conditions were rather severe, therefore the applicants for the post were limited in number, and nearly all unsatis- factory. One day, however, I received an answer to my advertisement in pretty feminine Italian handwriting on perfumed notepaper. The pen- manship of ladies in my youth was not the characterless, back-handed, coar6o vrawling it has since become, but dainty and light as threads of gossamer.

The chara'cter of the writing charmed me at sight. The perfume, strange and penetrating, intoxicated me, and set me dreaming of the dead past. Ninevah and Babylon in their van- ished splendour rose before me like glorious el. halation. •resolved to see the author of that magical letter. The following day Ashtaroth came to my appointment and answered my questions in a manner that filled me with much wonder for her erudition, as the exquisite loveliness filled me with admiration—nay, not admiration, bet a sudden and passionate Jove, such as only a Frenchman can experience. I took her soft, small hand, and looked into her fathomless, dark eyes, and immediately I was her slave for ever. Need I add, that I engaged her without asking for references or stipulating terms? I am a true son of Gaul. Ashtaroth was the most lovely woman I had ever looked upon. That .was sufficient for me. . . .

^She was dark-skinned, but radiant in colour- ing like a glowing flower. Her features were delicate and classic; her form divine. Her man- ners were bewitching; while the same delightful perfume stole from her as had intoxicated me when reading her letter. Her costume, also, was perfect. Several weeks passed in the most delightful commune-4110 sweet. blending of arehreology and ardent tenths/mess. Every hour drew our hearts and souls more closely together, until there was no longer any disguise. She adored me, as most women did when I be, stowed upon them my attentions, while I felt that at last I had met my fate. Ashtaroth was a specialist, and her speciality was Assyrian lore. Egyptology did not greatly interest her, although she was a passable scholar here also. Her intuition in deciphering the cuniform signs startled me in its unfailing promptitude and exactness. It was as if she translated her native language for my benefit. .

My curios' y was keenly roused to jearn her history; but she either could not, or would not, inform me respecting her nationality and parentage. All she told me was that her parents were Persians, and that her name, Ashtaroth, had been that of her mother. She had been taken from her native land when a child, after the death of her mother, and educated by a Russian lady. This patroness of her's having to fly for political reasons from Russia, had brought her to Paris, where for the past years they had lived in reduced retirement. Ashtaroth was alone now, and, with the exception of myself, her new friend, absolutely without an acquaint- ance. As for her Assyrian knowledge, she told me that this came naturally to her. she always felt at home in museums. I am a man of decisions, as Napoleon was, and honourable as I am truthful. Ashtaroth suited me exactly, and I had no one to consult respecting my domestic arrangements. Within ten days of our friendship I had offered my hand and heart to this incomparable woman, and was accepted with devotion and gratitude. The hours now became winged. My great book was shelved for the present, while we yielded ourselves to love and pleasure. We arranged to be married in a fortnight's time, and while Ash- taroth prepared for the great event, we enjoyed the interval like happy children. Now comes the amazing, the horrible, the fatal part of my story. Ashtaroth had examined the coloured bee. relief over soy dining-room fireplace, and con- firmed my own reading of the letters. But the single word puzzled her as it had done me. dream about it constantly," she said. "The Royal Hunter comes to me nightly, and speaks it. but as yet I cannot remember when I wake. Oh, Alphonse, I am frightened for that Assyrian king. His eye is filled with jealous hate when it looks at me in my dreams." The lovely creature hid her face on my breast as she told me this one night, three days previous to our intended marriage. We had finished a most recherche dinner, and felt tegder ympattivtio consequenco, J

quiver. remorseless, r,trong,,P and beardcd profile faced us, while the slave stretched his arm and pointed us out. For the moment I could not move. The weight of a dreadful nightmare was on roe. I could only wait and watch. . .

Once more the arrow was fitted, the bow drawn out and the string let go. Once more I saw the arr3w disappear, leaving one only in the quiver, then the pain struck me in the thigh. I vas wounded again, and had the sen- sation of a rock hitting me. But Ashtaroth was yet safe. fi she uttered no sound. Rapidly .1 took her in my arms and rolled with her to another part of the hall. We lay this time near the front door. If we could escape that last shaft, I felt we should be, safe. Where we now were the sculpture was hiddet from me, but from the open door spread a broad line of light across the hall. I watchtd that open door with abject and torrid horror. Suddenly the stream of light became broken, and to my amazement I saw the charioteer standing in the hall, with a fiendish grin on }li face and his arms outstretched, pointing o';0 place of refuge to the avenger inside. "Quick, Aslitaroth," I shouted, rising my feet, and dragging her to another pla.l, Too late. As I rose the charioteer disap. peared, while my love gave one shrill scream and then lay supinely in my arms. The last in. risible arrow had sped and slain her,

A mad rage now 'seized me. Lifting the warm corpse of my betrothed in my arms, I bore her into the dressing-room and laid her on the couch. Then I faced the accursed Assyrian piece of teulpture. It was the same as before, only the quiver" was now empty. The Royal Hunter had used his last shaft, and my darling lay dead before me. Dead, and seemingly with. out a wound.

_ Furiously I pulled at the hell until my valet And housekeeper appeared. Then I said: "Bring me a large hammer, Hortense, and Henri, run for the doctor." Before the doctor appeared I had broken that rare piece of sculpture into a thousand atoms ro demolish the ruthless face of that royal mur lerer gave me exquisite pleasure. I hammered him into minute fragments. When the physician arrived and had exa. mined my betrothed, he pronounced it to be r •:•ase of heart disease. S,onie sudden shock had 7mished up the poor girl, and, with this ver dict, he departed satisfied. But I know differently, for even to this day suffer from these wounds in my shoulder and thigh. At times I can feel, the arrow heads dia tinctly, where they rankle in my muscles, an I know too well that the third arrow head d the royal Assyrian hunter lies buried in tht iicart of the only woman who was worthy <A my love. _
ArKux

=flaked the perfumed tresses in my angel, as wit sat together on the couch and told her not to be afraid for I was there to protect her. Then I glanced defiantly at the bas-relief now lighted up by several wax candles. • It seemed to me that the painted eye of the king watched me fiercely, while the charioteer gazed also in our direction. Suddenly Ashtaroth sat up, disengaged herself from my embrace, and stared wildly at the sculpture. " I know the word now," she murmured. "He has said it again, and I remember it." She uttered a word in clear tones, as one speaks an invocation. I started Up amazed and horrified at the effect of that cabalistic word. _ .

A swarthy flush passed over the face of the king as it life was waking in him. The chari- oteer also made a distinct movement as if bend- ing his head to receive a command. With a' wild shriek of terror Ashtaroth sprang from the couch and fled towards the door. I also followed her quickly—to arm her retreat and protect her from this unknown danger. While she was fumbling at the door handle I saw the king raise his arm to his shoulder, draw one of the three arrows from his quiver, and St it quickly to the bow. Ashtaroth by this time had opened the door, and was in the lobby crouching in a 'dark corner and covering her face with her hands, when the arrow was launched frotn the bow in my direction. • _

I saw the bow strain and bend, then spring back to its former position as the arrow sped. But there was no twang, and no arrow came my way, yet I felt a sharp pain in my right shoulder as if it had been pierced; and as I koked. back, the .quiver only held two arrows. . .

Wildly I rushed over to where Ashtaroth was kneeling, and covered her with my body as a shield. Instinctively I understood that the rage af this king was directed to her rather than to me. Instinctively I. realised that in past ages she had been his property, and that jealousy had drawn his spirit back to possess and con- trol that work of art. It was horrible. Who could battle with a demon in this form, who utilised a slab of stone, and sent out arrows that became in- visible in their passage? While I knelt covering Ashfaroth in the dark; I glanced into that lighted chamber, and saw the king azain raise his arm towards his

div.head: OFFENCES OUT OF SCHOOL.
div.p: OFFENCES OUT OF SCHOOL.
POWERS OF TEACHERS TO PUNISH
CHILDREN.

The Cheshire County Education Committee, sitting at Crewe on Monday, had their attention called by the Director of Education to the following resolution passed by the mantgers of one of the schools in the Chester union area : The head teacher is desired to punish children for misbehaviour daring the dinner interval, and on the way to or from school.

Dr Hodgson, the chairmen, said they should be very careful how and in what way they gave definite per- mission to teachers to punish children for offences committed out of school. Thi4 was a matter for parents, and not for school teachers. The Rev W Bidlake stid that punishment might be given for off 4110 PS committed during the dinner hour if the children were on the school premises. Mr f T Wcbardson said be presumed the school managers would take the responsibility. The Chairman urged the committee to be careful ae to what instructions they gave to teachers. . .
Mrs Fergus Smith fer4ei it might lead to unfortunate complicatiors if teachers wore to punirl chiltion for oTermes outside the Bohol!.
T..e subject was referred to the Elsmentary Schools Committee.

The King went to London on Monday from Sandringham on purpose to visit the great Cattle Show, which was opened at the Agricultural Hall. His Majesty wits keenly interested in all the exhibits, and his tour of the Hall occupied nearly an hour and a-half.
Our photograph shows //fr. Cazalet's shorthorn steer, "Golden Arrow," winner of the Championship for the best steer, as well as the 100-guinea plate for the best beast in the show.

div.head: CANADA'S WINTER PORT.
div.p: CANADA'S WINTER PORT.

The opening this meLth of the winter steamship services of the Canadian Pacific and Allan Line steam- ships to St John is adding enorruonsly to the already great activities which have characterised that port during the present year. Uni sunny heavy traffic is anticipated by the railmayr, especially in view of the western wheat crop, which is being handl d through to the Atlantio winter ports for shipment to Europe. At the same time the city itself is in the throes uf great industrial developments. The bar bcur works in East St John already in progress will ultimately add several thousand men to the working population of Et John. Übe works include the largett dry dock, 1,150 feet long, in the world, and the reclaiming of an area of 200 acres near by upon which iron and steel works and ship build- ing plants are to be erected. All this will involve an expenditure of millions of dollare, and the British con- tractors are receiving the support of the city,provincial ard federal authorities in this undertaking. Additional enterm iSOS, induct:lig a suga refill( ry with a 'capacity of 2,100 barrels a day, cemert works, a brush factory, a brass foundry and new elevators are all in progress ; while proposals have been received by the city auth ties for sites for works for the production of coal tar, creosote and other prcducts, boot end shoe factory, paper big mills and breweries. The values of real estate in St John are naturally rising, but the charactr r and extent of the adjoining district, well suited for the expmsion of the city, should keep values within reasonable limils, and offer, therefore, attractive inducements to capital. Like other progressive cities of Canada, St John has placed the conduct of its affairs in the hands of a committee of five Commissioners, thereby ensuring administration on business principles and an active attention to the many and important interests that aro arisiog at present out of its develop- ment.

div.head: LANCASHIRE GIRLS AND CANADA.
div.p: LANCASHIRE GIRLS AND CANADA.
Labour Of ficials' Protest Against Suggested
Emigration-.

At a meeting of the fßackburn Board of Guardians on Saturday, the Bev H T Greaves moved a resolution approving the emigratien to Can .da of suitable girl inmates of the Clttage Homes. Having referred to pressure on the accommodation at the Homes and to the difficulty of finding suitable employment for girls, many of whom had returned from situations. Mr °reeves said be was strongly of opinion that they would have a bt ter chance in Canada, where there was a great tcarcity of female labour, and where the homes offered to girls were much supelior to those in this country. Mr Johnson (secretary of the Operative Spinbers' Aas.ociation) said that it would bo moro patriotic to provide good homes for the children in England than to emigrate them on the chance of their finding homes in the colonies. Blackburn could rot afford to sand girls to Canada if, as was sta'ed, 1,,500 operati yea were ' required to take charge of weaving looms in the town, and employers were seriously cons:deriog the a dvisn- bility of obtaining operatives from other countries. Mr Michael Brothels (secretary of the Card-room Workers' Association) expressed similar views, adding that thanks to trade unionism, women workers received the same scale of wages as men—conditions which did not exist anywhere cu.side Lancashire, It was unfair that the ratepayers should keep children until they reached worklng age and then drafted them out to another country. . .
The resolution was defeated by 15 votes to six.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Modern Christmas.—The decline-of the DickenS Christmas spirit is seen in the growing fashion among the middle classes for spending Christmas away from home. Those who are not going abroad to the sunny South, or for winter sports mostly have some or other plans for enjoying a brief holiday change, either with or wit'aitit the uAial family surroundings. If people are not going away and you ask them what they are doing at Christmas, the invariable reply is "nothing particular," which generally means that they propose to avoid Christmas social celebrations as far as possible. Christmas observances in accordance with traditioral custom, still prevail among the more humble classes,but to a great extent they have lost their hold upon the well-to-do, who can afford the luxury of spending Christmas at a smart hotel. Under these circumstances it is hardly surprising that Mr Charles Crombies pro- posed Dickens Centenary Christmas party at the Bull, Itches ter, has fallen through owing to lack of support It was prorosed to get together a party of forty, who were to drive down from Londen to Rochester in four co ches in the Id-fashioned style. The guests were all to be in the costumes of a hundred years ago, and %ere to take poseession of the Bull lon, the scene of al many incidtnts in the Pickwick story, for three or four days over Christmas. There were to have bean dinners end daners, Pitiewickian revels, and old-time mark ments, but in the end it was found tint only six enthusiasts were ready to carry out the programme,and it ' would seem that they elore, cut of numeroui promises of support thought they could stand or enjoy so much old-fashioned Christmassiog.

'I he World Travellers and Artists Cln's.—lf a girl is able to look after herself, social convention no longer places any obstacle in the way of her travelling alone —and seeing the world—to use a vulgarism on her own:' Such womea may be met wi hin all tae capitals of Europe, and the great cities of America. Some are travelling for pleasure, others are studying at the Universities, and every great centre of learning has rts cosmopolitan col( try of women students. At the same time, the problem of lodging often presents diffi- culties for the unittached girl, ford a fresh attempt to make things easier for her when travelling is being made by a number of inflential women on both sides of the Atlantic. This organization has taken the form land title of the World Travellers and Artiste Club, of which a London branch was opened recently. It is Intended to serve as a club-house, a residential hostel, a general information bureau affording all such services at what might be called cot price. It is proposed to open similar institutions in Paris, Berlin, Rouse, Vienna, and all the great cities of the United States and Canada, offering educatie nal and social advantages •c, women who are travelling and studying ahroad, removed from the ~are aol intiu 'n ;es of hums hien I Sombre Masculine Attire.—The masculine dress reformers are orce more trying to lure the" mere marl" to return to the silts end satins and laces of his ancestors. Ile is reminded of tbe splerchd appear- ance of the man of fashien of the eighteenth century, and invited to foreswesr his negative fashions, his arab and uninta,esting, utilitarian style of dress. Every now and Resin the enthusiasts get the pendulum a little on the swing, ard the mere outfitters fill our shop w'ridons with fancy wa'stcoats, highly col mred socks and ties, and a more picturesque style of headgear. Then, just as they are waiting for the smart and distin- guished man to sink his self-consci usness, and array himself in a brighter and more artistic fashion, the periculum stops, cud the men of fashion returns to his old moncs. and sombre drabness. The average rami bat(a new clothes, both in the ordering,and trying them on, and rerorm himself in the light of the gay costumes of the Georgian period, he will not. One hardly sees how he can in these days of commercialism, which have forced the Highlander into treusers, and have affected not only the entire middle class, tut a great number of the aristocracy. The House of Lords is c.mposed largely of business men, or ex-business men, and business life, like our climate, does rot encourage an exotic taste in dress. Moreover the woman who has to look after the clothes of her men folk, will be Wise not to support the agitation for more elaborate scheme's of masculine attire. The Matinee Hat and Frock,—The cult of the small hat, has led milliners to attempt once more to design a sty le of hat that nay be worn in the theatre without' any fear of a request for its removal,—and this time it would veem that their efforts have been crowned with Success. Nothing crud be more charming than the models now being shown, that in almost each instance deserve rather the term cap, than hat, One in parti- cular of gorgeous embroidery, fitted as closely to the head as the baby's cap of long ago, and was similar in shape. Framing the face was a border of soft fur. The matinee dress is almost as burning a question as the hat. The severe typo of tailor-made is decidedly unsuitable, but the artistic may be worn without fear of ineorru:ty, should the bat be removed. Perhaps the ideal sty e for such functions is a smart afterneon diets, over shich the comfortable long fur coat is a correct garment. This Seasons' Furs.—Many furs once considered harsh, stiff, and unplisble, have been rendered quite the opposite, by the mode rdopted by furriers in mount- ing them. Notably is this the case with this years skunk. By dividing the skins into strands, stoles and scarves may be draped round shoulders, as gracefully as if these accessories were built of the softest silk or satin. Large skunk muffs match these stoles, and are finished with tails arranged as fringes. The shapes of stoles and muffs may be described as legion, and theY are made to suit every type of figure. For the tall woman there are scarves that drape the fLture and give quite as much warmth as fur-lined coats. For the petite individt al, the very opposite is provided in the shape or simple little ties, that do not detract front, but rather add to the height of the we irer. These may be worn with or without muffs, and when Wee:red with a bunch sf ribbans are very smart indeed and, make most acceptable Christmas gifts. The Braided Tailor-Mae:le.—The lICW(et, tyres or tailor-mar'es are rather lavishly trimmed with silk braid in contrasting colcu-s. Thus a model of Davy blue sin( serge, or any rich material, is decorated partly with navy and partly with crimson silk braid, awl has porre" lain buttons of the latter calour. Another model in grey is similarly trimmed with braid of a darker shade of grey and sapphire blue, with buttons that match tbia colour exactly. A great deal of piping, consisting of very flee folds of black satin, is tarn used on tailored suits of whipcord, serge, and velours cloth. These p'pings accentuate more particularly the scams of this style of oustum‘. It is confidently P'°:. dieted that the three-quarter carat will ret un spring, and in confirmation of this prediction it may IT remarked that this lengthy coat is being at the momes' very much worn in Paris, with dresses of cashmere of chiffon cl.Jth iii 1/ghter shades. The Servant Tax.—When the Insurance Act was being passed many society won's,' declared that they would defy the law, and have nothinz to do with it. Mostly they have since thought letter of it, hut there are some exceptions, and among them is Laly Mimic° FitV Gerald, of Johnstown Castle, Onuaty Wexford. Sh° appears to be a record-breaker, in having bum the recipient of no fewer than one-hund ed and fiftY seven summonses in respect of 20 servants, and failing to stamp their cirds. Lady Maurice is auut to the present Duke of Leinster and it was a Maurice Fitz; Gerald who was the companion and trusted lientense' of Strong-Bow. The Fitzge aids are descended fOni the Gherardine of Florence, one of whose chiefs becalr! a great favourite with Edward the Confessor. BOWLING CLUB DINNER.—On Thursday night the annual dinner of the Bowling Club held in connection 1 with the Green Dragon Hotel, Bentley, was held at its headquarters. There was a large attendance of members and friends who did justice to the admirable catering of the landlord, Mr Richardson. Some of the prize winners were :—President's (Mr \V H Sutton) handicap : 1, marble clock and bronzes, Mr L Wilson •, 2, gold watch, Mr J Hincle. WESLEYAN CHURCH ENTERTAINMENT.—EmboIdened by the success that attained Miss Mitchell's recital last October the local Wesleyans made the venture of having a still higher class elocutionist in the person of Mr Pella Mills, F.R.0.5., for their recital of Wednes- day evening last. Mr Mills was able, by varying his items, which consisted of humorous songs musical sketches, recitations and story telling, to talc() charge of, and carry the programme throughout without wearying his audience in the least, in fact, as humour predomiated, the audience were carried along with roars of laughter from beginning to end. As each item was exceptionally good and well rendered it would be a difficult matter to decide which was the most popular piece. The programme contained the following ; Humorous songs, " The football craze," " Ladies in Parliament," "Isn't that like a man," and " When father carves the duck "; musical sketches, " A railway journey " including " Don't forget the porter !" " The silver wedding in which the various characters were cleverly impersonated ; a whistling sketch " An adventure up the Rigi " ; humorous storks about the Jew ; and a recitation with a moral `• The old man goes to town." Pianoforte accompaniments were cleverly played by Mr H S Brown, and Mr W Cooke, F.R.C.O. There was a very good attendance considering the very

wet evening. - DEATH OF MRS. G. GHOVES.—II is with regret that we announce the passing away of another well known Lymm inhabitant in the person of Mrs Groves, who died at her residence, "Newfield Villa," on Sunday morning. The deceased lady was the widow of the late Mr George Groves, whose connection with Cherry-lane Tanyard extended over a long period. Mrs Groves was one of the oldest people in Lymm, having attained her ninetieth year of age last February, and despite her advanced years maintained a keen interest in all local affairs. Her only son, Mr William G Groves, is the well known Booth's Hill representative on the Lymm Urban District Council where he is the highly respected chairman, having enjoyed the unique distinc- tion of holding the position for two terms of office ; he is also one of the local magistrates and is interested in the welfare of the poor people in the district. Of her two daughters, Mrs Hewitt, wife of Mr Richard Hewitt of Booth's Hill, is the better known locally, whilst the other, Mrs Copeland, lives at Manchester. The funeral took place at the Parish Church on Thursday afternoon, when the Rev G B Thurston, M.A., was the cificiating clergyman The chief mourners were Mr and Mrs R Hewitt, Mr and Mrs W G Groves, and Mrs Copeland. A number of beautiful coral tributes were received. HIGHER-LANE BAPTISTS.—The members of the Higher-lane Baptist Chnrch and Sunday School are always pleased to receive a visit from their esteemed friend Mr E Parker, but since that gentleman concluded his studies at the Baptist College last summer he has accepted the call to the pastorate of a church in Leicester,hence his duties will prevent him from paying more than an occasional visit to Lymm and therefore additional importance was made of the Rev E Parker's stay amongst his many L3mm friends last week-end. On Sunday morning he preached from the words "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands ; thy walls are continually before rue," Isaiah xlix, H. In the evening he delivered another striking sermon, this time choosing as his topic the story of the man sick of the palsy. Matt. xi., 2. —There was an interesting gathering of Sunday School officials and scholars in the schoolroom on Monday night, when the Rev E Parker gave a most touching address on the experiences he has had during his three mouths ministry, especially in relation to the testimony of two children in his Church who have been the means Of bringing souls to the Saviour. iss A Brundrett, on behalf of the Sunday School officials and scholars, pre- sented Mr Parker with a silver tea pot as a token of their high esteem. A list of the autographs of all who had contributed to the gilt was also handed to Mr Parker who was deeply affected by their kind thought and in responding said that they would never know how Painful it had been to him to decline the pastorate of Lynam. During the evening several musical items and recitations were given. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHOIR SociAL.-At the Primi- tive Methodist Church on Monday night the annual choir social tea and concert was brought to a successful con- clusion. There was a capital muster of friends present to partake of the choice and ample supply of food that bad been provided for them by Mesdames G W Cross, Edwards, E Moss, and It W B Whiteway, and the Misses Goodwin and Welford. After tea a concert was given by the choir members, the principal part of which consisted of folk-songs, England being represented by " Annie Lisle " in which Miss Millicent Clare took the solo ; Ireland was depicted in " The dear little Shamrock," solo by Miss Bessie Cross ; Scotland was remembered by 139 Mr George Appleton who sang " Annie Laurie' Whilst Mr Harry Brooks put in the Welsh share with the song "Land of my fathers." The part songs " Swabian folk-song." "Thuringian folk-song," "The belfry tower " and " Arise, my love "were most credit - • ably given. Miss Dora Cross contributed the song Happy Moments." Humorous element was pro- vided by the quartette " A very bad cold "by Miss M J Appleton. Miss M Clare, Mr G APoleton, and Mr A Appleton; a nonsense "og "John henry" by the choir and a s)lo " Michael Roy "byMr A Appleton. Mr A Appleton also contributed a well-delivered recitation, "Gone With a handsomer man," and as an encore " John Oswald." The terminating item was a dialogue," The 4500 prize," in which the various parts were well sus- tained by Mies D Cross as Miss Cripps •, Miss B Cross as Kitty; Mr H Clare as Mr Compound; Mr J Atherton 48 Tommy ; and Mr A Appleton as Corporal Jones. The liastinted applause and demands for encores proved that If the concert was not a classical one yet it was a most P °Pular one. The training for the musical items had "!aen thoroughly carried out by Mr J Edwards, the v,t,loirmaster. The accompaniments were provided by 'iiSs Shore. A vote of thanks to the workers was pro- posed by the Rev RWBW hiteway, the chairman, and Passed with acclamation. •

WESLEY G ull,D.—At the weekly meeting on Wednes- day last, Mr Wilcockson gave a lecture entitled "Devonshire Cream," being an account of a cycling holiday spent in that country. The lecture was illus- trated with original lantern slides. Mr Wilcockson who has great taste for architecture, showed many beautiful photographs of churches and buildings as well as country scenery. Owing to the very inclement weather the audience was rather small. .

SCALDING FATALITY.—A sad accident occurred in the village on Tuesday night, when a child of six 3ears, the youngest son of Mr and Mrs S Woodward fell over a bucket of boiling water end was badly scalded. The shock to his system must have been very great for he died the next morning at seven o'clock. Much sympathy is felt for the family. The inquest was held on Thursday afternoon and a verdict of "Accidental death," returned.

ST. THOMAS'S FISHERNIEN.—On Saturday evening the members of St. Thomas's Men's Bible class (B) Fishing Club, sat down to an excellent potato pie supper supplied by Mrs Dean in the Parish Room. After supper, Mr Hallows in distributing the prizes, said how pleased he was to know that they had had a successful season. div.head: FIRE BELL.
div.p: THE FIRE BELL.

The Clerk read a letter from the Architect to the County Council, expressing the opinion that the lire bell standard proposed to be fited at the Police Station was much too high, that it lighter erection, at the most twelve feet high, was all that was required, and that the arrangements should be such that the bell could he rung by any civilian from outside the side gate, for the gate would be kept locked and the police would accept no responsibility for opening the gate, or for ringing the bell. The position suggested for the bell standard appeared to be suitable. Mr Wright said the bell was a heavy one and no lighter standard would carry it. The letter was referred to the Fire Appliances Committee.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH PETTY SESSIONS.

SMART FINE FOR POACHING.—At the Stockton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday before Mr J Cherlton Parr (presiding) and other magistrates, Thomas Dobson Kimberley-drive, and Philip Berry, Southern-street, both of Stockton Heath, were summoned for unlaw- fully entering enclosed land at Acton Grange, in the occupation of Peter Hall, at 12.45 a.m. on November 17th, for the purpose of taking game. Defendants pleaded guilty.—Mr T D Amos (Messrs Robert, Davies and Co.) prosecuted on behalf of Sir Gilbert Greenall Bart. He said this was not an ordinary case of poach- ing, but of night poaching, and the Bench had the power to ask the defendants to give sureties to the effect that they would not commit the offence again. Last July he appeared to prosecute two other offenders, and in that case he did not ask the Bench to be severe' but unfortunately, the leniency then exercised had not proved a deterrent. The covert in which the defendants were found was the most valuable one, but so far as rabbits and bares were concerned, it had been poached upon so much that there were few alive. On November 17th, at 12.45 a.m., five men, including the defendants, were seen crossing a field at Acton Grange. On seeing Mr Smith, the head gamekeeper,to Sir Gilbert Greenall and fcur other gamekeepers approaching, the men took to their heels. Three of them proved swift, enough to get away, but the two defendants were caught. The men were armed with bludgeons, and one of the men who succeeded in escaping at•saulted one of the keepers, who was laid up for a week. The Bench had power to believe and assume that the bludgeons were to be used for offensive purposes. Be asked them to inflict the maximum penalty.—Defendants were fined £3 and costs each, or two months' imprisonment, and the nets and bludgeons were confiscated. MOTORIST SAYS PROSECUTION IS "MALICIOUS AND ABSURD."—Bertram S Newcombe, Great Sankey, was summoned for not having a light attached to his motor car at the extreme right on November 24th at Stockton Heath.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.—lnspector Breese said that at 9 p.m. on the date in question he saw defendant driving a motor car along Walton road. He noticed that there was only one lamp in the centre of the car. Defendant stopped when called upon to do so, and on being asked whether he was aware that he should have a light on the extreme right of the car, he replied, " Yes, but I have a good headlight, and that is sufficient. Witness told defendant he would report him, and he said he did not care ; he had driven the car for thousands of miles without an accident. Witnese agreed, in cross-examination, that the defendant was driving carefully.—The defendant protested against the prosecution which, he declared, was malicious and absurd." He had driven the car between 150,000 and 200,000 miles without an accident, and the lights bad been in that position practically the whole time. The following night he put a lamp on the car in the position suggested by the Inspector. The headlight was not in the centre, but was some short distance towards the right side.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. A DRUNKEN HUSBAND.—Tbos. Mitchell, Warburton- street, Stockton Heath, was summoned by his wife,who alleged that he was an habitual drunkard, and applied for a separation order.—Mr CH Unswortb ,who appeared for the complainant, told a sad story of repeated out- breaks of drunkenness, beginning in 1903 when the defendants wife, who carried on business at Golborne, got into difficulties because he took the money and spent it in drink. In 1909 he was sent to an inebriates' borne, where be

remaineil six months. He returned home, but "broke out " amain. Defendant afterwards reformed and got work at Darwen as a wallpaper designer, but during the six months be was there he only sent his wife £3. He was practically never sober. He lost his position in Damen end went out to New Zealand, and while he was out there his father died, baying settled on the defendant money which brought in something like £OO a year. On his return from New Zealand he persuaded his wife to come back to him, and said he would make a fresh start. They took op their residence in Stockton Heath, hut before he had b-en there a week he resumed his drinking habits, and had been drunk practically ever since.—Complainant having given evidence,a separation der was granted with alimony of £1 a week.

PADGAT E. PARISH COU NcIL—A special meeting was held on Friday evening last week to consider plans submittect for the opening of a new road and the formation of a new bridge across the railway. Mr Denham presided and all the members were present. No resolstions were passed, and there is to be another meeting at an early date. _ .

WESLEY GUILD.—The usual weekly meeting was held on Monday evening, presided over by Mr W G Proffitt, in the univoideble absence of the Rev E Morgan. A paper of special interest was read by Mr W A Birchall, his subject being—" The Romance of Foreign Travel." In his capacity of wireless telegraph operator on board several vessels, Mr Birchall has had considerable experi- ence, and his personal reminiscences were listened to with great appreciation by the members present.—ln felicitous terms, Mr Joseph Dakin proposed a vote of thanks to Mt Bi rchall for his admirable paper, and remarked that he had followed with great int3rest his graphical description of the voyage down the Mediterranean, but regretted that although that particular spot had alwa3s held a peculiar fascination for him, it had not yet been his good fortune to "see Naples and die."—The proposition was seconded by Mr E Lunt and carried.—The Chairman was also accorded a vote of thanks, on the proposition of Mr J H Mason, seconded by Mr Thomas Leach.

CONCERT—The second of the series of entertainments in aid of the reduction of the debt on the new Wesleyan School premises was held there on Tuesday evening. Mr Thos Duckwoith presided over the meeting at which there was but a moderate attendance. The Orpheus Quartette contributed in their usual pleasing style the following items : " Robin Adair "; "Nellie Way "; " Annie Laurie "; "Farewell ". Mr J H Draper was well received in" Eleanore" and "1 hear you calling me "; Mrs A Booth's fine rendering of the "April Song' and " Valley of Laughter," was greatly appreciated. Mr W Moores, whose appearance in various characters, caused great met riment, gave a welcome touch of humour to the evening's entertainment by his songs : " My word," "Captain Ginger," " 0.T.," and "Mary Ann, she's after me." In the songs, "The pipes of Pan " and " alorious Devon " Mr F Fieldhouse was heard to great advantage. The duet " Watchman, what of the night " was ably given by Mr 3 H Draper and Mr F Fieldhonse, though the blend of voices was not se good as we have heard. Miss Nicholson whose natural manner charmed the audience, met with an enthusiastic reception in her sympathetic interpretation of the songs "In the chimney corner " and "My dear soul." Each artiste was complimented by an encore, and responses were made in every case. The concert was well worthy a better audience, but as the chairman remarked, the poor attendance was no doubt mainly due to the unfavourable conditions of the weather. Mr Thomas Duck worth voiced the thanks of the audience to the artiste; including the accompanists, and a pleasurable evening was brought to a close by the sing,ng of the National Anthem.

div.head: VISIT OF REV. DR. MALDWYN HUGHES, OF SOUTHPORT.
div.p: VISIT OF REV. DR. MALDWYN HUGHES, OF SOUTHPORT.

For some time past the visit -of the above mentioned gentleman to the Wesleyan Church has been pleasurably anticipated, and those who bad beard his sermon on Thursday afternoon and his lecture on the evening of the same day enjoyed a great treat. Mr C E Parker, of Penketh, presided at the lecture and was supported upon the platform by Revs Dr Hughes, W A Beckett and E Morgan who conducted the opening prayer. In opening his lecture Dr Hughes said that a friend had told him that a certain firm of distillers were advertising one of their products as " The spirit of the age." (Laughter.) Of course he did not propose to deal with that kind of spirit. The term " The spirit of the age " seemed to imply that each age had its own peculiar spirit. Thus we considered the early years of Christianity as the age of despair and expectancy. The days of feudalism as the Age of Chivalry. The 15th century was the age of discovery, the 16th century was called the revival of learning, the 18th century was the age of revolt. It should be borne in mind that the "Spirit of the Age "was not necessarily the " Spirit of the World." The present day was characterised by advance in our ideas of pity and brotherhood and in the conception of justice and in the develop- ments of social consciousness, statesmen of all parties were obsessed by the idea of the State There could be no social reform without coming hack to the individual. There could be DO ideal society without ideal individuals. One of the dangers of this age was the growth of plutocracy. The unscrupulous capitalists are the real anarchists of to-day. Another danger was the unwillingness to respond to any other influence than that of force. Christianity is not built up on force—love and sacrifice are the chief attributes of God. There is more in the Gospel than we yet realize. Whether we like it or not the destiny of our ..country is in the hands of the working classes. If there are no wrongs there need I be no fear, but if men have wrongs unredressed in the long run they will be invincible. Another sign of our times was the growth of the spirit of strife and rivalry among the nations. The growth of armaments had increased during the past twenty years in France 100 per cent, Britain 150 per cent, United States America 500 per cent, Germany 740 per cent, Japan 050 per cent. To those who took only a superficial outlook these were terrible figures, but the nations were linked together by science, economy, and commerce. The searchlight of the press permeated everywhere ; where the newspapers had no accurate news they might generally be relied upon to fabricate (Laughter.) The Lecturer here strongly recom. mended the small book recently published by Mr Norman Angell " The great illusion." Speak- ing of the book he said it was epoch making and it was said it had even converted Lord Northcliffe though he had not as yet noticed any of the fruits of repentance in the "Daily Mail." Dr Hughes proceeded to show that self interest was against war entirely. No nation could permanently destroy the trade and commerce of another by war. An argument against war was that no defeated nation could provide an adequate indemnity. For England to conquer Germany would cost at least £500,000,000. "How could you get it?" Not in securities, not in gold Germany would have to borrow ruthlessly all over the world, and the hank roll would rise to 7 or 8 per cent, and the English bankers would be begging the Government to forgive the indemnity to Save Our country from ruin. A victorious nation cannot destroy the competition of a country it has defeated. One nation cannot capture the trade of another by a powerful navy. Trade seems independent of military matters, for the small nations were better in many ways than the larger ones. Belgian 3 per cent's stand at 96 while German are only 82. Russian 31 per cent's stand at 81 while Norway, with an army about as large as the Warrington Police Force—(laughtter)—bas 31's at 10.2 Another sign of the times is the lessening of the respect for the authority of parents. The words " Children obey your parents "'sad been altered to "Parents obey your children "—and many of them do it. (Laughter.) It was complained that no men of outstanding charater command this age, as in bygone years. That was because men were beginning to think for themselves. There should be a conservative element in every progressive. Theology has had to re-state some of its doctrines, but that was nothing to be ashamed of. It would have been had they net been restated. Quoting, the lecturer said "Science has filled the Temple of Theology with ruins, but the only things it has destroyed are idols." Speaking of the higher criticism, Dr Hughes said that "Revelation is progressive and men should be measured by the age in which they lived. We have learnt that ' the twin streams of Judaism and Christianity form a great river viith many tributaries. The poor attendance at public worship of recent years was due to booming trade. The diminishing authority of the churches is due to the people beginning to think for themselves. An era of adversity would cause many to renew their connection with the churches. A vote of thanks to chairman and lecturer was accorded on the proposition of the Rev W A Becket seconded by Mr Frank A Harris. Mr CE Parker replied on behalf of Pr Hughes and for himself and said that he felt sure that the lecturer hoped to come again to Padgate. He also urged the study of Mr Angell's book and remarked that now-a-days there was not so much relatively in nationality. There was more affinity between h.nglish and German miners than between the men and those who employ them. Collections were taken on behalf of the new school premises.

CHRISTMA'S. PARCELS. The London and Notth-Western Railway Co have made complete arrangements for the collection quick transit and prompt delivery of Christmas parcels in all the principal towns on their system, and all parts of Wales, Scotland, and Ireland. Special parcel trains will be run and through Vall3 will also be attached to the principal passenger trains for the accommodation of the traffic, and additional delivery and collection services by parcel vans and carts between the receiving officers and the station wi;l be in operation during Christmas and the preceding week. Senders are advised as an extra precaution a duplicate address label should be enclosed in each parcel so that the name of the con- signee may be ascertained in the event of the outside address becoming detached or defaced.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES COUNCILLOR TO RESIGN.

Mr J W Towers, Liberal representative for Widnes South, has intimated his intention to resign at tie expiry of his term, owing to business pressure. The letter was received with regret by the executive com- mittee of the association, and he was thanked for his services. The executive committee decided to leave the matter of a successor in the hands of the officers of the association. The north portion of the town is represented by the Mayor (Alderman F Neil), a Conser- vative, as the result of an arrangement between the two political parties. ASKED FOR AND GIVEN. -

At Liverpo-oTint;rn;ediate Sesame on Tuesday Harry Stockton (34), labourer, pleaded guilty on two charges of office-breaking at Widnes, between the 22nd and 29th October, and also a charge of theft at Liverpool, on October 6th.

Prisoner handed to the bench a statement in which he said there were no extenuating circumstances in his case. Everything was deliberately done, and the chisel and jeromy were bought for the purpose. The justices would see his previous record,and it was his firm deter- mination to continue his recent career until lent to penal servitude. The Chairman said such a statement as that made by prisoner gave the bench much pain. He would have to go to penal servitude tor three years. RUNL ORN ENTERTAINMENTS.

At Runcorn Sessions on Monday, Mr Quayle, of Southport, applied on behalf of Mr Henry Thomas Aulton, Southport, for a cinematograph and musio and dancing licence for a building to be erected on a plot of land adjoining the Royal Hotel, High-street. The building would seat 800, and the plans provided for leight emergency exists. Mr Laycock made an application on behalf Alfonso Smith, of Salford, for a licence for stage plays and also for music and dancing for a building to be erected on laud adjoining Bank Chambers. This site, he stated, had been for years spoken of as an ideal spot for the erection of a hall for public) purposes, and was in the best part of the town. I he bench adjourned the applications for a fortnight, and the clerk ruled that they had no power to grant a provisional licence to allow the building to be pro- ceeded with at once. WIDNES FREE CHURCHES. COUNCIL'S NEW PRESIDENT.

The Widnes Free Church Council on Monday night appointed Mr A E Calvert to be its president next year. A resident of Widnes of twenty-seven years' standing, he was the first layman president two years after the inception of the coun3ll, and be has held several offices in connection with that body, including that of secretary. Mr Calvert is a Primitive Methodist and a member of Frederic-street Church. On the Widnes Education Committee he represents the Free Church Council, and also sits on the Library Com- mittee as a co-opted member. He holds the position of vice-chairman of the Higher Education Committee. The son of the late Rev Jonathan Calvert, he is con- nected with the Liverpool and District Primitive Methodist Connexion and the Manchester and Liverpool districts of the Ministerial Association. He is also a very enthusiastic Liberal.

div.head: WIDNES LIBERALISM.
div.p: WIDNES LIBERALISM.

SPEECH BY YOUNG LIBERALS' CANDIDATE. The choice of the Young Liberals of Widnes to con- test the division in opposition to Colonel Hall Walker, has fallen on Mr J B Martindale, vice-president of the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation, a member of the '95 Club, Manchester, and a partner in the woollen firm of Messrs J Ball and Co., of Manchester. At a recent meeting of that body a resolution was passed, suggest- ing to the Liberal Executive of the division the name of this promising young politician. The senior organisation has also looked with favour on the proposal and it is practically certain that Mr Martindale will be asked to tight this strong Tory constituency. Mr C Poole presided over a meeting at the Liberal Club on Wednesday evening, when Mr Martindale was the chief speaker. Mr Martindale said the Tories told them that when the Liberal party had dealt with Home Rule, Welsh Disestablisbment, and one man one vote, they wonld not have anything more to talk about. Liberalism was not for a time, but for all time ; and they must recog- nise that Liberalism coloured the whole aspect of their life. If their Liberalism was founded on that basis, come what may. They had a Government in power which was doing much hard work ,and they had to assist them, and the sooner Home Rule was given to Ireland, the Welsh Disestablishment Bill passed, and one man one vote became law, the sooner other pressing problems would be tackled. Liberalism would never depart from the principles of Free Trade, because in those principles lay the welfare of the great mass of the people. Present-day landlordism was altogether against the comfortable living of the poor. Schemes of providing tenements for the working classes of the country had not been a success, because the tenants were barracked and had not the freedom of a proper English home. The only solution was to place I the matter in the hands of county and town councils to buy or build property on the outskirts of towns and so get the people away from slum areas. The citizens of the land were entitled to have decent homes to live in, and in the National Insurance Act provision had been made to obtain this. Undeveloped land was another problem which was to be dealt with. The Liberals would not countenance apoilation but they were going to see that the community should be pro- tected. He regretted the attitude of the doctors toward the Insurance Act, and he was of opinion that before January 15th there would be a medical service to work the bill. Liberals had a very live future, although it was often said that the country was suffer- ing from a surfeit of legislation. What was wanted was some system of legislation which would not waste time over the old problems, but which would ensure prompt attention to other pressing problems which came along. (Cheers.)
