div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

SEPTUAGENARIAN'S FATAL DRAUGHT. The death took place on Tuesday, under distressing circumstances, of Mr James Hall, watchmaker and jeweller, of Eccleston-street, Prescot. About four o'clock Police Constable Bridgham heard the bell on the shop door ring, and, on looking through the glass panel in the door, saw Mr Hall sitting on a chair. The officer asked what was the- matter. Mr Hall replied that he drunk something and showed the constable a bottle which contained aqua fortis. The officer adminis- tered an emetic and summoned Dr Green, but Mr Hall died shortly afterwards, lie was seventy-two years of age, and at one time was an officer in the Army. He leaves a widow but no family. .‘

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
EARLESTOWN " CO-OPS" AND THE INSURANCE ACT.

In the House of Commons on Monday Viscount Wolmer asked the Secretary to the Treasury whether he was aware that the Earlestown Industrial Co-operative Society had not yet received the special order under section 47 of the National Insurance Act promised to them, and whether he could explain why there had been this delay ? Mr Masterman replied :—A special order extending the provisions of section 47 of the National Insurance Act to the employees of the society mentioned in the question will be published in the course of a few days, and will he brought into force at once. The order is the first of its kind, and some time has necessarily been occupied in settling questions of legal form and in making arrangements to enable the order to be brought into force as a provisional order without its having been subject to the waiting period of not less than fifty-one days, which must in normal circumstances elapse before a special order becomes effective.

20Th ANNIVERSARY SALE OF JEWELLERY. " Davies's, Low Hill," is the name of a firm which can always be relied on, and which wonderfully helps one in the purchase of jewellery. Davies's 20th Anniversary Sale which is now proceeding, offers great bargains to suit all purses. The windows of the shop are now ablaze and aglitter with genuine sparkling diamonds and gems. The prices marked in plain figures show a saving of fully lOs in every £. Several fine old heirloom diamonds have been remounted to current fashion showing a wonderful saving compared to ordinary prices. A visit to this noted store will be well repaid. Being situated in Low Hill and not in Church-street many,hundreds a year is saved in rent and taxes ; the benefit is offered to buyers of Christmas presents.

div.head: MOTORIST HEAVILY FINED.
div.p: MOTORIST HEAVILY FINED.
Mr Firth; lam not browbeating him. Mr Roberts : I think so. Mr Firth : You ought not to think so. The Chairman : You want magistrates who don't think at all.

Mr Firth : I like intelligent gentlemen who do think. Such remarks are unfair when you have not heard the defence. Mr Roberts : There is no bias whatever. Mr Pirth : I hops not. will accept that. Continuing, : P.C. Andrews said the men in the car were dressed alike. Acting Sergeant Hewitt, who was on duty in Bridge- street, said the dress of the men in the car was like that worn by motor racers. The car was travelling at a rapid rate snd he whistled to the driver to stop. P.C. Edwards and P.C. Corbett spoke as to the car travelling at a fast rate.

The Chief Constable (Mr Martin Nicholls) corro- borated counsel's statement with regard to the inter- view in his office, the visit to Huyton and the corres- pondence which bad passed between far Beecham his solicitor Mr Firth, and himself. ANOTHER COMPLAINT.

_ The Chief Constable was giving evidence when he was stopped by Mr Firth, who complained that he was proceeding too quickly. The Chief Constable remarked that he imagined it was impossible to go too fast for him. Mr Firth: You must not imagine that which is impossible. The Chairman : Proceed.
Mr Firth : He has no right to make such observations. The Chairman : You have no right to speak to him in that manner.

Mr Firth : You ought to blame him. The Chairman : We are not inclined to tolerate it. Cross-examined by Mr Firth : Did you ask for an appointment with Mr Beecham on the 19th November ? —No. I did not. Do you know the other two people who had access tc. the car besides Mr Beecham and the two chauffeurs were the Misses Beecham ?—I don't know. Do you think it was right and proper to dress as a private individual and go to a gentleman's premises ? When I have to travel I don't usually go in uniform. You seem to think it is compatible with your duty to visit .a law-abiding citizen in plain clothes and instead of going to the front door to enter by the backway ?—Yes. I do. I did not expect to find the chauffeur in the drawing-room. Why did you go in this surreptitious way ?—I see no objection, when as you say Mr Beecham was desirous of giving all the information he could. Is it not a fact, that Mr Beecham said to you" I will help you all Loan ?"—I don't agree. You have told the magistrates about Mr Beecham coming to see you at your office when he said "I suppose the conversation is to be treated as private ?" —Yes.
Immediately after that you broke the compact with Mr Beecham ?—There was no compact. Why did you assure him the conversation was private ?—I told him it was private; no one else being there.
Do you want to suggest that Mr Beecham came to you in a free deliberate manner uninvited by you ?—I don't know what be came for. -
Was it not a fact you had a long conversation with him ?—Yes.
_ Did he not tell you one of the chauffeurs was always with him and took a turn at the steering wheel ?—He did not.
I suggest that you used this conversation to trap him and to issue process against him ?—Nothing of the sort How did you know he was in the car ?—Robinson the chauffeur admitted it.

Can you conceive it was impossible for Mr Beecham to give you the necessary information ?—No I cannot. Toe chauffeur, a man named Robinson, was then called. He said he was in the car on the day in ques- tion with Mr Beecham. They took it in turns at the wheel. He could not say what time the car left Huytoo or at what time they arrived at Leicester, He admitted having said to the Chief Constable in an interview that he would rather not say who was in the car with him. At that time he aid not know who the Chief Constable was.

By Mr Acton : Did Mr Beecham or yourself drive through Warrington ?—I don't remember. For the defence it was contended by Mr Firth that he had,no case to meet. The miserable exploits of the police in that case were such that he ventured to think no magistrates would countenance or confirm. No less than tour summonses had been issued for one and the same alleged offence. The prosecution had tried to build up their case on letters which were intended to erpress indignation at the way the defendant had been treated. He would also like to point out that the summons was bad on account of duplicity and he asked that the case should be dismissed an the ground of the summons being illegal. He had a further objection—there was no plane stated on the summons where the alleged offence occurred. The Chief Constable himself bad shown an enormous amount of bias in the case which he (Mr Firth) had ventured to describe in one of the letters as a conspiracy to trump up a case against Mr Beecham. It was a strange thing that a man like the Chief Constable instead of looking after serious burglary cases should go out to this private residence in plain clothes and enter by the back premises. Did he think that Sir Joseph Beecham and Mr Harry Beecham were so mean that if he had gone to the front door he might have been turned assay? If Mr Harry Beecham had shown an antagonistic spirit he could have understood it. There would then have been some excuse. He did not care to dwell on the incident in the Chief Constable's office. It was admitted that the conference was of a private character. That was not the sort of treatment that English gentlemen were going to put op with. Very drastic methods would be used if measures were carried so far. It was beneath the dignity of an official of a big borough. like Warrington. The threat in that letter was never used at the interview and the fact that Mr Beecham had gone their uninvited gave the lie to the evidence of the Chief Constable Mr Beecham did not keep a record of where he went by motor every day or they might have been able to supply the details. How could they remember who was driving when going long journeys? It was impos- sible for him to say who was driving at any particular time. Another fact which bore out the defendants story was that Robinson said in the witness be; that Mr Beecham had made inquiries. The Bench retired and on their return the Chairman, said the legal points raised had been over ruled and that they had decided to convict. A tine of £2O and costa, with the endorsement of the licence, was imposed. Mr Acton made an application for a special order as to costs which was opposed by Mr Firth. The Magistrates allowed £l5 costs. The other three charges of a similar nature were with drawn.

A further charge was preferred against the defendant of, failing to notify the authority in whose area the car was registered of the change in the colour of the car. The charge was dismissed on payment of 40s. costs.

Latchford Hockey Club Dance. The annual dance in connection with the Latchford Hockey Club was held last evening week at the King's Cafe and proved an unqualified success. About seventy persons were present, and dancing was kept up until an early hour to the strains of Mr T Broad- hurst's band. Messrs WII Minards and J B Wilkin- son were capable M.C.'s and Mr F W Isherwood ably carried out the duties of secretary.

div.head: MR. H. BEECHAM AND THE POLICE.
div.p: MR. H. BEECHAM AND THE POLICE.
REMARKABLE CASE.

An important and rather unusual motor prosecution was heard at the Borough Police Court on Thursday, before Mr J Rymer Young (in the chair), and Messrs W Roberts, J Upson, A J Jolley and Dr Naden. The summons was against Mr Harry Beecham, son of Sir Joseph Beecham, of Ewanville, Huyton, near Liverpool, and was taken under Section 1, sub-section 3 of the Motor Car Act, 1903. The section imposes upon the owner of a motor car an obligation to give any informa- tion which is in his power which may lead to the identity or apprehension of a driver who had committed an offence under the Act.

Mr E Acton, barrister (instructed by the Town Clerk), prosecuted on behalf of the police and Mr Steplee-Firth, of London, defended. Mr Acton. in outlining the case, said the defendant was a gentleman of considerable means and resided at Huyton. lie was the owner of a sixty horse power car which bore the identification mark of LA 7784. On Sunday, November 3rd, about 10.10 a.m., when the streets were fairly thronged with people going to church, the defendant's car was driven through the streets of Warrington at a very great speed in a manner which was dangerous to the public. Mr Firth : That is not admitted.

Mr Acton : Of course it is not admitted. Continu- ing, Mr Acton said there were two persons in the car, one wearing goggles and both wearing skull caps, which made it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to recognise them • Four police officers saw the car at different points and attempts were made to stop it, but in vain. It proceeded at a great pace across Warrington Bridge in the direction of Knutsford and was driven in a way which was a danger to the public. The reason it was not stopped was because the driver took no notice of the warnings. The fact was reported by all the officers. On the following evening about 6.20 one of the officers P.O Andrews, who saw the car the morning previous, was in company with Sergeant Woolacott when they saw the car coming from the direction f Knutsford. The car was stopped by P.O Andrews who called upon the driver to produce his licence. The driver was the defendant, and a licence was produced which showed he was the registered owner of the car. A conversation took place and defendant was told by Andrews that he had been reported for driving the car in a manner which was dangerous to the publio on Sunday morning through Warrington. The driver turning to his com- panion, said "Why we were in Leicester." No answer was made by his companion. Defendant further said to the officer "You must be mistaken in the nurxber of the car," to which officer replied that there was no mistake. The driver then said "Why did'nt you stop me at the time "and Andrews replied. "I put up my band to you but you took no notice and went on" To these remarks the defendant answered "That is Bosh " and drove on in the car. Some communications passed between Mr Nicholls and Mr Beecham. On the 14th of November Mr Harry Beecham called by appointment on the Chief Constable: He informed Mr Nicholls that he understood application had been made for information by the Lancashire County Police. He had sent a note to them that if they wanted any questions answering they must put them in writing. The defendant was told by the Chief Constable what had taken place, and be was given a full explanation of the obligation he was under. At all events the defendant did not give any information to the Chief Con- stable and in consequence a letter was written request- ing the defendant to supply him with the name nnd address of the person who drove the car along Sankey. street and Bridge-street on Sunday Nov. 3rd on which date, it was alleged by officers of the police force that the car was being driven at a speed dangerous to the public. If the information was refused, an application for process would be made to the magistrates. There was no answer from the defendant, but a 'reply was received from the firm Mr Firth represented, that all applications must be put in writing. Another letter dated November 26 was received by the Chief Constable, in which it was stated that Mr Beecham had made inquiries of the different drivers who had access to the car, but he had been unable to obtain any information which would lead to the identification of the driver at the time and place mentioned. That letter, commented counsel, was an evasion deliberately put together for the purpose of keeping back such information which might be obtained from the owner of a motor car. On the 27th November in order if possible to get some further information the Chief Constable along with Superintendent McLean of the County Police went to the defendant's residence. He saw the defendant and chauffeurs Robinson and Underwood, but he got no information whatever. He was told that anything he required must be put in writing. Two days later the Chief Constable received the following letter.

"We have received a report from our client to the effect that you and another policeman paraded in plain clothes entered the back of private premises at Huytoo and endeavoured to browbeat and cajole certain servants there and moreover that either you or some of your emissaries have had the insolence to ring up our clients private telephone and put certain questions to the servants of the house. Unless you apologise forth- with and undertake not to repeat such annoyance we shall report the whole matter to the Home Office or proceed in the High Court for an injunction against you for trespass. It is quite obvious that you are endeavouring to hatch up a wicked conspiracy against our client and unless we have the above assurance we shall take very drastic steps to put an end to your outrageous conduct.—Yours faithfully, FIRTH. _ _ _

- In conclusion, Mr Acton said if it were a fact, as eeemed to be suggested in these letters, but never stated, that the car was being driven by someone with- out authority or without the knowledge of Mr Harry Beecham, he thought those letters would have been the very last that would have been written. P.O Andrews said that he was on duty at Market Gate on the day in question. He saw a cpr come along Sankey-street. The driver signalled his intention of proceeding into Bridge-street. After receiving witness's signal the driver increased his speed and went round the corner of Bridge-street at the rate of 15 to 18 miles an hour. The car proceeded down Bridge-street at a speed of 30 miles an hour. He called upon the driver to stop but be did not seem to notice the signal. On the following day he saw the same car and stopped the driver. The conversation which took place between the defendant and himself as related by Mr Acton was perfectly true. Police-Constable Andrews was cross-examined by Mr Firth with regard to the description of the clothing of the motorists. Mr Firth said he wanted it in plain English so as he could understand. _

The Chairman (Mr Rymer Young): He cannot give it plainer. We perfectly understand. Mr Firth : If your worships are going to prejudice the case I am going to sit down. It was a remark which ought not to have been made. The Chairman : Go on. Mr Firth : I am afraid lam not going on if you are going to interrupt. Mr Roberts (another magistrate) : We shall protect our police. Mr Firth They are not your police. This man is a witness.
Mr Roberts : Thcre is no reason why he should be browbeaten.

div.head: EYENING MEETING.
div.p: EYENING MEETING.

-- T 1 e evf n'ng meeting was presided over by Mr .1 Long- land w. o after the epetiing hymn end prayer by the Rev la Ogden declared his great pleasure in being pre- sent at teet meeting. tie rememnered the days when Uel bort e- tra et friends worshipped in the tin tabernacle in By lato.-street and it was a pleasure to see now such beautiful buildings. I was hardly credible that so lovely a school room could be reared upon the extinct ashes ot the old premises. But now the buildings were iii the pssession of the church he hoped that the Baptists would he able to take a position in the social and religious life of the town in consonance with the great traditions of the denomination. There was a wide scope for Baptist work and these new premises should give the right impetts. (Hear, hear.) Mr E WYNNE JONES then gave his statement in the course of which he stated that the estimated cost of the scheme would be £2,450. They had received in sub- scriptions and a few amounts raised by a sale of work and a bazaar held some time ago in the Parr Hall, together with a grant of £5OO from the Baptist Union, a total of £1,500. They had therefore to raise a Wince of nearly £l.OOO. The total raised as a result of that day's effort realized the splendid sum of £llO. The Rev H V Tfiomas, of Manchester, is an old and honoured visitor at Golborne-street. As Secretary of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches, be has had much to do with the new scheme.l Mr Thomas said be joined with the chairman in express- ing his delight with the new buildings, but no buildings were of any avail unless they were used. If Golborne- street did not become the centre of a great activity for God be should regret having raised his voice and urged the claims of school and church before the Council of the baptist Union. The buildings were not merely for their comfort but for pushing out the borders of God's Kingdom and widening the horizon of the power of Christ. He would draw attention to the need of the Sunday school. Every Church meeting should consider the state of the school. Every Church member should be interested in its welfare. Tbe best men should give their hest service. The management of the Church affairs should he in the bends ef the deacons, and the Church members should be eager to attend to the spiritual and social work of the place. (Applause). The Rev W G POPE of Liverpool, emphasised what Mr Thomas had said and made it manifest that when the nursery is alright the home will grow and thrive. He always inquired when he entered a church about the Simony school : Is the nursery thriving and fit? Then all is well. he wes glad they had started at the right end first ; they had begun with the school. It was an interesting coincidence that the day the school was opened was the day when the foundation stones of the new church front were placed. The children deserved our best, and less than the best was worse than nothing at all. (Applause). ' A votes of thanks to the speakers and choir was moved by Mr J K SLATER, Liverpool, who, speaking of money, said he had been treasurer of a church 43 years. There had never been a collection, never a sale of work. All meg done by the freewill offerings of the people. We must give to the point of sacrifice. Mr JAMES ENWORTHY seconded the vote and expressed delight with the excellent speeches they had listened to that night. Mr B Few and Mr H BUCKBY thanked the Chairman and the applause which greeted the motion was an evidence of the deep respect which is entertained by the Uolborne-street people for Mr Longland. The choir and children were under the able training of the choirmaster Mr Herbert Barnes. The two anthems by the choir" Great and marvellous" and "Onward " were effectively rendered and the children added colour by their singing of the " Forward March" and "Soldiers of Jesus." The Pastor, Rev H Ogden' added his thanks to the Building Committee which had worked so zealously.

div.head: LOCAL DOCTORS AND INSURANCE. Refusal to Work the Act.
div.p: LOCAL DOCTORS AND INSURANCE. Refusal to Work the Act.

By seventeen votes to fourteen the Warrington and Widnes Branch of the British Medical Association have decided against working the National Insurance Act. A previous meeting had been held but no decision was arrived at, opinions being so divided. The Deputy Town Clerk gives notice that invitations have been issued to the medical practitioners in Warrington to confer with the Insurance Committee as to the arrangements to be made with them for the administration of medical benefits.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A_WAERINGTON VAULTS
div.p: SUICIDE OF A_WAERINGTON VAULTS
MANAGER.

A verdict of " Suicide whilst of unsound mind " was returned at an inquest held at the Coroners Court yesterday, relative to the death of Joseph ClooneY, aged fifty-two, vaults manager at the Patten Arms Hotel, Warrington, who was found hanging lava- tory of the vaults on Wednesday. in a Wm Joseph Clooney, a son of the deceased, 17,Lovely- lane said his father sustained three injuries to his head which had caused him severe pains and failing eye- sight. Deceased was a jovial sort of fellow and as far as witness knew he had no home troubles.

A barman at the vaults 3poke as to seeing the deceased enter the lavatory and ,ock the door from the inside. Five minutes later be had occasion to call for deceased, but received no answer. On looking through the lavatory window he saw the deceased hanging by the window cord, which bad been passed four times round his neck. Life was extinct when the body was cut down.

div.head: Opening of tam tunday School at
div.p: Opening of tam tunday School at
tioiboine-strett.

Thursday was a memorable day in the history of the Baptist denomination in Warrington, to,: it witnessed the opening of the handsome 'anti well-appointed new sunday school which has been erected in connection with Golborne-street Baptist Church. The striking new church front is also nearing completion, and .o.pportuuity was taken to place several .memorial stones in position. The site for the school was of a restricted character, but full advantage has been taken of the area at the builder's disposal. . A large hall occupies the ground floor, accommodating over 300, a portion being capable of sub-division into seven *class- rooms by movable partitions. A young nien's institute room, 30ft. by 15ft. din., has been placed on the first floor, and there is ample accommo- dation for kitchen, minister's vestry, &c. The church front has been rebuilt with new central porch and side staircases. The materials for facing the front are Accrington facing bricks aa buff terracotta. The contract also provides for re-ceiling the existing building' and further ac- commodation at the gallery end of the church. The whole of the buildings are heated by hot water and fitted with electric light. The total cost is approximately .t 2,350. The building has been admirably carried out by Mr. G. Walling- ton, of Warrington, to the designs of Mr. H. H. Matley, of Manchester. The opening ceremony had been looked for- ' ward to with considerable interest, and there was a large gathering at the entrance of the church. The pastor (Rev. H. Ogden) presided, and amongst other present were : The Revs. J. S. Chedburn, G. Curtis, and W .Reid, Messrs. E. Wynne Jones, B. Few, E. England, W. Bes- wick, E. Lloyd Jones, T. Longshaw, J. Ken- worthy, Cr. Wallington, and T. F. Wallington. After the singing of the hymn, "This stone to Thee, in faith we lay," the offering of prayer by the Rev. Cr. Curtis, and the reading of Scrip- ture by the Rev. J. S. Chedbum, The Rev. H. Ogden said the church should always set an ideal to its immediate environment and give a tone to the neighbourhood in which it was placed. He thought no one would dis- pute that that church was now the best building in Golborne-street. (Applause.) It remained for the Town Council to do their part, for he under- stood it was their intention some day to widen the street and adorn it with suiable buildings. He was particularly glad that the lettering on the front of the church so boldly betokened the denomination to which it belonged. He hoped that in future the Free Churches of the town, in extending their buildings, or erecting new pre- mises, would be guided by the ideal of unity which had been placed by them by their own great secretary, the Rev. J. H. Shakespeare. There should be hearty co-operation, and the time of building one against the other should be relegated to the past. (Applause.) Mr. Ben Few (senior deacon), in placing the first stone, said he was prayerfully :anticipati#g very prosperous and progressive future for that church. (Applause.) Stones were also placed by Mr. Norman Balm- ford, Mrs. Morris (Southport), Mr. Thos. Long- shaw, Mr. Harry Hall (on behalf of the Bible Class) and Mr. B. England. Mr. England, in the course of a short address, referred to the great missionary and evangelising work of the Baptists, and to the worthy part which they had taken in the fight for religious liberty, justice and equality. In the present day they numbered in their ranks that great champion of education, Dr. Clifford, and that leading states- man who was doing so much for the benefit of humanity—Mr. Lloyd George. (Applause.) The assembly then proceeded to the entrance ot the new school, which was formally opened by Mr. James Kenworthy. Having accepted a •key presented by the archi- tect, Mr. Kenworthy said that in the past Gol- borne-street Church had done its fair share of the work of the town, although it had laboured under great difficulties. The chief obstacle had been lack of accommodation, but that had now been rectified, and they rejoiced in the opening of that school, where the rising generation would be instructed in the Word of God and all that was necessary for their eternal salvation. A short meeting was held in the school. The Rev. H. Ogden, who presided, said he wished the people to use the new premises as they would use their own homes. They could live their collective life and further their collective ideals. He would be disappointed if that building did not become the centre of all types of activities—religious and social and recreative. He never could under- stand why the world should have a monopoly ot pleasure. He was one of those who believed it was possible to play billiards to the glory ot God, and he hoped the young men would make good use of the institute. (Applause.) Empha- sising the importance of Sunday school work, Mr. Ogden said he had a great deal of admiration— for the way in which the Church of England and the Church of Rome sedulously looked after and nurtured -their young people. (Applause.) The Rev. G. Curtis moved a vote of thanks to those who had placed stones. Mr. E. Wynne Jones, in seconding, announced that Mrs. Morris had given a donation of £5O. (Applause.) , Souvenir mallets were presented to those who had performed the afternoon's ceremonies. The Rev. W. Reid proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Kenworthy. Ho said the Church was to-day paying the penalty f.r her mistaken atti- tude towards young life in the past, and she had problems to solve because of that neglect. She had happily awakened to the consciousness that if her work was to succeed, too much attention

div.head: " KING " CARSON'S VISIT.
div.p: " KING " CARSON'S VISIT.
--- Piquant Comments by Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crostield.

Some piquant comments on Sir Edward Car- son's recent visit to Warrington were made by Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield at another of the successful series, of ward socials in connection with the Warrington Women's Liberal Associa- tion on Thursday evening. The gathering, which was for the members .in Fairfield and Howley Wards, was held in the Bold-street Wesleyan School and attracted a very larie attendance. Excellent arrangements had beet# made by the ward captains—Mrs. Osborne (hen. secretary of , tke association) and Mrs. J. S. Hill. At the commencement the chair was occupied by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, and there were also on the plat- form : Miss Alison Garland (of the Women's Liberal Federation, London), Miss Crosfield, Mr. M. Llewellyn and members of the committee. A most enjoy-able musical programme had been arranged by Mrs. E. A. sanders, and afforded very great pleasure. Songs were pleasingly in- terpreted by Miss Lena Duckworth, Mrs. E. A. Sanders, Mr. Thos. Goostrey, and Mr. Ernest Walker, and a duet by Mrs. Sanders and Mr. Walker was also well received. Mr. W. VV. Whittle, in his humorous sketches, was a host ' in himself, and kept the audience in continual merriment, his "country curate" song being es- pecially popular. Mr. T. F. Wi llington was an able accompanist. Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, after, referring to the gratifying reports presented at the annual meet- ing of the association the previous day, said the members would be pleased to hear that the erec- tion of the new club premises would very shortly be commenced. Mrs. Crosfield, of Colwyn Bay, had intimated her desire to erect a hall in memory of the late Mr. John Crosfield—(applause) —and she hoped the Women's Liberal Associa- tion would be able to hold many successful meet- ings and entertainments in it. (Applause.) There would also be a—room in which Mrs. Os- borne, their capable secretary, would have an office, and acccomodation would be provided for the sewing club. The fancy dress ball, promoted by the association last year, proved a splendid success, and it had been decided to hold another early next autumn. Owing to the early date .at which Lent began, and to the heavy bookings of the Parr Hall, it would be impossible to hold the function during the present winter. She was going, to refer for a moment to SIR EDWARD CARSON'S MEETING.

(Much laughter.) She need not ask them why they laughed, because the Tories had indeed made a laughing stock of themselves. (Laughter.) On reading, Mr. Harold Smith's speech, she could not help thinking that he used a very happy illus- tration when he compared Sir Edward Carson to a barracks. (Laughter.) ,Did they not think that Sir Edward did resemble a barracks in den- sity. monotony, and dreariness? (Laughter and applause.) She congratulated Mr. Harold Smith on the simile, and as be seemed to be so fond of figures of speech, she would present him with another. •Let them suppose for a moment that Mr. Harold Smith was a mosquito—one of those tiny, disagreeable creatures that abounded in the East—and that he alighted on the neck of a bull which they would call Warrington. (Laugh- ter.) After bumming a song in that position for a considerable time he said to the WI : "Do I disturb you with my song? If so, I will de- part." (Laughter.) And the bull answered, very calmly and coolly, "Neither when you came did I perceive you, nor if you go will I mind it.' (Laughter and applause.) Mr. M. Llewellyn, in the course of a review ot the work of the Government; said there never was a time when the work done in Parliament came so near to the homes and lives of the workers as it did to-day. (Applause.) . _ _ .

- Miss Alison Garlad then delivered an inter- esting address. Referring to the change in the leadership of the Tory party, she said Mr. Balfour was regarded as too old-fashioned—he could not say enough disagreeable and rude things. (Hear, hear.) Consequently they exchanged him for Mr. Bonar Law, and everybody knew what had hap- pened. On a certain memorable occasion the Tories turned the House of Commons into a bear
garden. They had always associated the Tory, party and the Conservative cause with law and order but now they thought of it as LAW AND DISORDER.

(Laughter and applause.) The Tories made an- other great mistake recently, when, at a big meeting in London, they decided to throw over the Referendum. At the last election, just before the people had to vote, the Tories knew that Tariff Reform—or taxing the food of the people— was not very popular, so they promised that be- fore it was introduced they would again refer it to the people. On that understanding many Free Trade Unionists voted for Tory candidates, but, in face of the latest declaration, their support would not be forthboming in the future. Miss Garland referred at some length to the Reform Bill, and put in a strong plea for the enfran- chisement of women. Some people were apt to associate the cause with those women who smashed windows, interrupted meetings and interfered with the Post Office. They, however, were only one class of suffragists—a quite new and modern class. She asked that meeting to think of all the women who had been quietly agitating for enfranchisement for forty or fifty years. They had no more right to blame all the suffragists for the conduct of the few than they had to blame the Liberal ,members of Parliament because the Tories behaved so disgracefully in the House. (Applause.) Mr. A. H. Crosfield, on entering the room, was received with cheers and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow." He said that since he last addressed the Liberal women there had been an event which he, as a sane Imperialist, regarded as epoch-making in the history of our Empire. He meant the splendid evidence of loyalty pervading the vast dominion of Canada which had found expression in a generous and patriotic gift to our Imperial defences. (Loud applause.) If they considered the unrest which prevailed in Canada in the thirties of last cen- tury and what the healing power of self-govern- ment had shown itself capable of achieving there, as, in an even more striking degree, it had accom- plished in later days in South Africa—(applause), —did they not feel inclined to ask what was the use of Sir Edward Carson coming to Warrington to warn us of the disaffection which Ise said would ensue if we gave the Irish nation respon- sibility for its own affairs? His attitude was the more remarkable in view of the fact that the one man who, above all others, had acted in the North of Ireland in such a way as directly to lead not only to unrest but to ruffianism, was Sir Edward Carson himself. (Applause.) More. over, we had before us a score of Parliaments in the great system of self-government on which our Empire was founded more permanently aria loyally than any other Empire the world had ever known. (Applause.) It was indeed useless for Sir Edward Carson to try and persuade us that by extending that principle according to the circumstances. and needs of Ireland, we should be sowing seeds of unrest and revolution. Such talk would not go down. (Applause.) "Judg-

jog from the smiles I saw on your faces when I mentioned Sir Edward," continued Mr. Crosfield, "I suppose some of you did GO TO SEE THE BIT OF FUN in Warrington the other day. (Laughter and a voice : 'We were all there/ Of course, I read all about the display of rockets—(laughter),--but that struck me as being nothing new or uncom- mon, for I am old enough to have grown rather accustomed to Tory fireworks. (Laughter.) How- ever, I looked in the Warrington papers to see if they had brought along any of those wooden Cannons. '(Laughter.) I did think, while they were about it, they might have given us a little hit of a novelty in that way. (Laughter.) But 1 found no mention of cannons. (Laughter.) Be. fore Sir Edward came to Warrington I asked him _ . . _

whether, as a member of the.party which claimed in a very special way to be the Imperialist party, he quite appreciated the criticisms of newspapers of various political opinions in Canada of those methods of hooliganism in the House of Commons, which papers, even on his own side of politics in LOndon, had characterised as the 'methods of the pot-house brawler.' (Applause.) Sir Ed- ward skated rather lightly over that thin ice and tried to frighten us by talk of what would happen if Home Rule were granted. But that kind of argument won't wash—even with Perfec-
tion soap. (Laughter.) It is just about as little use, too, for _
MR. HAROLD SMITH

to come down to Lancashire to try and persuade us to put taxes on our bread and butter, on all foodstuffs, and on every article of clothing that we need in our households." Having emphasised the fact that the levying of taxes, according to Mr. Chamberlain's scale, would cost the workers pearly twice as much as they would be able to save by the remission of taxes on tea, sugar, coffee and cocoa, Mr. Crosfield said the goal to- wards which the Liberal party was steadily mov- ing was the free breakfast table—(applause)—and tariff "reform" would only render its realisation impossible. The last time Mr. Harold Smith was speaking in Warrington, he was talking abqut boots. "I don't know," commented Mr. Crosfield, "whether Mr. Smith means to suggest that I am indifferent to any legitimate means of fostering the British trade in boots. If so, he never made a bigger blunder, in his life. lam only too willing and anxious to encourage British trade in every legitimate way, but I decline to foster the boot industry by putting Protective taxes on it. (Ap- plause.) That is where I join issue with Mr. Smith. I wonder whether that POLITICAL INNOCENT —(laughter)—imagines he can put a tax on boots and stop at that. If he really does think that, all I can say is that if his party once got the power to impose such taxes, he would have a rude awakening. They would very soon find a • thousand other manufacturers demanding taxes on hats, on every stitch and shred of clothing, and on all the other articles in which the womern of England are more vitally interested than the men. The reign of dearness and scarcity would be inaugurated, and do you suppose that when the agricultural labourers of England were suf- fering, as they inevitably would, through the enhanced cost of necessaries, they would not also want some concessions? Do you suppose that the great agricultural industry, which is the back- bone of the Tory party, would not insist upon consideration? Of course, they will get it, for Mr. Chamberlain himself told us he would pro- tect them as producers of foodstuffs, and so you see the whole vicious circle completed—everybody taxing everybody else, things getting dearer all round, the cost of living of the worker and the cost of production of the manufacturer alike in- creased." Mr. Crosfield reminded his hearers of the resentment of the Protective policy which caused some of the most eminent of Conserva- tive statesmen to sever party ties rather than lend themselves to the establishment of such a system. At the present moment Conservative organs like the Liverpool Courier were exclaiming against the fatal step which Lord Lansdowne had taken in throwing over the Referendum pledge, and the old Spectator was also wringing its hands and writing in the most despairing way, while a Scottish Conservative nobleman—the Earl of Mar and Kellie—writing to the same journal, said Lord Lansdowne's declaration would be a knock- down blow to the Unionist party. He (Mr. Cros- field) noticed that Mr. Harold Smith kept pretty clear of the food taxes, and he was wise in his generation to do so. (Hear, hear.) "But I am rather surprised," continued Mr. Crosfield, "at the kind of stuff he has to put into his speeches and which some of his supporters publish in their papers. I admit that the Conservative party has gone through difficult times, and that it is rather demoralised—(hear, hear),—but really they are

div.head: AT A PRETTY LOW EBB
div.p: AT A PRETTY LOW EBB

when they have to turn to the sorry stuff to which they treat their supporters in Warrington. I notice that they suddenly developed a great interest in the comings and goings of my wife and myself—(laughter),—tind in our little in- nocent recreations. • (Laughter.) I am inclined to ask myself : What about pheasants and foxes, bunting and hounds? (Laughter and applause.) Hitherto I have not complained, but if people choose to amuse themselves by following hounds or shooting pheasants, I should like to know what they have got to say to me if I take a round of golf on the links? (Laughter and applause.) If they think fit to dress their member up in all sorts of characters, I would ask : What is to pre- vent my wife or myself putting on fancy costume for an evening's amusement? (Laughter.) What are you to think of a party which is reduced to the kind of stuff which they circulate in War- rington? We can afford to be thoroughly amused at the nonsense of the thing, and treat with not a little contempt the hypocrisy of it." (Applause.) Having expressed his satisfa6tion with the splen- did leadership of the Women's Liberal Associa- tion, Mr. Crosfield congratulated the members on the greatness of the causes which they were supporting, and upon the fact that in the whole history of England they never had in the House of Commons a band of men of a higher average level of ability and intellectual eminence than those who were at the head of the Liberal party to-day. (Applause.) He was talking the other day to a Labour membgr, who said : "Yes, they are a body of intellectual giants, while on the other side they have only intellectual puppies." (Laughter.) The present Government was well worthy of their. strongest backing, and he was thankful that they in Warrington were giving the Premier and the Cabinet such splendid and loyal support. (Loud applause.) It was announced that the following prizes had been awarded : Bread competition : Mrs. Roberts, Ellesmere-street, Mrs. Carey, Steel- street, and Mrs. Hamblett ; collar-ironing com- petition : Miss Willett, Dalton Bank; Mrs. Mas- sey, Wellington-street.

div.head: LOCAL MAGISTRATES RETIRE.
div.p: LOCAL MAGISTRATES RETIRE.

The Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster has, at their own request, removed the names of four magis- trates from the Commission of the Peace for the borough. They are : Mr. Ernest Morland Crosfield, who was appointed in 1889. Mr. Ziba Armitage, who was appointed in 1880. Dr. Karl E. Markel, who was appointed in 1007. Mr. Fred Stott, who was appointed in 1007. It is assumed that owing to change of residence or other reasons, these gentlemen have found it impos- sible to continue to die charge the duties of justices. Mr. E. M. Crosfield is the only surviving local magistrate who bolds the Crown Commission, and as long as his name appears on that Commission he will still remain a magistrate of the borough.

div.head: Alleged Fraud on the Railway..
div.p: Alleged Fraud on the Railway..

At the Clerkenwell Police Court on Priday last Arthur Wilcox, 24, a tea merchant, of Forest-street, Warrington, was before Mr d'Eyncourt, charged with travelling from Rugby to Ruston, with intent to avoid payment of fate-6s 10d. William Woodwell, ticket examiner, on the London and North-Western Railway, said he found the prisoner in a third-class compart- ment of the 10.30 a.m from Rugby. He produced a ticket from Latchford to Euston. The date had been written in ink, and in blue-pencil, were the words " press broken." The prisoner said he purchased the ticket, and that the booking clerk said tbat the date press was broken. As a number of the tickets had been stolen from the offices at Latchford, the prisoner was asked for his name, and gave that of Jack Platt, Electricity-street, Warrington. He was detained. Detective-Inspector Robinson, bf the company's police, said that the prisoner admitted to him that he wrote the words and date on the ticket. He wore four names and addresses altogether. The prisoner now said that he found the ticket some time ago in the lavatory at Latchford, and kept it. Ho offered the fare, but be was given into custody. Mr d'Eyucourt remanded the accused for inquiries.

div.head: WIDNES COUNCILLOR TO RESIGN.
div.p: WIDNES COUNCILLOR TO RESIGN.

Mr 3 W Towers, Liberal representative for Widnes South, has intimated his intention to resign at the expiry of his term, owing to business pressures The letter was received with regret by the executive Com- mittee of the association, and he was thanked for his services. The executive committee decided to leave the matter of a successor in the hands of the officers of the association. The north portion of the town is represented by the Mayor (Alderman F Neil), a Conser- vative, as the result of an arrangement between the two political parties.

BISHOP ON DIVORCE. Speaking on the reports of the Divorce Commission, on Wednesday, the Bishop of Liverpool pointed to what he described as the laxity and indifference of American society in regard to divorce, and asserted that they did not want to have the same deteriorating public moral opinion in England. As 'Christians they should set their faces like a flint against any increase in the grounds of divorce, and in the sharp conflict that was fast coming on they were convinced that if they bad the main body of motherhood and womanhood on their side, a law to make divorce easy dare be passed by no House of Parliament.
